<rss version="2.0" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"><channel><title>Kubernetes Blog</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/</link><description>The Kubernetes blog is used by the project to communicate new features, community reports, and any news that might be relevant to the Kubernetes community.</description><generator>Hugo -- gohugo.io</generator><language>en</language><image><url>https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/master/logo/logo.png</url><title>The Kubernetes project logo</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/</link></image><atom:link href="https://kubernetes.io/feed.xml" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Hardening Container Storage with Bind Mount Options and EmptyDir Permissions</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/16/kubernetes-v1-37-hardening-container-storage/</link><pubDate>Wed, 16 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/16/kubernetes-v1-37-hardening-container-storage/</guid><description>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 brings important storage security features: <code>emptyDir</code> permission modes and bind mount options. They help application programmers and security professionals implement rigorous security policies, for example, prohibiting deletion of files across containers or execution of arbitrary binaries from writable volumes, directly in Kubernetes without any complicated circumvention.</p>
<h2 id="linux-storage-and-permission-fundamentals">Linux storage and permission fundamentals<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#linux-storage-and-permission-fundamentals" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Before diving into the new Kubernetes features, let us briefly review the low-level Linux security mechanisms that make them possible.</p>
<h3 id="bind-mount-flags">Bind mount flags<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#bind-mount-flags" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>When Linux mounts or remounts a directory, Virtual File System (VFS) flags control what actions are permitted on that filesystem:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>noexec</code></strong>: Do not permit direct execution of any binaries on the mounted filesystem.</li>
<li><strong><code>nosuid</code></strong>: Do not allow set-user-identifier or set-group-identifier bits to take effect.</li>
<li><strong><code>nodev</code></strong>: Do not interpret character or block special devices on the file system.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="directory-permissions-and-the-sticky-bit">Directory permissions and the sticky bit<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#directory-permissions-and-the-sticky-bit" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Standard Unix permissions regulate access across three scopes: Owner, Group, and Others (e.g., <code>0755</code> or <code>0777</code>).</p>
<p>Beyond standard read, write, and execute bits, Linux supports the <em>sticky bit</em> (as in mode <code>01777</code>).
When applied to a directory, the sticky bit ensures that a file inside that directory can only be deleted or renamed by the file's owner or root. This is essential for shared writable directories like <code>/tmp</code>.</p>
<h2 id="motivation-for-the-improvements">Motivation for the improvements<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#motivation-for-the-improvements" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Why does Kubernetes need bind mount options and <code>emptyDir</code> permissions?</p>
<p>The primary goal of these features is to increase the security of Kubernetes workloads by allowing security-related bind mount options on volume mounts. By default, volumes are bind-mounted into containers by the container runtime and kubelet without <code>noexec</code>, <code>nosuid</code>, or <code>nodev</code> flags. This default can undermine security. For example, with <code>noexec</code> missing, a compromised process can use any writable volume (<code>emptyDir</code>, PersistentVolume, etc.) to download, <code>chmod +x</code>, and execute arbitrary binaries even when the container has a read-only root filesystem (<code>readOnlyRootFilesystem: true</code>). Supporting <code>noexec</code>, <code>nodev</code>, and <code>nosuid</code> gives users a native way to harden volume mounts to match security benchmarks and policy.</p>
<p>The gap is most visible with <code>emptyDir</code> volumes, which are the most common writable volume type and have been the subject of multiple security findings:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48912">Issue #48912</a>: Recognized security gap - the inability to set mount options on <code>emptyDir</code> was flagged in an audit but remained unresolved until now.</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119627">Issue #119627</a>: Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit (Finding NCC-E003660-7HM) - external auditors specifically noted that the inability to mount <code>emptyDir</code> with <code>noexec</code> represents a security failure.</li>
</ul>
<p>However, the same gap applies to all volume types. PersistentVolumes have a <code>mountOptions</code> field, but those options are filesystem-level flags applied by the CSI driver at the node, so they do not reliably translate into bind mount flags inside the container. Previously, there was no mechanism to set <code>noexec</code>, <code>nosuid</code>, or <code>nodev</code> on the bind mount that the container runtime creates for any volume type.</p>
<p>Additionally, the <code>emptyDir</code> volume type defaults to creating directories with a hardcoded mode of <code>0777</code>.
This previously meant that <strong>any</strong> process that can discover the volume could read, write, and delete anything in the volume, regardless of who created it.</p>
<p>You could - and still can - use an initial container to set a different access mode, but this is more complex, and hard to verify for compliance.</p>
<p>This causes real problems:</p>
<ul>
<li>Multi-container pods sharing an <code>emptyDir</code> could not prevent one container from deleting another's files. The sticky bit (<code>01777</code>) solves this, but there was no native way to set it.</li>
<li>Some applications and security frameworks expect <code>/tmp</code> directories to have the sticky bit set (mode <code>01777</code>). Without native support for setting the <code>emptyDir</code> mode, users had to use init containers or alternative volume types to meet this requirement.</li>
<li>Platform engineers who want tighter permissions (e.g., <code>0750</code> for owner and group only) have to use init containers running <code>chmod</code>, which adds unnecessary complexity.</li>
</ul>
<p>The <code>emptyDir</code> volume type was a notable gap.
As one of the most common writable volume types in Kubernetes, it had no way to control its creation permissions.</p>
<h2 id="real-world-use-cases">Real-world use cases<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#real-world-use-cases" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Application developers, working closely with security engineers, are responsible for maintaining the security posture of their applications and ensuring workloads do not pose risks to the wider infrastructure. These features allow development teams to confidently address critical security scenarios:</p>
<p><strong>Preventing Privilege Escalation on Writable Mounts:</strong> An application developer configuring temporary workspace volumes (like <code>emptyDir</code> or <code>/tmp</code> mounts) can ensure they are mounted with <code>nosuid</code> and <code>noexec</code>. This guarantees that even if the application is compromised and a malicious payload is downloaded, the workload cannot execute the payload or use it to escalate privileges on the node.</p>
<p><strong>Securing Shared Scratch Space in Multi-Container Pods:</strong> A developer configuring CI/CD pipeline pods often needs multiple containers (e.g., a builder container and a sidecar logger) to share a workspace. By setting <code>mode: 01777</code> on an <code>emptyDir</code>, the developer ensures the shared workspace behaves like a traditional Unix <code>/tmp</code> directory. Each container can write files independently, but a compromised process in one container cannot delete the build artifacts produced by another.</p>
<p><strong>Enforcing Principle of Least Privilege for Application Data:</strong> An application developer deploying a database pod can lock down access to the database's temporary storage. By setting <code>mode: 0750</code> on the <code>emptyDir</code>, the developer ensures that only the specific database user and group can read or write to the volume, explicitly denying access to any other processes or sidecars in the same pod.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Both features are behind Alpha feature gates in Kubernetes v1.37. To use them, enable <code>VolumeBindMountOptions</code> and <code>EmptyDirVolumeMode</code> on the API server and kubelet.</p>
<h2 id="example-1-enforcing-bind-mount-options">Example 1: Enforcing bind mount options<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#example-1-enforcing-bind-mount-options" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This full Pod manifest mounts an <code>emptyDir</code> volume at <code>/tmp</code> with <code>bindMountOptions: [noexec, nosuid]</code>.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">hardened-bindmount-pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">default</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">os</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">linux</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">hardened-app</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">image</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">alpine:latest</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">command</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="s2">&#34;sleep&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;3600&#34;</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">securityContext</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">readOnlyRootFilesystem</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">volumeMounts</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">temp-storage</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">mountPath</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">/tmp</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">bindMountOptions</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="l">noexec</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="l">nosuid</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">volumes</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">temp-storage</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">emptyDir</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span>{}<span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="example-2-emptydir-volume-permission-mode-with-sticky-bit">Example 2: <code>emptyDir</code> volume permission mode with sticky bit<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#example-2-emptydir-volume-permission-mode-with-sticky-bit" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This full Pod manifest creates an <code>emptyDir</code> volume using <code>mode: 01777</code> to enforce standard Unix <code>/tmp</code> sticky bit protections across containers.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">hardened-emptydir-pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">default</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">os</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">linux</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">app-container</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">image</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">alpine:latest</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">command</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="s2">&#34;sleep&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;3600&#34;</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">volumeMounts</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">shared-tmp</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">mountPath</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">/tmp</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">volumes</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">shared-tmp</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">emptyDir</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">mode</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">01777</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="verifying-the-features-in-linux">Verifying the features in Linux<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#verifying-the-features-in-linux" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>To verify that these features are actively enforcing restrictions, you can run <code>kubectl exec</code> into the container. The following examples simulate attempts to perform actions that are successfully blocked by these features.</p>
<h3 id="verifying-noexec">Verifying noexec<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#verifying-noexec" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Attempt to write and run a script on a volume mounted with <code>noexec</code>:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 1. Exec into the pod</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl <span class="nb">exec</span> -it hardened-bindmount-pod -- sh
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 2. Create an executable script on the mounted volume</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nb">cd</span> /tmp
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s1">&#39;#!/bin/sh&#39;</span> &gt; test.sh
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s1">&#39;echo &#34;Executing untrusted code...&#34;&#39;</span> &gt;&gt; test.sh
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">chmod +x test.sh
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 3. Attempt to run the script</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">./test.sh
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Expected result:</p>
<pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-none" data-lang="none">sh: ./test.sh: Permission denied
</code></pre><p>Even if an executable file is created, the Linux kernel refuses execution because <code>MS_NOEXEC</code> is enforced at the bind mount level.</p>
<h3 id="verifying-the-sticky-bit">Verifying the sticky bit<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#verifying-the-sticky-bit" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Attempt to delete another user's file in an <code>emptyDir</code> with <code>01777</code> permission mode:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 1. Exec into the pod</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl <span class="nb">exec</span> -it hardened-emptydir-pod -- sh
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 2. Verify directory permissions on /tmp</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">ls -ld /tmp
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Output: drwxrwxrwt 2 root root ... /tmp (Notice the &#39;t&#39; indicating sticky bit)</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 3. Create a file as the guest user</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">su -s /bin/sh -c <span class="s2">&#34;touch /tmp/guest_file&#34;</span> guest
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 4. Attempt to delete that file as nobody</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">su -s /bin/sh -c <span class="s2">&#34;rm /tmp/guest_file&#34;</span> nobody
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Expected result:</p>
<pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-none" data-lang="none">rm: can&#39;t remove &#39;/tmp/guest_file&#39;: Operation not permitted
</code></pre><p>The kernel blocks deletion because the sticky bit (<code>01777</code>) restricts file removal strictly to the owner of the file.</p>
<h2 id="things-to-know">Things to know<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#things-to-know" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Keep these key details in mind as you begin using these features. Full details are available in the official documentation for <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-bind-mount-options/">bind mount options</a>, <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-emptydir-volume-mode/"><code>emptyDir</code> volume mode</a>, and <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/volumes/#emptydir"><code>emptyDir</code> volumes</a>.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Default unchanged:</strong> If you omit <code>bindMountOptions</code> or do not set an <code>emptyDir</code> <code>mode</code>, you get standard default behaviors (like <code>0777</code> permissions) exactly as before.</li>
<li><strong>Broad volume support:</strong> <code>bindMountOptions</code> works with <code>emptyDir</code>, PersistentVolumes, CSI volumes, projected volumes, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and more. The only exception is image volumes, which are explicitly unsupported. The <code>mode</code> field works with all <code>emptyDir</code> medium types: default (disk-backed), <code>Memory</code> (tmpfs), and <code>HugePages</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Runtime capabilities matter (for <code>bindMountOptions</code>):</strong> The container runtime <strong>must</strong> support the CRI <code>mount_options</code> field and advertise it via <code>runtimeFeatures</code>.
The scheduler uses <em>node declared features</em> to avoid placing pods on incompatible nodes.
If a pod reaches such a node anyway, the kubelet rejects it. There is no silent degradation.
However, using <code>mode</code> for an <code>emptyDir</code> does not require runtime support.</li>
<li><strong>Not the same as PV mountOptions:</strong> PersistentVolume <code>mountOptions</code> apply at the storage layer via the CSI driver. The new <code>bindMountOptions</code> controls bind mount flags applied inside the container by the runtime. They operate at different layers and do not conflict.</li>
<li><strong>fsGroup interaction:</strong> If <code>fsGroup</code> is set in the pod's security context, the group permissions applied by <code>fsGroup</code> will override the <code>mode</code> specified for the <code>emptyDir</code> volume.
This is the same behavior that exists for <code>defaultMode</code> on Secret and ConfigMap volumes.</li>
<li><strong>Linux only:</strong> Flags like <code>noexec</code>, <code>nosuid</code>, <code>nodev</code>, and Unix permission modes are Linux concepts.
<code>bindMountOptions</code> has no effect on Windows nodes.
On Windows, the <code>mode</code> field is also skipped for <code>emptyDir</code> volumes, since Windows does not support Unix-style file permissions.</li>
<li><strong>Version skew safety:</strong> Both features are additive. For <code>emptyDir</code> <code>mode</code>: if the API server has the gate enabled but the kubelet does not, the field is accepted but ignored - the kubelet falls back to <code>0777</code>. For <code>bindMountOptions</code>: the scheduler uses Node Declared Features to prevent placing pods on nodes without runtime support; if a pod reaches such a node, the kubelet rejects it rather than silently ignoring the options.</li>
<li><strong>Feature Gates:</strong> Both capabilities are available as Alpha features in Kubernetes v1.37:
<ul>
<li><code>VolumeBindMountOptions</code>: Controls bind mount flags on volume mounts.</li>
<li><code>EmptyDirVolumeMode</code>: Controls creation permission modes on <code>emptyDir</code> volumes.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="how-do-i-get-involved">How do I get involved?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-do-i-get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>These new features are driven by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a> and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/storage/">SIG Storage</a>.
You can find more details in the KEPs for these enhancements: <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5855/">KEP-5855</a> (bind mount options) and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5502/">KEP-5502</a> (<code>emptyDir</code> permission mode).</p>

<li><a href="https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/kubernetes-sig-node">Mailing list</a></li>
</ul>
<p>Reach out to SIG Storage:</p>
<ul>
<li>Slack: <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/messages/sig-storage">#sig-storage</a></li>
<li><a href="https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/kubernetes-sig-storage">Mailing list</a></li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Pod-Level Resource Managers graduated to Beta</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/15/kubernetes-v1-37-pod-level-resource-managers-beta/</link><pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/15/kubernetes-v1-37-pod-level-resource-managers-beta/</guid><description>
<p>With the release of Kubernetes v1.37, the <strong>Pod-Level Resource Managers</strong>
feature has graduated to <strong>Beta</strong> status (disabled by default)!</p>
<p>First introduced as an Alpha feature in
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/05/01/kubernetes-v1-36-feature-pod-level-resource-managers-alpha/">Kubernetes v1.36</a>,
this enhancement builds on
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/22/kubernetes-v1-34-pod-level-resources/">Pod-Level Resources</a> by
equipping Kubelet's Topology Manager, CPU Manager, and Memory Manager to use
Pod-level resource declarations (<code>.spec.resources</code>) directly when making
hardware placement decisions.</p>
<h2 id="bringing-pod-level-resources-to-node-managers">Bringing pod-level resources to node managers<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#bringing-pod-level-resources-to-node-managers" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Before this feature, obtaining exclusive NUMA-aligned CPU cores or memory for
latency-critical applications forced cluster operators into an all-or-nothing
choice: assign integer resource requests to <em>every</em> container in the Pod, or
forfeit exclusive NUMA alignment entirely. For modern workloads running
lightweight sidecars (such as logging agents or telemetry exporters), allocating
dedicated physical cores to auxiliary containers was wasteful.</p>
<p>Pod-Level Resource Managers solves this challenge by enabling hybrid allocation
models. The Kubelet can reserve exclusive NUMA-aligned resources for primary
application containers while placing non-Guaranteed sidecars into a pod-isolated
shared pool. This ensures primary workloads get unthrottled, NUMA-local
performance while sidecars benefit from running in a pod-isolated shared pool,
enjoying local NUMA alignment and protection from external node interference
without consuming dedicated physical cores.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-new-in-beta">What's new in Beta<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-new-in-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Graduating to Beta brings key operational and API enhancements:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Graduation to Beta:</strong> Controlled by the <code>PodLevelResourceManagers</code> feature
gate, available to opt in (disabled by default) in Kubernetes v1.37.</li>
<li><strong>PodResources API Reporting:</strong> The <code>v1</code> PodResources gRPC service
(<code>PodResourcesLister</code>) introduces top-level <code>cpu_ids</code> and <code>memory</code> fields on
<code>PodResources</code> responses. Monitoring tools and device plugins can query
pod-level exclusive assignments directly without double-counting container
allocations.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="getting-started-and-providing-feedback">Getting started and providing feedback<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#getting-started-and-providing-feedback" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>For a deep dive into the technical details and configuration of this feature,
check out the official documentation:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/resource-management/pod-level-resource-managers/">Pod-level resource managers</a></li>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/node/pod-level-resource-managers/">Pod-level resource managers reference</a></li>
</ul>
<p>To follow a step-by-step tutorial on configuring and deploying workloads:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/cluster-management/use-pod-level-resource-managers/">Use pod-level resources with Kubelet resource managers</a></li>
</ul>
<p>To learn more about how to assign resources to pods:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/assign-pod-level-resources/">Assign Pod-level CPU and memory resources</a></li>
</ul>
<p>As this feature moves through Beta toward GA, your feedback is invaluable.
Please report any issues or share your experiences via the standard Kubernetes
communication channels:</p>
<ul>
<li>Slack: <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/messages/sig-node">#sig-node</a></li>
<li><a href="https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/kubernetes-sig-node">Mailing list</a></li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/community/labels/sig%2Fnode">Open Community Issues/PRs</a></li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes Changed Block Tracking API - Beta Differences</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/14/csi-changed-block-tracking-beta/</link><pubDate>Mon, 14 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/14/csi-changed-block-tracking-beta/</guid><description>
<p>Changed Block Tracking (CBT) support for CSI drivers
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/25/csi-changed-block-tracking/">shipped as Alpha</a> in
September 2025. With the March 2026 <code>v1.0.0</code> release of the
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshot-metadata">external-snapshot-metadata</a>
project, the feature moved to <strong>Beta</strong>.</p>
<p>If you aren't yet familiar with <em>changed block tracking</em> for storage in
Kubernetes, the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/25/csi-changed-block-tracking/">Alpha announcement</a> covers
the motivation, the three primary components (the CSI <code>SnapshotMetadata</code>
gRPC service, the SnapshotMetadataService CRD, and the
<code>external-snapshot-metadata</code> sidecar), and a walkthrough of how to use the
API. CBT currently applies to block volumes; file-volume and network
file-share changed-list tracking is not covered by this feature. This post
focuses on what is different in Beta.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-new-in-beta">What's new in Beta<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-new-in-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The main change in that release was the promotion of the
SnapshotMetadataService CRD from <code>v1alpha1</code> to <code>v1beta1</code>. The CRD used to
advertise a driver's metadata service now serves
<code>cbt.storage.k8s.io/v1beta1</code>. The schema itself is unchanged, but this
release <strong>removed</strong> <code>v1alpha1</code> (rather than serving it alongside the new version).
If you are upgrading from Alpha, you need to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Re-apply the CRD definition shipped with <code>v1.0.0</code>.</li>
<li>Update SnapshotMetadataService manifests to use
<code>apiVersion: cbt.storage.k8s.io/v1beta1</code>.</li>
<li>Update any client or controller code that talks to the CRD.</li>
</ul>
<p>This is a one-time change. There is no automatic conversion between the two
versions.</p>
<h2 id="compatibility">Compatibility<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#compatibility" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>Minimum Kubernetes version: <strong>1.33</strong></li>
<li>CSI spec: <strong>1.10 or newer</strong></li>
<li>Container image: <code>registry.k8s.io/sig-storage/csi-snapshot-metadata:v1.0.0</code></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="trying-it-out">Trying it out<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#trying-it-out" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/25/csi-changed-block-tracking/#getting-started">Getting Started section in the Alpha
blog</a> still
applies. In short:</p>
<ol>
<li>Make sure your CSI driver supports volume snapshots and ships the
<code>external-snapshot-metadata</code> sidecar.</li>
<li>Install the SnapshotMetadataService CRD (the <code>v1beta1</code> definition from
the <code>v1.0.0</code> release).</li>
<li>Create a SnapshotMetadataService resource for your driver.</li>
<li>Use a client — <code>snapshot-metadata-lister</code>, or your own implementation —
to call <code>GetMetadataAllocated</code> and <code>GetMetadataDelta</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p>If you want to see the full flow end-to-end, the
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-driver-host-path/blob/master/docs/example-ephemeral.md">hostpath driver example</a>
is a good starting point.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-next">What's next?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The focus for the rest of the Beta cycle is wider CSI driver adoption and
operational feedback before the feature moves towards GA. If you maintain a
CSI driver, this is a good time to evaluate adding support. If you are
building a backup application on top of the API, feedback on the streaming
clients and the iterator package is very welcome.</p>
<h2 id="where-can-i-learn-more">Where can I learn more?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#where-can-i-learn-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>The <a href="https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/external-snapshot-metadata.html">CSI developer
documentation</a>
for snapshot metadata.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3314/">KEP-3314</a>.</li>
<li>The
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshot-metadata">external-snapshot-metadata</a>
repository.</li>
<li>The gRPC
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshot-metadata/blob/main/proto/schema.proto">schema</a>.</li>
<li>The
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshot-metadata/tree/main/examples/snapshot-metadata-lister">snapshot-metadata-lister</a>
example client.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="how-do-i-get-involved">How do I get involved?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-do-i-get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This work is the result of contributions from many people across SIG Storage.
A big thank you to everyone who helped review, code, and test the feature
through Alpha and into Beta:</p>
<ul>
<li>Ben Swartzlander (<a href="https://github.com/bswartz">bswartz</a>)</li>
<li>Carl Braganza (<a href="https://github.com/carlbraganza">carlbraganza</a>)</li>
<li>Daniil Fedotov (<a href="https://github.com/hairyhum">hairyhum</a>)</li>
<li>Ivan Sim (<a href="https://github.com/ihcsim">ihcsim</a>)</li>
<li>Nikhil Ladha (<a href="https://github.com/Nikhil-Ladha">Nikhil-Ladha</a>)</li>
<li>Praveen M (<a href="https://github.com/iPraveenParihar">iPraveenParihar</a>)</li>
<li>Rakshith R (<a href="https://github.com/Rakshith-R">Rakshith-R</a>)</li>
<li>Xing Yang (<a href="https://github.com/xing-yang">xing-yang</a>)</li>
</ul>
<p>If you would like to get involved with CSI or storage in Kubernetes,
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/master/sig-storage">SIG Storage</a>
is the place to start. The <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/15tLCV3csvjHbKb16DVk-mfUmFry_Rlwo-2uG6KNGsfw/edit">Data Protection Working
Group</a>
also holds regular meetings, and new attendees are always welcome.</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Memory QoS Graduates to Beta</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/14/kubernetes-v1-37-memory-qos-graduates-to-beta/</link><pubDate>Mon, 14 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/14/kubernetes-v1-37-memory-qos-graduates-to-beta/</guid><description>
<p>Memory QoS has graduated to Beta in Kubernetes v1.37 and is now enabled by
default. On Linux nodes running cgroup v2, the feature uses the memory controller
to give the kernel better guidance on how to treat container memory. It was first introduced as
Alpha in v1.22, and expanded in v1.36 with tiered memory reservation.</p>
<p>This post covers what changed in v1.37, what the Beta promotion means for
cluster operators, and how to configure the feature.</p>
<h2 id="what-changed-in-v1-37">What changed in v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-changed-in-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="memory-qos-is-beta-and-enabled-by-default">Memory QoS is Beta and enabled by default<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#memory-qos-is-beta-and-enabled-by-default" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>MemoryQoS</code> feature gate is now Beta in v1.37.
This means every v1.37 <code>kubelet</code> has the feature gate turned on without any
configuration change. Turning on the feature by default is safe because the
default <code>kubelet</code> configuration does not enable memory throttling or memory
reservation. No <code>memory.high</code>, <code>memory.min</code>, or <code>memory.low</code> values are
written to cgroups unless you explicitly configure them.</p>
<p>You can opt into specific behaviors through <code>kubelet</code> configuration fields:</p>
<ol>
<li>Set <code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> (for example, <code>0.9</code>) to enable <code>memory.high</code> throttling on Burstable and BestEffort containers. The default is <code>null</code>, which means no throttling.</li>
<li>Set <code>memoryReservationPolicy</code> to <code>TieredReservation</code> to enable tiered memory protection via <code>memory.min</code> and <code>memory.low</code>. The default is <code>None</code>, which means no memory reservation.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="default-memorythrottlingfactor-changed-to-null">Default <code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> changed to null<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#default-memorythrottlingfactor-changed-to-null" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In earlier Alpha releases, <code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> defaulted to <code>0.9</code>, which
meant enabling the feature gate caused the <code>kubelet</code> to set
<code>memory.high</code> on containers. In v1.37, the default is <code>null</code>, so the <code>kubelet</code>
does not set <code>memory.high</code> unless you configure a value.</p>
<p>This change was made because, with the feature gate now on by default, an
automatic <code>memory.high</code> could throttle workloads that were previously running
without throttling. Making it <code>null</code> ensures that upgrading to v1.37 does not
change runtime behavior for existing clusters.</p>
<p>If your <code>kubelet</code> configuration file already contains an explicit
<code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> value, that value is preserved during the upgrade and
throttling continues to work as before. If your configuration file does not
include <code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code>, the <code>kubelet</code> uses the new <code>null</code> default and
stops setting <code>memory.high</code>. To keep throttling in that case, add
<code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> explicitly:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">memoryThrottlingFactor</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">0.9</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="how-to-configure-memoryqos-in-v1-37">How to configure MemoryQoS in v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-configure-memoryqos-in-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>For full details on configuring Memory QoS, see <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#memory-qos-with-cgroup-v2">Memory QoS with cgroup v2</a>, <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#configuring-memory-reservation">Configuring memory reservation</a>, and <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#system-requirements">System requirements</a></p>
<h3 id="enable-memory-throttling-only">Enable memory throttling only<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#enable-memory-throttling-only" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Set <code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> to a value between 0 and 1. The <code>kubelet</code> uses this
factor to calculate <code>memory.high</code> for Burstable and BestEffort containers. See
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#memory-throttling">Memory throttling</a>
for how <code>memory.high</code> is calculated for each QoS class.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">memoryThrottlingFactor</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">0.9</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="enable-memory-throttling-and-tiered-reservation">Enable memory throttling and tiered reservation<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#enable-memory-throttling-and-tiered-reservation" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">memoryThrottlingFactor</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">0.9</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">memoryReservationPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">TieredReservation</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="enable-tiered-reservation-without-throttling">Enable tiered reservation without throttling<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#enable-tiered-reservation-without-throttling" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">memoryReservationPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">TieredReservation</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="disable-memory-qos-entirely">Disable Memory QoS entirely<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#disable-memory-qos-entirely" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To disable the feature after upgrading, set the feature gate to <code>false</code>
and ensure a compatible kubelet configuration. The <code>kubelet</code> rejects the configuration if
<code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code> is set to anything other than the former default of <code>0.9</code>, or if
<code>memoryReservationPolicy</code> is <code>TieredReservation</code>, so remove or adjust those fields if you set them.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">featureGates</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">MemoryQoS</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>When the feature gate is off, or <code>memoryReservationPolicy</code> is not <code>TieredReservation</code>, the
<code>kubelet</code> resets stale protection at startup on cgroup v2 nodes: <code>memory.min=0</code> and <code>memory.low=0</code>
on the root kubepods cgroup, and <code>memory.low=0</code> on the Burstable QoS cgroup.
For containers, stale <code>memory.high</code> values are reset to <code>max</code> on reconciliation paths such as restart or resize.</p>
<h2 id="known-limitation-memory-reservation-is-node-wide">Known limitation: memory reservation is node-wide<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#known-limitation-memory-reservation-is-node-wide" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><code>memoryReservationPolicy</code> applies to every pod on the node. With <code>TieredReservation</code>, every Guaranteed pod gets <code>memory.min</code> and every Burstable pod gets <code>memory.low</code>; there is no way to opt individual pods in or out. A node that mixes workloads needing hard reservation with workloads that should stay reclaimable has to choose one policy for all of them.</p>
<p>Hard reservation also covers everything charged to the container's cgroup, including page cache, so a pod that reads large files can hold memory the kernel would otherwise reclaim to serve its neighbors.</p>
<p>SIG Node is tracking both in <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140246">kubernetes/kubernetes#140246</a>. If this affects you, that issue is the best place to describe your workload.</p>
<h2 id="what-to-expect-next">What to expect next<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-to-expect-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The next milestone for Memory QoS is graduation to GA. Feedback from Beta
users will shape any remaining adjustments before that step. If you run into
issues, please file bugs at
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues">kubernetes/kubernetes</a>.</p>
<h2 id="how-can-i-learn-more">How can I learn more?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-can-i-learn-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/2570/">KEP-2570: Memory QoS</a></li>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/">Pod Quality of Service Classes</a></li>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#memory-qos-with-cgroup-v2">Memory QoS with cgroup v2</a></li>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/">Managing Resources for Containers</a></li>
<li><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/cgroups/">Kubernetes cgroups v2 support</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html">Linux kernel cgroups v2 documentation</a></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="getting-involved">Getting involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#getting-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This feature is driven by
<a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>. If
you are interested in contributing or have feedback, you can reach out through:</p>
<ul>
<li>Slack: <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/messages/sig-node">#sig-node</a></li>
<li><a href="https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/kubernetes-sig-node">Mailing list</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/#meetings">SIG Node meetings</a></li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Native Histograms Graduates to Beta</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/11/kubernetes-v1-37-native-histograms-beta/</link><pubDate>Fri, 11 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/11/kubernetes-v1-37-native-histograms-beta/</guid><description>
<p>I'm excited to announce that native histogram support for Kubernetes metrics is graduating to Beta and is enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.37!</p>
<p><em>Native histograms</em> (previously introduced as Alpha in Kubernetes v1.36 under <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5808/">KEP-5808</a>)
bring high-resolution, low-cardinality observability to Kubernetes metrics.
By adopting <a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/native_histograms/">Prometheus Native Histograms</a>, Kubernetes components now expose latency and duration metrics with far greater accuracy while significantly reducing telemetry storage and scraping overhead.</p>
<h2 id="why-move-beyond-classic-histograms">Why move beyond classic histograms?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-move-beyond-classic-histograms" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Since the early days of Kubernetes observability, duration and latency metrics (such as API server request latencies or scheduling durations) have relied on <strong>classic Prometheus histograms</strong>.</p>
<p>Classic histograms require metric authors to define a static list of cumulative bucket boundaries (<code>le</code> labels), such as <code>0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10</code>. While familiar, this approach introduces three major challenges:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>The Bucket Guessing Game</strong>: If a workload's latency profile changes, for example, shifting into microsecond ranges or experiencing long-tail tail latencies beyond the highest bucket, the histogram loses visibility. Specifying bucket boundaries upfront requires knowing the distribution before observing it</li>
<li><strong>High Cardinality &amp; Storage Cost</strong>: With classic histograms, each bucket boundary is exported as a separate time series (<code>_bucket{le=&quot;...&quot;}</code>). A histogram with 10 buckets across multiple labels multiplies the number of time series by 10, increasing memory consumption in Prometheus and inflating time series database (TSDB) storage costs</li>
<li><strong>Interpolation Error in Quantiles</strong>: Calculating percentiles using <code>histogram_quantile()</code> relies on linear interpolation between static bucket boundaries. When bucket spans are coarse, quantile calculations can suffer from significant estimation error</li>
</ol>
<h2 id="what-are-prometheus-native-histograms">What are Prometheus native histograms?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-are-prometheus-native-histograms" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/native_histograms/">Prometheus Native Histograms</a> replace static user-defined buckets with <strong>dynamic, exponential buckets</strong>.</p>
<p>Instead of emitting a separate time series for every single bucket boundary, a <em>native histogram</em> is stored as a single time series containing a rich schema of positive and negative spans, zero thresholds, and exponential scaling factors.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>High Resolution Automatically</strong>: Exponential buckets dynamically adjust to any value range — from nanoseconds to hours — without requiring pre-configured bucket boundaries</li>
<li><strong>Up to 90% Fewer Time Series</strong>: By consolidating buckets into structured spans within a single time series, scraping and storage overhead are dramatically reduced</li>
<li><strong>Accurate Quantile Calculation</strong>: Quantiles can be calculated with mathematical bounds on error (≃5% worst-case relative error under default settings) across the entire spectrum of observations</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="how-native-histograms-work-in-kubernetes">How native histograms work in Kubernetes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-native-histograms-work-in-kubernetes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In Kubernetes, native histogram support is implemented directly inside the shared metrics subsystem (<code>k8s.io/component-base/metrics</code>).</p>
<p>Figure 1 illustrates how native histogram metrics are processed and exposed across Kubernetes components.</p>
<figure class="diagram-large "><a href="https://kubernetes.io/images/blog/2026-kubernetes-1-37-native-histograms-beta/native-histograms-flow.svg">
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/images/blog/2026-kubernetes-1-37-native-histograms-beta/native-histograms-flow.svg"
alt="Diagram showing native histogram metric registration, exponential options configuration, and dual exposition flow in Kubernetes components"/> </a><figcaption>
<p>Figure 1. Native histogram processing and dual exposition flow in Kubernetes.</p>
</figcaption>
</figure>
<h3 id="1-dual-exposition-for-zero-breaking-changes">1. Dual exposition for zero breaking changes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#1-dual-exposition-for-zero-breaking-changes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>A primary design requirement for KEP-5808 was <strong>zero disruption</strong> for existing observability stacks. When the <code>NativeHistograms</code> feature gate is enabled, Kubernetes components use <strong>dual exposition</strong>:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Classic buckets (<code>h.Bucket</code>)</strong> are still emitted alongside native spans. Existing Prometheus servers, dashboards, and alerting rules that rely on traditional text scraping or classic bucket labels continue to work unmodified</li>
<li><strong>Native spans (<code>h.Schema</code>, <code>h.PositiveSpan</code>)</strong> are included in the same Protobuf payload for collectors that understand native histograms</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="2-tuned-default-exponential-configuration">2. Tuned default exponential configuration<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#2-tuned-default-exponential-configuration" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>When <code>NativeHistograms</code> is enabled, the <code>k8s.io/component-base/metrics</code> package automatically applies standardized exponential options to all histogram metrics:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>BucketFactor: 1.1</code></strong>: Configures exponential buckets where each bucket is at most 10% wider than the preceding one. This guarantees a mathematically bounded worst-case relative error of at most ~5% for quantile calculations regardless of whether an operation takes 1 millisecond or 10 seconds.</li>
<li><strong><code>MaxBucketNumber: 160</code></strong>: Caps the maximum number of buckets per histogram to 160. Following OpenTelemetry SDK recommendations for base-2 exponential histogram aggregation, this limit protects component memory usage even under extreme outlier distributions.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="3-broad-component-support">3. Broad component support<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#3-broad-component-support" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Because native histograms are integrated into <code>component-base/metrics</code>, all major Kubernetes control plane and node components inherit support automatically, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>kube-apiserver</code></strong> (e.g., <code>apiserver_request_duration_seconds</code>, authentication/authorization metrics, validation latencies)</li>
<li><strong><code>kube-scheduler</code></strong> (e.g., <code>scheduler_plugin_execution_duration_seconds</code>, <code>scheduler_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds</code>)</li>
<li><strong><code>kubelet</code></strong> (node-level container runtime and pod lifecycle metrics)</li>
<li><strong><code>kube-controller-manager</code></strong> and <strong><code>kube-proxy</code></strong></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="how-to-scrape-native-histograms">How to scrape native histograms<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-scrape-native-histograms" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The simple answer: upgrade to Kubernetes v1.37, and it works.</p>
<p>Because Kubernetes v1.37 enables <code>NativeHistograms</code> by default, your cluster is already emitting dual-exposition metrics. How you configure Prometheus to scrape native histograms depends on your Prometheus version:</p>
<h3 id="1-prometheus-scrape-configuration-by-version">1. Prometheus scrape configuration by version<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#1-prometheus-scrape-configuration-by-version" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Prometheus 3.0+ (Recommended)</strong>: Use explicit per-job configuration in your <code>scrape_configs</code> rather than global flags (the global <code>--enable-feature=native-histograms</code> flag is deprecated in Prometheus 3.9+):</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">scrape_configs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">job_name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s1">&#39;kubernetes-apiservers&#39;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">scrape_native_histograms</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">always_scrape_classic_histograms</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="c"># Recommended during transition</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>You must read the caution in <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/native-histograms/#migrating-dashboards-and-alerts">Migrating dashboards and alerts</a> in the Native Histograms documentation. In summary: always set <code>always_scrape_classic_histograms: true</code> during your transition period. Without this setting, Prometheus will only ingest the native format and stop ingesting classic <code>_bucket</code>, <code>_count</code>, and <code>_sum</code> series. Setting <code>always_scrape_classic_histograms: true</code> ensures existing dashboards (<code>histogram_quantile(..._bucket...)</code>) and alerts continue to work while you migrate them to native histograms.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Prometheus 2.40 – 2.x</strong>: Enable Native Histograms globally by starting Prometheus with the feature flag:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">prometheus --enable-feature<span class="o">=</span>native-histograms
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Note that in Prometheus 2.x, this is an all-or-nothing setting for all scrape targets.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="2-verify-protobuf-dual-exposition">2. Verify Protobuf dual exposition<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#2-verify-protobuf-dual-exposition" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Standard Prometheus text scraping (<code>application/openmetrics-text</code> or plain text format) only transfers classic buckets. When <code>scrape_native_histograms</code> is enabled, Prometheus automatically negotiates <strong>Protobuf format</strong> with Kubernetes endpoints.</p>
<p>You can verify that a Kubernetes component is exporting native histograms using <code>curl</code> with an <code>Accept</code> header specifying Protobuf. For example:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1">## THIS IS NOT SECURE. ONLY DO THIS IN A TEST CONTEXT.</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">curl --insecure <span class="se">\
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="se"></span> -H <span class="s2">&#34;Accept: application/vnd.google.protobuf;proto=io.prometheus.client.MetricFamily;encoding=delimited&#34;</span> <span class="se">\
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="se"></span> --header <span class="s2">&#34;Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="k">$(</span>cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token<span class="k">)</span><span class="s2">&#34;</span> <span class="se">\
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="se"></span> https://localhost:6443/metrics
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>When decoded, the returned <code>MetricFamily</code> for histogram metrics (like <code>apiserver_request_duration_seconds</code>) will contain both traditional <code>bucket</code> entries and populated <code>schema</code> / <code>positive_span</code> fields.</p>
<h2 id="querying-native-histograms-in-promql">Querying native histograms in PromQL<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#querying-native-histograms-in-promql" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Once native histograms are ingested into Prometheus, you can query them using standard PromQL histogram functions without needing static <code>le</code> bucket labels or <code>_bucket</code> suffixes:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-promql" data-lang="promql"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># 1. Calculating P99 latency for a single target:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c1"># Classic histogram (requires _bucket suffix):</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="kr">histogram_quantile</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mf">0.99</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kr">rate</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nv">apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="s">5m</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="o">))</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c1"># Native histogram (operates directly on the metric name):</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="kr">histogram_quantile</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mf">0.99</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kr">rate</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nv">apiserver_request_duration_seconds</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="s">5m</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="o">))</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c1"># 2. Aggregating across multiple instances (e.g., all API servers):</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c1"># Classic histogram (requires sum by (le) to preserve bucket boundaries):</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="kr">histogram_quantile</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mf">0.99</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">sum</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">by</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nv">le</span><span class="o">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kr">rate</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nv">apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="s">5m</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="o">)))</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c1"># Native histogram (no grouping by le required!):</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="kr">histogram_quantile</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mf">0.99</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">sum</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kr">rate</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nv">apiserver_request_duration_seconds</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="s">5m</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="o">)))</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>With native histograms, functions like <code>histogram_quantile()</code> operate directly on the dynamic exponential spans inside the time series, producing highly accurate quantiles without static bucket interpolation error.</p>
<p>For official documentation on querying Native Histograms in PromQL, see:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_quantile">PromQL <code>histogram_quantile</code> documentation</a></li>
<li><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_fraction">PromQL <code>histogram_fraction</code> documentation</a></li>
<li><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_count-and-histogram_sum">PromQL <code>histogram_sum</code> documentation</a></li>
<li><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_count-and-histogram_sum">PromQL <code>histogram_count</code> documentation</a></li>
<li><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_count">PromQL <code>histogram_count</code> documentation</a></li>
<li><a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_stddev-and-histogram_stdvar">PromQL <code>histogram_stddev</code> and <code>histogram_stdvar</code> documentation</a></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="dashboard-migration-rollback-strategy">Dashboard migration &amp; rollback strategy<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dashboard-migration-rollback-strategy" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="recommended-migration-workflow">Recommended migration workflow<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#recommended-migration-workflow" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To safely transition your monitoring infrastructure to Native Histograms without breaking existing alerts or dashboards, I recommend a four-step migration workflow:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Enable Both Formats</strong>: In your Prometheus 3.x scrape config, set <code>scrape_native_histograms: true</code> AND <code>always_scrape_classic_histograms: true</code> so both formats are collected safely during transition</li>
<li><strong>Migrate Queries</strong>: Update your Grafana dashboards and Prometheus alerting rules from classic quantile queries (<code>histogram_quantile(..._bucket...)</code>) to native histogram queries (<code>histogram_quantile(...)</code>), and replace references to classic <code>_count</code> and <code>_sum</code> series with <code>histogram_count(...)</code> and <code>histogram_sum(...)</code></li>
<li><strong>Verify in Staging/Production</strong>: Validate that all dashboards and SLO alerts fire and graph correctly using the new native histogram queries</li>
<li><strong>Unlock ~10x Storage Savings</strong>: Once migration is complete, set <code>always_scrape_classic_histograms: false</code>. Prometheus will stop ingesting the static <code>_bucket</code>, <code>_count</code>, and <code>_sum</code> time series, reducing your histogram time series count by up to 90%!</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="opt-out-and-rollback-flexibility">Opt-out and rollback flexibility<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#opt-out-and-rollback-flexibility" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Because native histograms are dual-exposed, using them is entirely opt-in from a collector perspective:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Instant Collector Rollback</strong>: If you need to stop ingesting native histograms, simply set <code>scrape_native_histograms: false</code> in your Prometheus job configuration. No Kubernetes restart is required, and Prometheus will immediately resume scraping only the classic format without data loss</li>
<li><strong>Component Feature Gate Rollback</strong>: Administrators can also disable the feature gate on Kubernetes components using <code>--feature-gates=NativeHistograms=false</code> (requires component restart)</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="what-s-next-how-to-get-involved">What's next &amp; how to get involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next-how-to-get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>As native histograms progress toward General Availability (GA) in future Kubernetes releases, SIG Instrumentation will continue evaluating ecosystem readiness, performance characteristics, and long-term plans for eventually deprecating static classic buckets once native histogram adoption becomes ubiquitous across the monitoring community.</p>
<ul>
<li>Read the <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5808/">KEP-5808 page</a> or the <a href="https://kep.k8s.io/5808">KEP GitHub issue</a> to learn more.</li>
<li>Read the <a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/native_histograms/">Prometheus Native Histograms specification</a> and <a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_quantile">PromQL querying functions documentation</a></li>
<li>Get involved with <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/main/sig-instrumentation">SIG Instrumentation</a> on Slack in <strong>#sig-instrumentation</strong> or join the weekly SIG meetings</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="acknowledgements">Acknowledgements<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#acknowledgements" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>A huge thank you to contributors across <strong>SIG Instrumentation</strong> and component owners who collaborated on the design, implementation, testing, and review of native histograms in Kubernetes!</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Scheduler Preemption for In-Place Pod Resize (Alpha)</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/10/kubernetes-v1-37-scheduler-preemption-for-in-place-pod-resize-alpha/</link><pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/10/kubernetes-v1-37-scheduler-preemption-for-in-place-pod-resize-alpha/</guid><description>
<p>In Kubernetes, resource allocation has historically been a static decision made during a Pod's initial scheduling and placement. With the graduation of the core <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/12/19/kubernetes-v1-35-in-place-Pod-resize-ga/">in-Place Pod resize</a> feature to General Availability in v1.35, application developers and cluster operators gained the powerful ability to dynamically adjust CPU and memory allocations of running containers without incurring disruptive restarts or application downtime.</p>
<p>However, in-place resizing introduced a unique resource scheduling gap: if a running Pod requested a resource scale-up that exceeded the host node's allocatable headroom, the Kubelet was forced to mark the request as <code>Deferred</code>. The Pod would remain parked in this state indefinitely, waiting for resources on the node to naturally free up.</p>
<p>To bridge this scheduling gap, Kubernetes v1.37 introduces <em>scheduler preemption for in-place Pod resize</em> (Alpha), behind the <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate.
This feature allows the Kubernetes scheduler to actively free up capacity on a fully-utilized node by preempting lower-priority workloads, enabling the pending in-place resizes of critical, higher-priority applications to succeed.</p>
<h2 id="the-deferred-resize-challenge">The &quot;deferred&quot; resize challenge<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-deferred-resize-challenge" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>To understand why this preemption mechanism is needed, it is helpful to look at how Kubernetes handles running Pod resizing. When a user or controller (such as the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/vertical-pod-autoscale/">Vertical Pod Autoscaler</a>) updates the resource requests of an active container, the Kubelet evaluates whether the underlying node has enough spare allocatable capacity to fulfill the increase.</p>
<p>If the node's resources are fully utilized and cannot satisfy the new limits, the Kubelet sets the container's <code>resizeStatus</code> (reported in the Pod's <code>status.containerStatuses[]</code>) to <code>Deferred</code>. Unlike an <code>Infeasible</code> resize request (which is immediately rejected because it exceeds physical machine boundaries, namespace limit ranges, or admission quotas) a <code>Deferred</code> status indicates that the request is valid but is temporarily unable to be actuated, waiting until node capacity becomes available.</p>
<p>Before the introduction of this preemption mechanism, a Pod's in-place resize scale-up request could become permanently blocked if the node was heavily utilized. Even when a critical application (such as an in-memory database or a real-time web server) required more memory to prevent an imminent out-of-memory (OOM) crash, and the node lacked free capacity, the resize remained <code>Deferred</code>.</p>
<p>In this scenario, cluster administrators had limited choices:</p>
<ol>
<li>Manually evict lower-priority Pods from the node to clear resource headroom.</li>
<li>Rely on the cluster autoscaler to eventually spin up a larger node and reschedule the Pod. However, this is an operation that is highly disruptive and violates the core &quot;no restart&quot; value proposition of in-place scaling.</li>
<li>Rely on a custom autoscaling solution, for example a cluster autoscaler that can trigger dynamic node resizing operations itself.</li>
</ol>
<p>Because the <code>kube-scheduler</code> was unaware of deferred resizes on running Pods, it could not leverage standard priority-based preemption to evict lower-priority workloads and make room for the higher-priority running Pod's resource growth.</p>
<h2 id="why-this-matters">Why this matters<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-this-matters" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In production Kubernetes environments, cluster administrators strive to maximize resource utilization and efficiency. A common strategy is to bin-pack unused capacity on not-yet-full nodes with lower-priority workloads, such as batch jobs, background data processing, or best-effort tasks.</p>
<p>Without scheduler preemption for in-place resizing, this created a major operational dilemma. If lower-priority workloads consumed the remaining headroom on a node, higher-priority applications running on that same node would become blocked (<code>Deferred</code>) when they needed to scale up to handle sudden traffic surges or memory spikes. Operators were forced to choose between running low-utilization clusters with idle buffer capacity or risking that critical workloads could not resize when needed.</p>
<p>With scheduler preemption for in-place Pod resize, you can confidently bin-pack unused space across your clusters with lower-priority workloads without worrying about them degrading higher-priority Pods or blocking their scale-up requests. If a high-priority workload requires an in-place resize that exceeds available node capacity, the scheduler automatically preempts the lower-priority Pods to clear headroom. You achieve high cluster utilization and cost efficiency while preserving the responsiveness and reliability of critical services.</p>
<h2 id="architectural-mechanics-how-it-works">Architectural mechanics: How it works<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#architectural-mechanics-how-it-works" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><strong>Scheduler preemption for in-place Pod resize</strong> integrates directly into the core scheduling cycle to coordinate resources dynamically and safely.</p>
<h3 id="centralized-scheduler-tracking">Centralized scheduler tracking<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#centralized-scheduler-tracking" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>kube-scheduler</code> monitors the cluster for running Pods with a <code>Deferred</code> resize status condition. Normally, Pods with <code>spec.nodeName</code> populated are considered successfully placed and bypass the active scheduling queue.
