Under this feature gate, the scheduler intercepts Pods carrying the <code>Deferred</code> condition, permitting them to remain in active scheduling evaluations specifically to trigger preemption. The scheduler maintains continuous tracking of these Pods until the Kubelet successfully completes the resize actuation.</p>
<h3 id="single-node-preemption-boundary">Single-node preemption boundary<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#single-node-preemption-boundary" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Unlike placement preemption, which evaluates all nodes in a cluster to find the best scheduling fit, preemption for in-place resizing is strictly localized to the Pod's currently assigned node. The scheduler identifies eligible lower-priority &quot;victim&quot; Pods on the same host and initiates their graceful eviction, freeing up local capacity. Preemption is strictly scoped to the same node where the deferred Pod is running; if a node cannot accommodate the resize even after evicting all eligible lower-priority workloads, the resize remains in the <code>Deferred</code> state.</p>
<h3 id="resource-reservation-safety">Resource reservation safety<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#resource-reservation-safety" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To prevent scheduling races and double-allocation, the scheduler treats resources requested for a resize as <strong>already consumed</strong>. This enables the Kubelet to actuate the resize once the preemption takes effect.</p>
<h3 id="separation-of-concerns-critical-admission">Separation of concerns &amp; critical admission<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#separation-of-concerns-critical-admission" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>When a node is under resource pressure, the Kubelet includes a local mechanism known as the <strong>critical Pod admission handler</strong>. During initial Pod admission, if a critical system Pod arrives on a node that lacks spare capacity, this local handler can directly evict lower-priority Pods on that node to guarantee admission for the critical workload.</p>
<p>A significant architectural benefit of this new feature is the strict separation of concerns between the Kubelet and the scheduler. Under the <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate, <strong>the Kubelet's critical Pod admission handler does not perform local preemption checks or trigger local evictions for in-place resizing operations.</strong> Instead, the Kubelet defers the request and delegates the preemption decision entirely to the scheduler. This guarantees that a single, centralized orchestrator manages all resize-related preemption logic, respecting global priorities, Pod disruption budgets (PDBs), and graceful termination policies.</p>
<h3 id="managing-competing-updates-races">Managing competing updates &amp; races<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#managing-competing-updates-races" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>If a competing, higher-priority resize request is submitted for another running Pod on the same node during an active preemption cycle, the Kubelet prioritizes the higher-priority request. The scheduler is designed to observe these updates and will dynamically trigger a new round of preemption if more capacity is required to fulfill the new state.</p>
<h2 id="node-level-preemption-configuration">Node-level preemption configuration<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#node-level-preemption-configuration" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Administrators and automated controllers (such as a cluster autoscaler) can disable preemption specifically for in-place resizes on particular nodes. This is configured using the new <code>spec.podPreemptionPolicy</code> field in the Node Spec:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Node</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">batch-workload-node</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">podPreemptionPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">disableResizePreemption</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="s2">&#34;cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/disable-preemption&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="s2">&#34;operator.example.com/policy-override&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>An example use case for this policy is when a controller would prefer to size down other pods or dynamically adjust the node capacity itself when possible, only enabling scheduler preemption as a last resort.</p>
<h2 id="try-it-out">Try it out!<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#try-it-out" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>To utilize scheduler preemption for in-place Pod resize:</p>
<ul>
<li>Your cluster must be running Kubernetes <strong>v1.37 or later</strong> across both the control plane and all worker nodes.</li>
<li>The <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate must be enabled across all control plane components (<code>kube-apiserver</code>, <code>kube-scheduler</code>) and the <code>kubelet</code>.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="mini-tutorial-observe-resize-preemption-in-action">Mini-tutorial: Observe resize preemption in action<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#mini-tutorial-observe-resize-preemption-in-action" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To see this feature in action locally, you can test scheduler preemption on a single-node <code>kind</code> cluster with constrained CPU headroom.</p>
<h4 id="1-create-a-kind-cluster-with-scheduler-resize-preemption-enabled">1. Create a kind cluster with scheduler resize preemption enabled<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#1-create-a-kind-cluster-with-scheduler-resize-preemption-enabled" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Create a <code>kind</code> cluster configuration file named <code>kind-config.yaml</code> with the <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate enabled:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c"># kind-config.yaml</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Cluster</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">featureGates</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Create the cluster using this configuration, passing the <code>--image</code> flag to ensure the cluster is running Kubernetes <strong>v1.37</strong> (or later):</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml --image kindest/node:v1.37.0
</span></span></code></pre></div>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="note"><h4 class="alert-heading">Note:</h4>Make sure that the node image you specify corresponds to a Kubernetes <strong>v1.37</strong> cluster or later (such as <code>kindest/node:v1.37.0</code>). Older Kubernetes releases do not support the <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate.</div>
<p>Once your cluster is ready, inspect the node to check how many allocatable CPU cores it has:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns<span class="o">=</span>NAME:.metadata.name,ALLOCATABLE_CPU:.status.allocatable.cpu
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>In a standard local <code>kind</code> environment, the output shows <strong>8</strong> allocatable CPU cores:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">NAME ALLOCATABLE_CPU
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kind-control-plane <span class="m">8</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="2-create-priorityclasses-and-deploy-pods">2. Create PriorityClasses and deploy Pods<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#2-create-priorityclasses-and-deploy-pods" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Create two PriorityClasses and deploy a low-priority Pod (requesting <code>3</code> CPU) alongside a high-priority Pod (requesting <code>4</code> CPU). Together, these workloads consume <code>7</code> of the <code>8</code> available CPU cores, leaving <code>1</code> CPU of free allocatable headroom on the node.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c"># preemption-demo.yaml</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">PriorityClass</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">high-priority</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">value</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">1000000</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">globalDefault</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;High priority workload&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">PriorityClass</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">low-priority</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">value</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">1000</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">globalDefault</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Low priority workload&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">low-priority-pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">priorityClassName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">low-priority</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">worker</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">image</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">nginx</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resources</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">requests</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">cpu</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;3&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">memory</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;500Mi&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">limits</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">cpu</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;3&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">memory</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;500Mi&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">high-priority-pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">priorityClassName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">high-priority</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">app</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">image</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">nginx</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resources</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">requests</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">cpu</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;4&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">memory</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">limits</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">cpu</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;4&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">memory</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Save this manifest to <code>preemption-demo.yaml</code> and apply it:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl apply -f preemption-demo.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Wait until both Pods are running on the node:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get pods
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Output:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">high-priority-pod 1/1 Running <span class="m">0</span> 9s
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">low-priority-pod 1/1 Running <span class="m">0</span> 9s
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="3-request-an-in-place-scale-up">3. Request an in-place scale-up<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#3-request-an-in-place-scale-up" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Patch the high-priority Pod to increase its CPU request from <code>4</code> to <code>6</code> (+2 CPU delta). Because only <code>1</code> CPU of headroom is free on the node, this resize request exceeds remaining allocatable capacity:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl patch pod high-priority-pod --subresource resize --patch <span class="se">\
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="se"></span> <span class="s1">&#39;{&#34;spec&#34;:{&#34;containers&#34;:[{&#34;name&#34;:&#34;app&#34;, &#34;resources&#34;:{&#34;requests&#34;:{&#34;cpu&#34;:&#34;6&#34;}, &#34;limits&#34;:{&#34;cpu&#34;:&#34;6&#34;}}}]}}&#39;</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="4-inspect-the-preemption-event-on-the-low-priority-pod">4. Inspect the preemption event on the low-priority Pod<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#4-inspect-the-preemption-event-on-the-low-priority-pod" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>With <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> enabled, the scheduler intercepts the <code>Deferred</code> resize condition on <code>high-priority-pod</code> and targets <code>low-priority-pod</code> for preemption.</p>
<p>To verify that the scheduler actively preempted the low-priority Pod, inspect its events:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name<span class="o">=</span>low-priority-pod
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>In the event stream (or via <code>kubectl describe pod low-priority-pod</code>), you will see a <code>Preempted</code> event emitted by the scheduler:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">LAST SEEN TYPE REASON OBJECT MESSAGE
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">5s Normal Preempted pod/low-priority-pod Preempted by pod 97dba925-6b5f-4e2f-99f9-d51c30016586 on node kind-control-plane
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">5s Normal Killing pod/low-priority-pod Stopping container worker
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="5-trace-the-resize-event-lifecycle-on-the-high-priority-pod">5. Trace the resize event lifecycle on the high-priority Pod<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#5-trace-the-resize-event-lifecycle-on-the-high-priority-pod" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Next, inspect the event history on <code>high-priority-pod</code> to observe how the resize progressed from being deferred to successfully completed:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name<span class="o">=</span>high-priority-pod
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>You will observe a sequence of events as the Kubelet coordinates with the scheduler:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">LAST SEEN TYPE REASON OBJECT MESSAGE
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">33s Warning ResizeDeferred pod/high-priority-pod Pod resize OutOfcpu: <span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;containers&#34;</span>:<span class="o">[{</span><span class="s2">&#34;name&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;app&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;resources&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;limits&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;cpu&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;6&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;memory&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="o">}</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;requests&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;cpu&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;6&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;memory&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="o">}}}]</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;generation&#34;</span>:2,<span class="s2">&#34;error&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;Node didn&#39;t have enough resource: cpu, requested: 6000, used: 3950, capacity: 8000&#34;</span><span class="o">}</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">32s Normal ResizeStarted pod/high-priority-pod Pod resize started: <span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;containers&#34;</span>:<span class="o">[{</span><span class="s2">&#34;name&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;app&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;resources&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;limits&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;cpu&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;6&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;memory&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="o">}</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;requests&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;cpu&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;6&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;memory&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="o">}}}]</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;generation&#34;</span>:2<span class="o">}</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">32s Normal ResizeCompleted pod/high-priority-pod Pod resize completed: <span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;containers&#34;</span>:<span class="o">[{</span><span class="s2">&#34;name&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;app&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;resources&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;limits&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;cpu&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;6&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;memory&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="o">}</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;requests&#34;</span>:<span class="o">{</span><span class="s2">&#34;cpu&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;6&#34;</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;memory&#34;</span>:<span class="s2">&#34;1Gi&#34;</span><span class="o">}}}]</span>,<span class="s2">&#34;generation&#34;</span>:2<span class="o">}</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><ol>
<li><strong><code>ResizeDeferred</code></strong>: The Kubelet initially marks the resize request as deferred (<code>Warning</code>) due to insufficient CPU headroom on the node (<code>OutOfcpu</code>).</li>
<li><strong><code>ResizeStarted</code></strong>: Once the scheduler preempts <code>low-priority-pod</code> and capacity is released, the Kubelet accepts the new allocation and begins actuating the resize.</li>
<li><strong><code>ResizeCompleted</code></strong>: The Kubelet successfully updates container cgroup limits via the container runtime without restarting the Pod.</li>
</ol>
<p>Finally, verify that the allocated CPU on the container reflects the new request (appending <code>{&quot;\n&quot;}</code> to the JSONPath query ensures a trailing newline in your terminal):</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get pod high-priority-pod -o <span class="nv">jsonpath</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s1">&#39;{.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources.cpu}{&#34;\n&#34;}&#39;</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Output:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="m">6</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>This confirms that the in-place resize succeeded.</p>
<h2 id="getting-involved">Getting involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#getting-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This feature represents a major step forward for resource scheduling, bringing enterprise-grade density control and workload prioritization to dynamic resource scaling. We invite cluster operators, platform architects, and developers to enable the <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate in their testing environments and share feedback.</p>
<p>If you want to share your experience with this feature, please get in touch with the community via <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling">SIG Scheduling</a> or <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node">SIG Node</a> channels!</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Introducing Node Lifecycle Conditions</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/09/kubernetes-v1-37-node-lifecycle-conditions/</link><pubDate>Wed, 09 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/09/kubernetes-v1-37-node-lifecycle-conditions/</guid><description>
<p>Kubernetes has many ways to describe what is happening on a Node. Readiness,
taints, Pod state, labels, annotations, and provider-specific APIs each expose
part of the picture. What has been missing is a shared, Kubernetes-owned way to
say that a Node is <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/">draining</a>,
undergoing maintenance, or undergoing <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-shutdown/">Graceful Node Shutdown</a>.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 introduces five well-known <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/node/node-status/#condition">Node conditions</a>
that provide that description:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>DrainInProgress</code></li>
<li><code>Drained</code></li>
<li><code>MaintenancePlanned</code></li>
<li><code>MaintenanceInProgress</code></li>
<li><code>GracefulNodeShutdownInProgress</code></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="the-new-node-lifecycle-conditions">The new Node lifecycle conditions<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-new-node-lifecycle-conditions" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Condition</th>
<th>What it reports</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>DrainInProgress</code></td>
<td>The Node is actively being drained according to the administrator's chosen drain criteria.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>Drained</code></td>
<td>The Node has reached the drain criteria selected by the administrator.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>MaintenancePlanned</code></td>
<td>The Node is expected to undergo a change in the future.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>MaintenanceInProgress</code></td>
<td>The Node is actively undergoing maintenance.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>GracefulNodeShutdownInProgress</code></td>
<td>Graceful Node Shutdown is determined to be in progress on the Node.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Maintenance can include hardware or software rollout, remediation,
decommissioning, or debugging. Whether maintenance requires a drain depends on
its impact. A Kubernetes upgrade usually should follow a drain, while a kernel
live patch might not need one.</p>
<p>Like other Node conditions, each lifecycle condition uses <code>status</code> to report
whether the observation is active:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>True</code>: the lifecycle state is currently observed.</li>
<li><code>False</code>: the lifecycle state is not currently observed.</li>
<li><code>Unknown</code>: Kubernetes cannot determine whether the lifecycle state is active.</li>
</ul>
<p>The <code>reason</code> provides a stable, machine-readable cause for the current status,
and <code>message</code> can provide additional human-readable detail.</p>
<p>For example, an authorized maintenance controller could publish:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c"># Node .status excerpt</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">status</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">conditions</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">MaintenancePlanned</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">status</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;True&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">reason</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">MaintenanceWindow</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">lastTransitionTime</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;2026-12-09T12:00:00Z&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">message</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Hardware maintenance is scheduled for this Node&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="what-changes-in-kubernetes-v1-37">What changes in Kubernetes v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-changes-in-kubernetes-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The v1.37 release reserves these names as well-known <code>NodeConditionType</code>
constants and introduces the Alpha <code>NodeLifecycleConditions</code> feature gate,
which is disabled by default. In v1.37 the gate is effectively a no-op: it does
not restrict who can set these conditions, and no core component reads them. It
exists so that the built-in behavior planned for future releases — controllers
that consume these conditions — can be opted into when it arrives. You do not
need to enable it to start publishing the conditions today.</p>
<p>For this release, an administrator or an administrator-authorized
controller is responsible for setting and clearing the lifecycle conditions.</p>
<p>In this first release, no core workload controller changes its behavior based
on these conditions, but an administrator can publish them to communicate
maintenance and drains to cluster users.</p>
<h2 id="how-to-use-lifecycle-conditions-today">How to use lifecycle conditions today<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-use-lifecycle-conditions-today" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The immediate value is operational clarity. Administrators and
lifecycle automation can use these conditions as a common status channel for
Node lifecycle work that already happens today.</p>
<p>For example, maintenance automation can set <code>MaintenancePlanned</code> when a future
maintenance window is scheduled, then set <code>MaintenanceInProgress</code> when work
starts. Drain automation can set <code>DrainInProgress</code> when it begins evicting Pods
and <code>Drained</code> when the administrator's selected drain criteria have been met.
The <code>GracefulNodeShutdownInProgress</code> condition can report that Graceful Node
Shutdown is in progress on the Node.</p>
<p>The recommended pattern is to use lifecycle conditions to report status, while
lifecycle operations are managed through other mechanisms. Continue to use
existing Kubernetes mechanisms such as <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_cordon/"><code>kubectl cordon</code></a>,
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/"><code>kubectl drain</code></a>,
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/">taints</a>, and
workload-specific controls to change scheduling or eviction behavior. Use
lifecycle conditions to make the state of that work visible to people,
dashboards, alerts, and automation that choose to consume the signal.</p>
<p>When setting a condition, use <code>True</code> while the lifecycle state is active. Set the
condition to <code>False</code>, or remove it, when the state is no longer active. Use a
stable <code>reason</code> value and a clear <code>message</code> so that both people and automation
can understand why the condition changed. Cluster administrators should also
decide which component owns each lifecycle condition to avoid conflicting writes.</p>
<h2 id="why-a-shared-signal-matters">Why a shared signal matters<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-a-shared-signal-matters" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Node lifecycle affects components across the cluster. The <code>kubelet</code>, node
lifecycle controller, workload controllers, scheduler, autoscalers, storage
operators, and external maintenance systems all need some understanding of what
is happening to a Node.</p>
<p>Today, each component has to reconstruct that understanding from indirect
signals. One controller might look at Node readiness, another at taints, and
another at Pods that are terminating or missing. Infrastructure providers and
operators often add their own labels or annotations.</p>
<p>Those signals remain useful for their intended purposes, but they do not answer
the same question. A taint can influence scheduling or eviction, for example,
but it does not attest that a drain is in progress or that an administrator's
drain criteria have been met. A <code>NotReady</code> Node does not explain whether the
cause is an unexpected failure, a graceful shutdown, or planned maintenance.</p>
<p>Without shared lifecycle context, independently correct components can make
conflicting decisions. A DaemonSet controller can replace a Pod that the
<code>kubelet</code> intentionally terminated during graceful shutdown. A Job controller can
wait indefinitely for a terminal Pod phase on a Node that an administrator is
removing. A storage operator might learn about maintenance only after drain has
already started.</p>
<p>The new conditions provide a stable place on the Node for that missing context,
as part of the
<a href="https://kep.k8s.io/5683">larger effort to enhance Node Lifecycle management</a>.</p>
<h2 id="the-foundation-for-lifecycle-aware-kubernetes">The foundation for lifecycle-aware Kubernetes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-foundation-for-lifecycle-aware-kubernetes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The value of a shared signal comes from what can consume it — core controllers,
administrators, or the ecosystem of lifecycle projects. Follow-up enhancements
can build on the conditions without every component inventing a different way to
infer Node lifecycle state.</p>
<p>Consider a long-standing DaemonSet rollout edge case. A Node that is broken or
undergoing maintenance can remain unavailable for reasons unrelated to the new
DaemonSet revision. That Node still consumes the rollout's availability budget,
which can slow or block the controller from progressing the rollout on healthy
Nodes.</p>
<p>The DaemonSet controller knows that a Pod is unavailable, but it cannot tell
whether the new revision failed or an administrator intentionally took the Node
out of service. Readiness, taints, and Pod state expose pieces of the situation,
but none provides authoritative maintenance context.</p>
<p>The <code>MaintenanceInProgress</code> condition creates a Kubernetes-owned place to publish
that context. Future work can define how the DaemonSet controller uses it for
rollout ordering, availability accounting, and status reporting. Those behaviors
still require careful design, but the goal is for administrators to no longer
have to manually adjust the rollout.</p>
<h2 id="future-expansions-and-getting-involved">Future expansions and getting involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#future-expansions-and-getting-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Node lifecycle is a cross-cutting problem. Solving it starts with
components sharing enough context to make compatible decisions.
The next stage is to build on Node Lifecycle Conditions to improve scenarios
such as Graceful Node Shutdown, drain, and maintenance. Longer-term lifecycle
coordination may require explicit ownership, locking, and potentially a
dedicated API.</p>
<p>The Kubernetes ecosystem already includes many solutions for Node maintenance,
remediation, drain, autoscaling, and fleet management. The experience behind
those projects is essential to building a foundation that works across
different environments and operational models. The Node Lifecycle Working Group,
SIG Node, and SIG Apps invite maintainers and users to share their use cases
and ideas to shape the future work.</p>
<p>Follow the work through <a href="https://kep.k8s.io/5683">KEP-5683: Node Lifecycle Conditions</a>.
To participate in our discussions, join one of our groups:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/wg/node-lifecycle/">Node Lifecycle Working Group</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/apps/">SIG Apps</a></li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Advancing Workload-Aware Scheduling</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/08/kubernetes-v1-37-advancing-workload-aware-scheduling/</link><pubDate>Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/08/kubernetes-v1-37-advancing-workload-aware-scheduling/</guid><description>
<p>AI/ML and complex batch workloads continue to push the boundaries of Kubernetes scheduling. Following the foundational workload-centric enhancements introduced in previous releases, Kubernetes v1.37 delivers the next major milestone in the Workload-Aware Scheduling (WAS) journey. In this release, the core Workload and PodGroup APIs—enabling gang scheduling—along with Workload-Aware Preemption (WAP) and shared DRA ResourceClaims for PodGroups, all graduate to Beta, solidifying their role in the Kubernetes ecosystem.</p>
<p>To address the hierarchical scheduling requirements of modern high-performance distributed workloads, v1.37 introduces the new <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/compositepodgroup-api/">CompositePodGroup</a> API.
This new API allows expressing multi-level topology constraints, gang scheduling, and preemption policies for complex, heterogeneous groups of Pods. Crucially, this architectural expansion unlocks native scheduling support for advanced workload structures commonly managed by higher-order extension APIs such as JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet (LWS).</p>
<p>Alongside these API additions, v1.37 focuses on streamlining adoption by introducing a new set of <em>controller integration APIs</em> and the <code>workloadbuilder</code> Go library. These provide standardized building blocks that significantly simplify how out-of-tree controllers can integrate with WAS capabilities.
Utilizing these new tools, the native Job controller integration has been upgraded to fully consume the expanded WAS APIs—enabling advanced scheduling policies, flexible disruption modes, and topology-aware scheduling for standard batch workloads.</p>
<h2 id="gang-scheduling-and-workload-podgroup-apis">Gang scheduling and Workload / PodGroup APIs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#gang-scheduling-and-workload-podgroup-apis" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Kubernetes v1.37 delivers a major milestone: <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/workload-api/">Workload</a> / <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/podgroup-api/">PodGroup</a> APIs and <em>gang scheduling</em>
are officially graduating to Beta. This graduation signals that native, &quot;all-or-nothing&quot;
scheduling for workloads is solidifying for wider adoption.</p>
<p>Key updates to the API and gang scheduling algorithm in this release include:</p>
<h3 id="beta-graduation-and-api-versioning-changes">Beta graduation and API versioning changes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#beta-graduation-and-api-versioning-changes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The core Workload and PodGroup APIs have been promoted to v1beta1, meaning they are now one step away from
General Availability (GA). For early adopters who have been testing these features,
take note of the alpha versioning transition: v1alpha2 has been entirely replaced by v1alpha3.
This transition introduces breaking changes designed to clean up the API structure around <code>disruptionMode</code>.</p>
<h3 id="native-podgroup-queueing">Native PodGroup queueing<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#native-podgroup-queueing" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>A significant under-the-hood improvement in v1.37 makes the PodGroup a first-class citizen in the scheduling queue.
Previously, even if belonging to a PodGroup, all member Pods were queued individually. Now, only the top-level PodGroup
object is queued. This ensures all Pods share the same queueing behavior and lays the groundwork
for more advanced PodGroup queueing strategies in the future.</p>
<h3 id="dynamic-elasticity-with-mincount-mutability">Dynamic elasticity with minCount mutability<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dynamic-elasticity-with-mincount-mutability" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In earlier iterations, the <code>minCount</code> field, which dictates the minimum number of Pods required
to successfully schedule a PodGroup, was strictly immutable. In v1.37, <code>minCount</code> is now mutable.
This API change unlocks flexibility for elastic workloads. Controllers can now dynamically
adjust the minimum required size of a gang on the fly, allowing workloads to gracefully degrade
or expand without interrupting already-scheduled Pods.</p>
<h2 id="workload-aware-preemption">Workload-aware preemption<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#workload-aware-preemption" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In Kubernetes v1.37 the separate
<code>WorkloadAwarePreemption</code> <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/">feature gate</a>
for <em>workload-aware preemption</em> was merged into the <code>GenericWorkload</code> feature gate,
becoming a core part of the gang scheduling effort.</p>
<p>While the core concepts of workload-aware preemption stay the same, there are some
differences between the v1.36 and v1.37 releases:</p>
<h3 id="performance-and-optimality">Performance and optimality<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#performance-and-optimality" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To check whether a preemptor can fit in the cluster thanks to preemption, the scheduler
simulates the removal of all potential victims and re-runs the scheduling algorithm. After
that it tries to reprieve as many victims as possible. In the v1.36 release, the scheduling
algorithm was run for each victim reprieval, verifying whether with the victim reprieved, the algorithm
can still find a valid placement for the preemptor. In v1.37, the scheduling algorithm is run only once
and the preemptor Pods are assumed based on its output. Later, the reprieval checks
whether a victim can still run in its place with the preemptor assumed.</p>
<h3 id="podgroup-as-a-victim">PodGroup as a victim<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#podgroup-as-a-victim" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>One of the limitations of v1.36 was the fact that the default preemption for single Pods
was not aware of PodGroups and was not respecting their <code>disruptionMode</code> fields, allowing
for disruption of single Pods even when the PodGroup had <code>disruptionMode: {all: {}}</code> set.
Kubernetes v1.37 removes this limitation; the default preemption now respects the PodGroup
<code>disruptionMode</code> field.</p>
<h3 id="rename-of-the-disruptionmode-fields">Rename of the <code>disruptionMode</code> fields<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#rename-of-the-disruptionmode-fields" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>During the promotion of the API to Beta, the <code>disruptionMode</code> field was changed to decouple
its naming from the PodGroup object, allowing consistent naming across PodGroups and CompositePodGroups.
The modes changed as follows: <code>PodGroup</code> became <code>all</code>, and <code>Pod</code> became <code>single</code>.</p>
<h3 id="support-for-preemptionpolicy">Support for <code>preemptionPolicy</code><a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#support-for-preemptionpolicy" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In v1.36, the PodGroup does not have a <code>preemptionPolicy</code> field. The PodGroup can perform
preemption as long as none of the Pods forming it has <code>preemptionPolicy: Never</code> set. In v1.37,
when the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#PodGroupPreemptionPolicy"><code>PodGroupPreemptionPolicy</code></a>
feature gate is enabled, a PodGroup also has a <code>preemptionPolicy</code> field. It serves as an authoritative field for whether
a PodGroup can perform preemption.</p>
<h2 id="compositepodgroup-api">CompositePodGroup API<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#compositepodgroup-api" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In Kubernetes v1.36, workload-aware scheduling established a clean separation between static workload templates (Workload) and runtime group state (PodGroup), but the supported scheduling policies were limited to a single, flat group. The CompositePodGroup API, introduced in Kubernetes v1.37, extends this model to support hierarchical scheduling requirements.</p>
<p>This API allows its consumers to express multi-level scheduling requirements by organizing a workload in a tree-shaped hierarchy consisting of CompositePodGroup and PodGroup objects. Each CompositePodGroup carries policies and constraints that apply to other groups (CompositePodGroups and/or PodGroups), similar to how PodGroups govern scheduling behavior for a flat group of Pods. The scheduler treats such a hierarchy as a single scheduling unit and aims to satisfy the requirements specified by every group within that hierarchy.</p>
<h3 id="defining-a-workload-hierarchy">Defining a workload hierarchy<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#defining-a-workload-hierarchy" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To express multi-level scheduling requirements, you define a hierarchy of templates in a Workload object. Controllers then create the corresponding CompositePodGroup and PodGroup objects from that hierarchy.</p>
<p>To support this, the Workload API is extended with the <code>spec.compositePodGroupTemplates</code> field. Each CompositePodGroupTemplate defines a template for a parent CompositePodGroup and directly nests the templates (<code>podGroupTemplates</code> and/or <code>compositePodGroupTemplates</code>) from which its child groups derive.</p>
<p>Below is a sample Workload object that defines a two-level template hierarchy:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>After creating <code>example-workload</code>, a controller can stamp out the corresponding runtime group objects from these templates:</p>
<ol>

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">parentCompositePodGroupName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-root-group</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-workload</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">templateName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">workers</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minCount</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">4</span><span class="w">

<h3 id="how-multi-level-gang-scheduling-works">How multi-level gang scheduling works<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-multi-level-gang-scheduling-works" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To schedule a hierarchical workload, <code>kube-scheduler</code> evaluates the entire group tree as a unified scheduling unit:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Recursive evaluation</strong>: The scheduler traverses the hierarchy from the root CompositePodGroup down to the leaf PodGroup objects. At each level, a parent CompositePodGroup is considered schedulable only when its child groups satisfy its scheduling policy (for example, placing at least <code>minGroupCount</code> of child groups when using the gang policy), while each leaf PodGroup must satisfy its own Pod-level policy (for example, placing at least <code>minCount</code> of member Pods when using the gang policy).</li>
<li><strong>All-or-nothing scheduling</strong>: Once a valid combination of child groups is found that satisfies the requirements of the root CompositePodGroup, the Pods across the entire hierarchy are scheduled and bound atomically. If the root group cannot satisfy its policy constraints, the entire hierarchy remains unschedulable and no Pods are bound, preventing partial deployments and deadlocks.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="workload-aware-preemption-for-the-compositepodgroup-api">Workload-aware preemption for the CompositePodGroup API<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#workload-aware-preemption-for-the-compositepodgroup-api" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 extends workload-aware preemption to support CompositePodGroup hierarchies as well. Specifically, if a CompositePodGroup cannot be scheduled due to insufficient capacity in the cluster, the scheduler can invoke preemption to evict lower-priority workloads in order to fit the Pods belonging to that CompositePodGroup.</p>
<p>A CompositePodGroup can be selected for preemption as well. To specify the desired behavior during preemption, workload owners can specify an appropriate <code>disruptionMode</code> in the CompositePodGroup spec:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>single</code></strong>: Allows individual child groups within the CompositePodGroup to be preempted and disrupted independently. This is the behavior when <code>disruptionMode</code> is not set.</li>
<li><strong><code>all</code></strong>: Enforces &quot;all-or-nothing&quot; disruption semantics across the entire CompositePodGroup hierarchy. If any Pod within the descendant subtree must be preempted, the scheduler evicts all Pods across the entire hierarchy together.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="topology-aware-scheduling">Topology-aware scheduling<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#topology-aware-scheduling" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In Kubernetes v1.37, topology-aware scheduling expands to support complex, multi-level workload hierarchies and delivers performance improvements for existing single-level deployments.</p>
<h3 id="multi-level-topology-aware-scheduling">Multi-level topology-aware scheduling<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#multi-level-topology-aware-scheduling" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In Kubernetes v1.36, we introduced foundational topology-aware scheduling, allowing you to define co-location constraints directly on a PodGroup. While effective for single-level groupings, complex distributed workloads—such as large-scale AI/ML training, JobSet deployments, or disaggregated inference via LeaderWorkerSet (LWS)—often require co-location across multiple levels of cluster infrastructure simultaneously.</p>
<p>For example, an entire workload may need to run within a single availability zone, while different parts of that workload (such as specific worker groups or driver processes) require strict co-location within specific server racks.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes v1.37, alongside the new CompositePodGroup API (<code>scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha3</code>), topology-aware scheduling expands to support <em>multi-level topology-aware scheduling</em>. You can now express complex co-location requirements by specifying topology constraints at different levels of a group hierarchy.</p>
<h3 id="top-down-topology-constraint-resolution">Top-down topology constraint resolution<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#top-down-topology-constraint-resolution" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>During hierarchical scheduling, the <code>kube-scheduler</code> resolves multi-level topology constraints in a <strong>top-down</strong> manner. Specifically, topology domains that are considered during the scheduling of a child group are confined within a topology domain that corresponds to the placement assumed by the parent group.</p>
<h3 id="configuration-and-runtime-execution">Configuration and runtime execution<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#configuration-and-runtime-execution" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Using the updated Workload API (<code>scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</code>), you can configure multi-level topology constraints directly within <code>compositePodGroupTemplates</code>. In the example below, the parent template constrains the overall workload to a single availability zone (<code>topology.kubernetes.io/zone</code>), while child templates for <code>workers</code> and <code>driver</code> constrain their respective Pods to server racks (<code>topology.example.com/rack</code>) within that selected zone:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Workload</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">multi-level-tas-workload</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">job-ns</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kubernetes.io/description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Workload defining zone-level co-location for the root group and rack-level co-location for child groups.&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">compositePodGroupTemplates</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">root</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minGroupCount</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">2</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingConstraints</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">key</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology.kubernetes.io/zone</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">podGroupTemplates</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">workers</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minCount</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">8</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingConstraints</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">key</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology.example.com/rack</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">driver</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minCount</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingConstraints</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">key</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology.example.com/rack</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>When a controller creates an instance of this workload at runtime, it spawns the corresponding runtime objects from these templates:</p>
<ol>
<li>The root CompositePodGroup referencing the <code>root</code> template, carrying the availability zone topology constraint and the hierarchical gang scheduling policy.</li>
<li>The two child PodGroup objects (<code>tas-workload-workers</code> and <code>tas-workload-driver</code>), each referencing the root CompositePodGroup as their parent group via the <code>parentCompositePodGroupName</code> spec field:</li>
</ol>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha3</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">CompositePodGroup</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">tas-workload-root</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">job-ns</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kubernetes.io/description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Root group constraining the entire workload to a single availability zone.&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadRef</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">multi-level-tas-workload</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">templateName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">root</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minGroupCount</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">2</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingConstraints</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">key</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology.kubernetes.io/zone</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">PodGroup</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">tas-workload-workers</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">job-ns</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kubernetes.io/description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Worker group requiring 8 Pods co-located within a single rack in the selected zone.&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadRef</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">multi-level-tas-workload</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">templateName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">workers</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">

</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">PodGroup</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">tas-workload-driver</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">job-ns</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kubernetes.io/description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Driver group requiring 1 Pod placed in a rack within the selected zone.&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">parentCompositePodGroupName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">tas-workload-root</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadRef</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">workloadName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">multi-level-tas-workload</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">templateName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">driver</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minCount</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingConstraints</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">key</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology.example.com/rack</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>During scheduling, the scheduler evaluates multiple candidate availability zones across the cluster for <code>tas-workload-root</code>. For each candidate zone, it subdivides the nodes by rack topology to explore feasible rack placements for <code>tas-workload-workers</code> and <code>tas-workload-driver</code> strictly within that zone, systematically evaluating multiple combinations across available zones and racks before making a scheduling decision.</p>
<p>By allowing topology constraints to be modeled hierarchically, Kubernetes v1.37 provides a structured way to express multi-level co-location requirements across complex cluster infrastructures.</p>
<h3 id="performance-improvements-for-single-level-tas">Performance improvements for single-level TAS<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#performance-improvements-for-single-level-tas" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Alongside the Alpha introduction of multi-level hierarchies, Kubernetes v1.37 reduces the cost of placement evaluation for existing single-level topology-aware scheduling. We are continuously working to optimize the efficiency of placement evaluation algorithms in <code>kube-scheduler</code> and plan to deliver further performance improvements in future releases.</p>
<h2 id="controller-integration-apis">Controller Integration APIs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#controller-integration-apis" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Kubernetes v1.37 introduces new standard building blocks so that every controller can expose the same scheduling primitives in their own APIs, and share the same logic for translating them into scheduling objects.
These primitives express specific scheduling behaviors — such as policies or disruption logic — while
leaving the field naming flexible for each controller. A prime example of this is the native Job
controller, which we detail in the next section.</p>
<p>Types prefixed with <code>WorkloadPodGroup</code> describe a leaf group of Pods; types prefixed with
<code>WorkloadCompositePodGroup</code> describe a group of groups. A controller embeds them verbatim into
its own API, under whatever field name fits its domain:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>WorkloadPodGroupSchedulingPolicy</code> — either <code>basic</code>, meaning standard Pod-by-Pod scheduling, or <code>gang</code> with a <code>minCount</code>. The composite variant takes a <code>minGroupCount</code> instead.</li>
<li><code>WorkloadPodGroupSchedulingConstraints</code> — the topology constraints (<code>topology[].key</code>) the group's Pods must be co-located within.</li>
<li><code>WorkloadPodGroupDisruptionMode</code> — <code>single</code> or <code>all</code>, with the preemption semantics described earlier in this post.</li>
<li><code>WorkloadPodGroupResourceClaim</code> — the ResourceClaims shared across the group.</li>
</ul>
<p>Only the shapes are shared, so controllers retain full autonomy over how they name and nest these fields in their own APIs.</p>
<p><strong>The <code>workloadbuilder</code> library</strong> turns that intent into the scheduling objects. A controller describes its workload as a tree of <code>WorkloadItem</code> nodes — a node with children compiles to a <code>CompositePodGroupTemplate</code>, a node without children to a <code>PodGroupTemplate</code> — and attaches its own defaults plus the user-supplied building blocks to each node. From there, <code>Validate()</code> reports problems back at the exact field path within the controller's own API, <code>BuildWorkload()</code> compiles the tree into a Workload, and <code>NewPodGroup()</code> and <code>NewCompositePodGroup()</code> stamp out the runtime group objects.</p>
<p>Validation is deny-by-default: a controller declares the policies and disruption modes it actually supports through <code>AllowedPolicies</code> and <code>AllowedDisruptionModes</code>, and anything outside those lists is rejected. Building blocks added in future releases therefore stay unavailable until a controller explicitly opts into them.</p>
<p>For hierarchical workloads where a parent controller owns the Workload and delegates group creation to its children, <code>NewBuilderFromExistingWorkload</code> lets a child materialize only its own PodGroup from the parent's Workload.</p>
<p>Neither the building blocks nor the library have a feature gate of their own; they become user-visible through whichever controller adopts them. The native Job controller is the first to do so, and we detail it in the next section.</p>
<h2 id="integration-with-the-job-controller">Integration with the Job controller<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#integration-with-the-job-controller" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Building upon the new <em>controller integration</em> APIs, the Job API now features an explicit <code>.spec.scheduling</code> field, so you can declare how a Job should be scheduled instead of relying on the Job controller to infer it from the Job's shape. This expands support well beyond static, indexed, and fully-parallel Jobs.</p>
