<p><code>.spec.scheduling</code> is composed of the building blocks described above:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>schedulingPolicy</code> — <code>basic</code> for standard Pod-by-Pod scheduling, or <code>gang</code> for all-or-nothing scheduling.</li>
<li><code>schedulingConstraints</code> — the topology domain the Job's Pods must be co-located within.</li>
<li><code>disruptionMode</code> — whether the Job's Pods can be preempted individually (<code>single</code>) or only as a whole (<code>all</code>).</li>
<li><code>resourceClaims</code> — the ResourceClaims shared by all of the Job's Pods.</li>
</ul>
<p>For example:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">batch/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Job</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">distributed-training-job</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kubernetes.io/description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Distributed Job using explicit WAS scheduling with gang policy and zone topology constraints.&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">parallelism</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">8</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">completions</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">8</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">scheduling</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingPolicy</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gang</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span>{}<span class="w"> </span><span class="c"># minCount omitted → defaults to parallelism (8)</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingConstraints</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">topology</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">key</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology.kubernetes.io/zone</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">disruptionMode</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">all</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span>{}<span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">template</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">...</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Omitting <code>.spec.scheduling</code>, or omitting <code>schedulingPolicy</code> within it, selects the <code>basic</code> policy, which behaves exactly like standard Job scheduling today.</p>
<p>For every Job it manages, the controller compiles this configuration into a Workload and a PodGroup
owned by the Job, and sets <code>.spec.schedulingGroup.podGroupName</code> on each Pod it creates so the scheduler
treats them as one group. Once created, <code>.spec.scheduling</code> is immutable, with one exception:
<code>schedulingPolicy.gang.minCount</code> can be updated, which lets you resize a running gang.</p>
<h2 id="dra-resourceclaim-support-for-workloads">DRA ResourceClaim support for workloads<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-resourceclaim-support-for-workloads" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>As the core WAS APIs mature, so do their integrations with <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/resource-management/dynamic-resource-allocation/">Dynamic Resource Allocation</a>
(DRA). Kubernetes v1.36 introduced the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#DRAWorkloadResourceClaims"><code>DRAWorkloadResourceClaims</code></a>
feature gate. The associated feature allows <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/resource-management/dynamic-resource-allocation/dra-api/#resourceclaims-templates">ResourceClaims</a>
to be replicated and reserved for entire PodGroups and shared by all their
member Pods:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">PodGroup</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">training-job-workers-pg</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">...</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resourceClaims</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">pg-claim</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resourceClaimTemplateName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">my-claim-template</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">topology-aware-workers-pg-pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">...</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">schedulingGroup</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">podGroupName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">training-job-workers-pg</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resourceClaims</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">pg-claim</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resourceClaimTemplateName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">my-claim-template</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>In Kubernetes v1.37, the <code>DRAWorkloadResourceClaims</code> feature gate graduated to Beta.</p>
<p>While the API and core functionality of the feature remain unchanged, one change
eliminates some potentially surprising behavior when disabling the feature.
Previously when one of a Pod's <code>spec.resourceClaims</code> referenced a
ResourceClaimTemplate and matched one of its PodGroup's <code>spec.resourceClaims</code>
and the <code>DRAWorkloadResourceClaims</code> feature gate was <strong>disabled</strong>, a ResourceClaim was created for the Pod instead
of the PodGroup. In that scenario in v1.37, no ResourceClaim is created at all.
This change prevents Kubernetes from creating a flood of ResourceClaims from a
ResourceClaimTemplate and potentially exhausting DRA resources when a
claim intended to be shared by a whole PodGroup is replicated for each and every
Pod in the group.</p>
<p>For more information, see the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/resource-management/dynamic-resource-allocation/dra-api/#workload-resource-claims">feature documentation</a>.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-next">What's next?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/wg/workload-aware-scheduling/">Workload-Aware Scheduling Working Group</a> (WG WAS) is currently finalizing its plans for the Kubernetes v1.38 release cycle. While the roadmap is still taking shape (stay tuned!), the following key initiatives are already planned:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Graduation of Workload and PodGroup APIs to GA:</strong> Solidifying the core foundation of workload-aware scheduling as a stable Kubernetes API.</li>
<li><strong>Graduation of Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS) and CompositePodGroup (CPG) to Beta:</strong> Bringing these advanced placement and hierarchical scheduling features to Beta stability.</li>
<li><strong>Graduation of controller integration building blocks to Beta:</strong> Further refining the integration APIs to ensure a robust developer experience.</li>
<li><strong>Increased adoption and integration:</strong> Expanding the ecosystem by integrating workload-aware scheduling with other controllers, with a particular focus on hierarchical orchestrators such as <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset">JobSet</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Kueue Integration:</strong> Fostering closer alignment between WAS and <a href="https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/">Kueue</a>. In the near term, we aim to ensure Kueue is fully aware of WAS features for seamless interoperability. In the long term, we envision Kueue leveraging WAS as its underlying engine for capabilities like gang-scheduling and topology-aware placement.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="getting-started">Getting started<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#getting-started" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Many of the workload-aware scheduling improvements are now available as Beta features in v1.37, while new advanced capabilities are introduced in Alpha. Both Beta and Alpha features here are disabled by default and require manual enablement.</p>
<p><strong>Beta features:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Workload API, gang scheduling, and preemption:</strong> The
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#GenericWorkload"><code>GenericWorkload</code></a>
feature gate (which now integrates gang scheduling and workload-aware preemption) is Beta and disabled by default on the <code>kube-apiserver</code>, <code>kube-controller-manager</code> and <code>kube-scheduler</code>.
Ensure your manifests are updated to use the <code>scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1</code>
<a class='glossary-tooltip' title='A set of related paths in the Kubernetes API.' data-bs-toggle='tooltip' data-bs-placement='top' href='https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/kubernetes-api/#api-groups-and-versioning' target='_blank' aria-label='API group'>API group</a>.</li>
<li><strong>DRA ResourceClaim support for workloads:</strong> Enable the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#DRAWorkloadResourceClaims"><code>DRAWorkloadResourceClaims</code></a>
feature gate on the <code>kube-apiserver</code>, <code>kube-controller-manager</code>, <code>kube-scheduler</code> and <code>kubelet</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Alpha features:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Topology-aware scheduling:</strong> Enable the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling"><code>TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling</code></a>
feature gate on the <code>kube-apiserver</code> and <code>kube-scheduler</code>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>CompositePodGroup API:</strong> Enable the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#CompositePodGroup"><code>CompositePodGroup</code></a>
feature gate on the <code>kube-apiserver</code>, <code>kube-controller-manager</code> and <code>kube-scheduler</code>, and ensure the <code>scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha3</code> API version is enabled.
Note that enabling <code>CompositePodGroup</code> on the <code>kube-controller-manager</code> also requires the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling"><code>TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling</code></a> feature gate to be enabled.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Workload API integration with the Job controller:</strong> Enable the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#WorkloadWithJob"><code>WorkloadWithJob</code></a>
feature gate on the <code>kube-apiserver</code> and <code>kube-controller-manager</code>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>PodGroup <code>preemptionPolicy</code>:</strong> Enable the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#PodGroupPreemptionPolicy"><code>PodGroupPreemptionPolicy</code></a>
feature gate on the <code>kube-apiserver</code> and <code>kube-scheduler</code>.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Controller integration APIs:</strong></p>
<p>The new <code>workloadbuilder</code> library is available to developers building both out-of-tree and in-tree controllers who want to integrate with WAS. It does not require a feature gate. You can explore the library and find usage examples directly in the <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/component-helpers/tree/master/scheduling/schedulingv1/workloadbuilder"><code>kubernetes/component-helpers</code></a> repository.</p>
<p>We encourage you to try out workload-aware scheduling in your test clusters
and share your experiences to help shape the future of Kubernetes scheduling.
You can send your feedback by:</p>
<ul>
<li>Reaching out via <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0AHLJ0EAEL">Slack (#wg-workload-aware-scheduling)</a>.</li>
<li>Joining the <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/wg/workload-aware-scheduling/">WG Workload-Aware Scheduling</a> or <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/#meetings">SIG Scheduling</a> meetings.</li>
<li>Filing a new <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues">issue</a> in the Kubernetes repository.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="learn-more">Learn more<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#learn-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>To dive deeper into the architecture and design of these features, read the KEPs:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4671/">KEP-4671: Gang Scheduling Support in Kubernetes</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5710/">KEP-5710: Workload-aware preemption</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5732/">KEP-5732: Topology-aware workload scheduling</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6012/">KEP-6012: CompositePodGroup API</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6089/">KEP-6089: WAS: Controller Integration APIs</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5547/">KEP-5547: WAS: Integrate Workload APIs with Job controller</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5729/">KEP-5729: DRA: ResourceClaim Support for Workloads</a></li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: KubeletInUserNamespace (aka Rootless mode) Graduates to Beta</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/04/kubernetes-v1-37-rootless-beta/</link><pubDate>Fri, 04 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/04/kubernetes-v1-37-rootless-beta/</guid><description>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 promotes the <code>KubeletInUserNamespace</code> feature gate to beta.
With this feature enabled, all of the node components (kubelet, CRI and OCI runtimes,
CNI plugins, and kube-proxy) can run as a non-root user on the host, using a
<a href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/user_namespaces.7.html">Linux user namespace</a>.
This technique is also known as <em>rootless mode</em>.
The work started as an experiment in 2018, and was merged into Kubernetes v1.22 (2021)
as an alpha feature (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/2033/">KEP-2033</a>).</p>
<p>This feature should not be confused with <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/user-namespaces/">user namespaces for pods</a>
(<code>hostUsers: false</code> with the <code>UserNamespacesSupport</code> feature gate, GA since v1.36),
which puts pods in user namespaces but still runs the node components as root.
These two features do not conflict.
Moreover, they can be combined to nest Kubernetes inside Kubernetes without resorting to
the full <code>privileged: true</code>.</p>
<h2 id="why-run-the-node-components-in-a-user-namespace">Why run the node components in a user namespace?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-run-the-node-components-in-a-user-namespace" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Because the node components have historically had container-breakout vulnerabilities
that could compromise full root privileges on the host.</p>
<p>Examples of such vulnerabilities include:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-0811">CVE-2022-0811</a>
(&quot;cr8escape&quot;): CRI-O could be tricked into setting arbitrary sysctls, such as
<code>kernel.core_pattern</code>, resulting in arbitrary code execution as root on the host</li>
<li><a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-27561">CVE-2023-27561</a>:
runc could be tricked into bypassing the masked paths of a container via a volume
mount race, exposing the host's procfs files (a regression of CVE-2019-19921)</li>
<li><a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-10220">CVE-2024-10220</a>:
the kubelet could be made to execute arbitrary commands as root via <code>gitRepo</code> volumes
(<code>gitRepo</code> volumes had a similar vulnerability,
<a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-11235">CVE-2018-11235</a>, back in 2018 too)</li>
<li><a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-31133">CVE-2025-31133</a>:
runc could be tricked into bind-mounting attacker-controlled paths and writing to the
host's procfs files, such as <code>/proc/sysrq-trigger</code> and
<code>/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern</code></li>
<li><a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53488">CVE-2026-53488</a>:
containerd could be tricked into executing arbitrary commands on the host, via
crafted labels in a container image</li>
</ul>
<p>By running the node components in a user namespace, the potential damage is confined to
the non-root user's account.
Notably, an attacker cannot conceal their intrusion by modifying the kernel, the boot
loader, or the firmware.</p>
<p>It should still be noted that user namespaces are not effective for mitigating
vulnerabilities in the kernel itself.
User namespaces should be used in conjunction with traditional hardening measures such as
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/security/seccomp/">seccomp</a> to prevent containers from invoking
unnecessary system calls.</p>
<h3 id="use-cases">Use cases<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#use-cases" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><ul>
<li><strong>Production clusters</strong>: mitigate potential container-breakout vulnerabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Shared machines (e.g., HPC)</strong>: users can deploy Kubernetes without asking the machine
administrator for root privileges, and without the risk of accidentally breaking
other users' environments.</li>
<li><strong>Laptops</strong>: prevent a local cluster from accidentally breaking the host system configuration,
e.g., the host iptables rules used for VPNs.</li>
<li><strong>AI sandbox</strong>: a Kubernetes application developer may create a dedicated local user account for
running an AI coding agent and a test Kubernetes cluster.
This setup is useful for preventing the AI agent from breaking the host when it is deceived by
malicious information on the Internet.</li>
<li><strong>Kubernetes-in-Kubernetes</strong>: a nested cluster can run inside a parent cluster as a user-namespaced
pod (<code>hostUsers: false</code>), isolating workloads more strictly than Kubernetes API namespaces do.</li>
<li><strong>Bootstrapping</strong>: a temporary unprivileged cluster can be used to bootstrap an actual
cluster, e.g., with Cluster API.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="how-does-it-work">How does it work?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-does-it-work" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>A Linux kernel <em>user namespace</em> maps a host level non-root user (e.g., UID 1000) to a <em>fake root</em> user inside the namespace. The UID 0
privileges are limited to the inside of the namespace.
The fake root is enough for most of the node components' tasks: mounting volumes,
creating cgroups, and configuring the network namespaces of pods.
It still comes with some <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/2033/#notesconstraintscaveats-optional">caveats</a> that may break compatibility with specific CNI and CSI drivers, though.</p>
<p>The user namespace has to be created outside of Kubernetes.
For example, <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/rootless/">Rootless</a> Docker can be used to prepare the user namespace in which Kubernetes runs.</p>
<p>The <code>KubeletInUserNamespace</code> feature gate itself is quite &quot;boring&quot;: basically it just lets the kubelet
ignore permission errors that occur when <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0-beta.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L499-L517">setting some sysctl values</a>
(e.g., <code>vm.overcommit_memory</code> and <code>kernel.panic</code>)
and when <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0-beta.0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L586-L601">watching kernel messages via <code>/dev/kmsg</code></a>.</p>
<p>See <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/">Running Kubernetes Node Components as a Non-root User</a>
for further information.</p>
<h2 id="what-changed-from-alpha-to-beta">What changed from Alpha to Beta?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-changed-from-alpha-to-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>The <code>KubeletInUserNamespace</code> feature gate is now enabled by default.
Enabling the gate does not put the kubelet into a user namespace automatically, so nothing
changes for existing &quot;rootful&quot; clusters.</li>
<li><code>kubectl get nodes -o yaml</code> now reports whether nodes are running in a user namespace via
the <a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#NodeSystemInfo"><code>runningInUserNamespace</code></a> property.
A cluster administrator can use this property to set node labels or taints, to avoid scheduling workloads
that need real root privileges (e.g., some CNI plugin installers) onto rootless nodes.</li>
<li>For Kubernetes' own CI/CD testing, the node conformance end to end tests now run on a rootless cluster
(<a href="https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-rootless">ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-rootless</a>).</li>
</ul>
<p>Several related improvements have also happened outside the promotion of the feature gate itself:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Linux kernel v6.3 (2023)</strong>: added support for <a href="https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.3">idmapped tmpfs</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Kubernetes v1.33 (2025)</strong>: enabled the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/user-namespaces/"><code>UserNamespacesSupport</code></a> feature gate
by default, allowing user-namespaced pods (<code>hostUsers: false</code>) to be created without extra configuration.</li>
<li><strong>containerd v2.1 (2025)</strong>: added support for <a href="https://github.com/containerd/containerd/releases/tag/v2.1.0">writable cgroups</a>.</li>
</ul>
<p>With these improvements, a Kubernetes cluster with <code>KubeletInUserNamespace</code> can now also be nested
inside Kubernetes pods with <code>hostUsers: false</code> (<code>UserNamespacesSupport</code>).</p>
<h2 id="how-to-use-it">How to use it<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-use-it" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="kind">kind<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kind" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The easiest way is to use <a href="https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/">kind</a> (a Kubernetes SIG Testing project)
to run a Kubernetes cluster in rootless Docker, rootless nerdctl, or rootless Podman:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Example using Docker</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kind create cluster
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Depending on the host configuration, you may need additional configuration for
systemd, kernel modules, sysctl, etc.</p>
<p>See the <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/rootless/">Docker documentation</a> and
the <a href="https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/rootless/">kind documentation</a> for further information.</p>
<h3 id="minikube">minikube<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#minikube" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/">minikube</a> (a Kubernetes SIG Cluster Lifecycle project)
also supports running a Kubernetes cluster in rootless Docker or rootless Podman:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">minikube start --driver<span class="o">=</span>docker
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>See the <a href="https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/drivers/docker/">minikube documentation</a>
for further information.</p>
<h3 id="usernetes">Usernetes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#usernetes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://github.com/rootless-containers/usernetes">Usernetes</a> (a third-party project)
is a distribution of rootless Kubernetes, maintained by the author of this article.
The project began in 2018, and it is where the <code>KubeletInUserNamespace</code> feature gate
originally came from.</p>
<p>Unlike kind and minikube, Usernetes supports creating a cluster with multiple rootless
Docker / Podman / nerdctl nodes, connected using VXLAN via the Flannel CNI plugin.</p>
<p>Usernetes also experimentally supports a <a href="https://github.com/rootless-containers/usernetes/tree/master/kubernetes">Kubernetes-in-Kubernetes</a> mode.</p>
<h3 id="k3s">k3s<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#k3s" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://k3s.io">k3s</a> (a CNCF Sandbox project) also supports <a href="https://docs.k3s.io/advanced#running-rootless-servers-experimental">rootless mode</a>.
Unlike kind, minikube, and the current generation of Usernetes, rootless k3s does not rely on an external runtime such as rootless Docker.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-next">What's next?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Depending on feedback and adoption, the Kubernetes project plans to graduate this feature to
General Availability (GA) in a future release. If you have feedback on this feature, please
open an issue in the <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes">kubernetes/kubernetes</a> repository.</p>
<p>The project is also discussing several Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals that may contribute to
simplifying Kubernetes-in-Kubernetes with this feature:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5474/">KEP-5474: Enable Writable cgroups for unprivileged containers</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5714">KEP-5714: Allow specifying whether to unshare cgroup namespaces</a></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="getting-involved">Getting involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#getting-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>We always welcome new contributors. If you would like to get involved, you can join the
<a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">Node Special Interest Group</a>
(SIG Node).</p>
<p>If you would like to share feedback, you can do so on our
<a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/messages/sig-node">public Slack channel</a>
(visit <a href="https://slack.k8s.io/">https://slack.k8s.io/</a> for an invitation if you need one).</p>
<p>Special thanks to everyone who helped design and implement this feature,
including but not limited to (in alphabetical order):</p>
<ul>
<li>Bing Hongtao (<a href="https://github.com/HirazawaUi">HirazawaUi</a>)</li>
<li>Jordan Liggitt (<a href="https://github.com/liggitt">liggitt</a>)</li>
<li>Sergey Kanzhelev (<a href="https://github.com/SergeyKanzhelev">SergeyKanzhelev</a>)</li>
<li>Tim Hockin (<a href="https://github.com/thockin">thockin</a>)</li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: DRA Updates</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/03/kubernetes-v1-37-dra-updates/</link><pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/03/kubernetes-v1-37-dra-updates/</guid><description>
<p>Kubernetes 1.37 is here and <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/dynamic-resource-allocation/">Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)</a> keeps pushing past where it started! This release brings DRA Extended Resource support to GA, a milestone the team has been building toward for three straight releases. Several more features graduate to Beta or GA. A fresh batch of alpha features rounds out the release.</p>
<p>I'll dive into what's new for DRA in Kubernetes 1.37!</p>
<h2 id="what-s-stable-in-1-37">What's stable in 1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-stable-in-1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5004">DRA Extended Resource support</a> has graduated to GA. This is the mechanism that lets DRA drivers satisfy requests made through the traditional extended resource API, think <code>example.com/gpu</code> in a Pod spec, without requiring a separate device plugin alongside the DRA driver. An extended resource name can be set directly on a DeviceClass, and Pods requesting it get matched to a device through DRA with no ResourceClaim needed on the workload's part.</p>
<p>It's been on a steady path since KEP acceptance in 1.34. Alpha landed in 1.35, Beta in 1.36, and now it's Stable. For cluster operators, this is what makes DRA adoption gradual. Existing workloads written against extended resources keep working unmodified while the backend allocation logic moves over to DRA.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4817/">ResourceClaims status with possible standardized network interface data</a> adds a <code>devices</code> field to ResourceClaim <code>.status</code>, letting DRA drivers report per-device status, including, for network devices, the interface name, MAC address, and IP addresses. This gives users and controllers visibility into device state that was previously invisible once a device was configured in a Pod, and makes it possible to build things like network services that rely on a device's reported IPs.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5055/">DRA: device taints and tolerations</a> is now Stable; DRA drivers can mark devices as tainted so they're skipped for new Pod scheduling, and cluster admins can apply the same taints cluster-wide via a DeviceTaintRule, without reconfiguring drivers. Pods already using a tainted device can be evicted automatically, unless their ResourceClaim explicitly tolerates the taint. This mirrors node taints and tolerations, letting operators take a single device offline for maintenance or mark it degraded, without disrupting the rest of the cluster.</p>
<p><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/6072">Standard numaNode device attribute</a> standardizes <code>resource.kubernetes.io/numaNode</code> as a shared attribute name, so devices from different drivers can be compared on the same NUMA node instead of each driver inventing its own name for it. It landed directly as stable in 1.37, since it's a naming/registration KEP with no feature gate or in-tree behavior change.</p>
<h2 id="feature-promoted-to-beta">Feature promoted to Beta<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#feature-promoted-to-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5729">ResourceClaim support for workloads</a>
graduates to Beta behind the <code>DRAWorkloadResourceClaims</code> feature gate, which stays disabled by default.
In a cluster that has the feature enabled, Workloads and PodGroups can reference ResourceClaims directly, so
a single claim can be shared across an entire group of Pods. This is instead of claims being capped at 256
Pods through the old per-Pod reservation limit.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5304/">DRA Device Attributes Downward API</a> is aimed at
supporting device injection into KubeVirt VMs. Drivers populate a <code>Metadata</code> field when preparing a claim,
and the framework writes it to a JSON file mounted into the container via CDI, letting workloads read a
device's PCI bus address, MAC address, and other attributes directly instead of requiring custom controllers
to watch and translate ResourceClaims and ResourceSlices.</p>
<h2 id="alpha-features">Alpha features<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#alpha-features" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5491">List types for attributes</a> moved into a second Alpha in 1.37,
letting a device attribute hold more than one value instead of a single scalar, such as a CPU that's
adjacent to more than one PCIe root. This makes it possible to match or distinguish devices based on
overlapping or non-overlapping sets of values, while single-value attributes keep working as they do today.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5517">Node allocatable resource requests</a> moved into Alpha 2. It
lets the scheduler and kubelet treat DRA-managed CPU, memory, and similar node resources the same way they
treat ordinary resource requests, so a node doesn't get oversubscribed and users no longer have to duplicate
the same request in both a ResourceClaim and the pod spec.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5677">Resource availability visibility</a> moved to a second Alpha in Kubernetes 1.37. Users create a ResourcePoolStatusRequest to get a point-in-time availability snapshot. To refresh it, delete and recreate the request; it is not a continuous monitoring API.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5945">DRA: Optional Node Operations</a> lets a driver skip kubelet's
prepare and unprepare calls for allocations that don't need any setup on the node. This makes it possible to
avoid an unnecessary dependency on the driver for allocations where there's genuinely nothing for it to do
locally.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6080">Derived Attributes</a> is a new feature that lets you use <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/cel/">CEL</a> expressions to match up devices based on your own
custom rules. Before this, pairing devices from different vendors (like a GPU/TPU and a NIC on the same NUMA
node) only worked if both drivers used the exact same attribute name. If one used <code>numa</code> and the other used
<code>numaNode</code>, the scheduler couldn't pair them together. Now, you can easily bridge these differences yourself
inside your manifest, meaning you don't have to wait for hardware vendors to agree on standardized attribute
names. Beyond just fixing naming differences, you can also use CEL to handle more complex scenarios like
slicing a specific ID out of a long, monolithic topology string, or grouping devices into custom performance
tiers based on their available capacity.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5963">DRA Device Compatibility Groups</a> lets drivers tag partitions
of a device, like MIG vs vGPU profiles on the same GPU, with compatibility groups, so the scheduler rejects
incompatible combinations up front instead of the driver failing at node preparation time. It's controlled by
the <code>DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups</code> feature gate, disabled by default.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6132">PreQueueingHint extension point</a> is new as Alpha in 1.37.
DRA ResourceClaim events used to trigger a full scan of every unschedulable pod, an O(N²) cost during large
scale-ups. The DRA plugin now uses a pod informer index to narrow that to just the pods actually affected,
cutting the requeue path to O(1) and roughly doubling scheduling throughput in early benchmarks. Controlled
by the <code>SchedulerPreQueueingHints</code> feature gate.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5075">DRA Consumable Capacity</a> now supports fractional values in
CapacityRequestPolicyRange, enabling more precise capacity requests and allocation for devices with fractional resources.
This improves flexibility for workloads that require fine-grained resource allocation. The enhancement is gated by the
<code>DRAFractionalCapacityRange</code> feature gate, which is in Beta in 1.37.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-next">What’s next<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>DRA continues to mature with every release. Several features currently in Alpha and Beta are on track to progress in the
coming releases, and the community keeps working on DRA's performance, scalability, and reliability. Expect another
ambitious set of DRA features in Kubernetes 1.38.</p>
<h2 id="getting-involved">Getting involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#getting-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>A good starting point is joining the WG Device Management <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0409NGC1TK">Slack channel</a> and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/wg/device-management/#meetings">meetings</a> which happens at US/EU and EU/APAC friendly time slots.</p>
<p>Not all enhancement ideas are tracked as issues yet, so come talk to us if you want to help or have some ideas yourself! We have work to do at all levels, from difficult core changes to usability enhancements in <code>kubectl</code> which could be picked up by newcomers.</p>
<h2 id="acknowledgments">Acknowledgments<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#acknowledgments" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The following KEP owners added or promoted a feature in the 1.37 release (in alphabetic order):</p>
<ul>
<li>Alay Patel (<a href="https://github.com/alaypatel07">alaypatel07</a>)</li>
<li>Byonggon Chun(<a href="https://github.com/bg-chun">bg-chun</a>)</li>
<li>Gaurav Ghildiyal (<a href="https://github.com/gauravkghildiyal">gauravkghildiyal</a>)</li>
<li>Jiefeng Xu (<a href="https://github.com/jiefeng-xu">jiefeng-xu</a>)</li>
<li>John A. Hull (<a href="https://github.com/johnahull">johnahull</a>)</li>
<li>Jon Huhn (<a href="https://github.com/nojnhuh">nojnhuh</a>)</li>
<li>Lionel Jouin (<a href="https://github.com/LionelJouin">LionelJouin</a>)</li>
<li>Patrick Ohly (<a href="https://github.com/pohly">pohly</a>)</li>
<li>Praveen Krishna (<a href="https://github.com/pravk03">pravk03</a>)</li>
<li>Shingo Omura (<a href="https://github.com/everpeace">everpeace</a>)</li>
<li>Troy Chiu (<a href="https://github.com/troychiu">troychiu</a>)</li>
</ul>
<p>This would not have been possible without the help of the reviewers and approvers.
So a huge thanks to everyone else who helped shape this release, in ways big and small. Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow and this release had plenty of them, watching closely and caring enough to make things better. DRA got better this cycle because of all of you.</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Scale Workloads to Zero with HorizontalPodAutoscaler</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/02/kubernetes-v1-37-hpa-scale-to-zero-beta/</link><pubDate>Wed, 02 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/02/kubernetes-v1-37-hpa-scale-to-zero-beta/</guid><description>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 includes API support for horizontal autoscaling of workloads down
to zero replicas. This feature is now Beta and enabled by default. A
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/">HorizontalPodAutoscaler</a>
(HPA) that uses a suitable <em>object metric</em> or <em>external metric</em> can now scale a
workload to zero replicas, then bring it back when the metric changes.</p>
<p>Before v1.37, you needed an add-on or external component, or you had to enable the
Alpha feature gate, to scale from zero. It is now part of core Kubernetes.</p>
<p>Scaling to zero removes the last idle Pod from workloads such as queue consumers and
batch processors. The savings are largest when each Pod reserves expensive resources,
including dedicated CPUs or GPUs.</p>
<p>The trade-off is cold-start time: the HPA must observe the metric, schedule a Pod, and
start the application. This works well when work can wait in a durable queue.</p>
<p>Kubernetes Services do not buffer requests while no Pods are ready, so HTTP and other
request-driven workloads need a separate buffering layer.</p>
<h2 id="why-scaling-from-zero-needs-a-different-metric">Why scaling from zero needs a different metric<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-scaling-from-zero-needs-a-different-metric" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The HPA commonly scales on CPU or memory usage. Both metrics come from running Pods.
Once the replica count reaches zero, there are no Pods left to measure and no signal
that can tell the HPA to scale back up.</p>
<p>Object and external metrics do not have that limitation. A queue length, for example,
exists independently of the workers that consume it. The HPA can continue reading the
queue length while no workers are running.</p>
<p>The following example scales a queue consumer to and from zero using an external
metric.</p>
<h2 id="configure-an-external-metric">Configure an external metric<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#configure-an-external-metric" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The following example uses a Prometheus metric named <code>queue_consumer_lag</code>. It assumes
that Prometheus already collects a series similar to this one:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-promql" data-lang="promql"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nv">queue_consumer_lag</span><span class="p">{</span><span class="nl">namespace</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="p">&#34;</span><span class="s">default</span><span class="p">&#34;,</span><span class="nl">name</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="p">&#34;</span><span class="s">worker_tasks</span><span class="p">&#34;}</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Kubernetes needs a metrics adapter to make that value available through the External
Metrics API. One implementation is the
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter">Prometheus Adapter</a>, which can
expose the series using an <code>externalRules</code> entry:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">externalRules</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span>- <span class="nt">seriesQuery</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s1">&#39;{__name__=&#34;queue_consumer_lag&#34;,name!=&#34;&#34;}&#39;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">metricsQuery</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">sum(&lt;&lt;.Series&gt;&gt;{&lt;&lt;.LabelMatchers&gt;&gt;}) by (name)</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resources</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">overrides</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resource</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">namespace</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>The exact adapter installation and discovery rules depend on your monitoring setup.
See the Prometheus Adapter guide to
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter/blob/v0.12.0/docs/externalmetrics.md">external metrics</a>
for the full configuration options.</p>
<p>Before creating the HPA, you can verify that Kubernetes can read the metric:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get --raw <span class="se">\
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="se"></span> <span class="s1">&#39;/apis/external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/queue_consumer_lag?labelSelector=name%3Dworker_tasks&#39;</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>The request should return the current value for <code>worker_tasks</code>. If it does not, fix the
metrics pipeline before configuring the HPA. An HPA cannot scale from zero when its
metric is unavailable.</p>
<h2 id="configure-the-hpa">Configure the HPA<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#configure-the-hpa" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The following HPA targets a Deployment named <code>queue-worker</code>. It allows between zero
and ten replicas, with one replica requested for each 30 queued tasks:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">autoscaling/v2</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">HorizontalPodAutoscaler</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">queue-worker</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">annotations</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kubernetes.io/description</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Scales queue-worker based on the number of queued tasks&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">scaleTargetRef</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">apps/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Deployment</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">queue-worker</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">minReplicas</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">0</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">maxReplicas</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">10</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">metrics</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">External</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">external</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">metric</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">queue_consumer_lag</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">selector</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">matchLabels</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">worker_tasks</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">target</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Value</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">value</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;30&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>When the queue is empty, the HPA can reduce the Deployment to zero replicas. When
tasks arrive, the external metric remains available and the HPA calculates a new
replica count, capped at ten by <code>maxReplicas</code>.</p>
<p>Start the Deployment with at least one replica. Manually setting a Deployment to zero
has always paused autoscaling. The HPA preserves that behavior and will not wake a
workload that it did not scale down itself.</p>
<p>Normal HPA behavior still applies. In particular, the default downscale stabilization
window is five minutes. The window prevents a short drop in queue length from
immediately removing all workers. You can configure the window through
<code>spec.behavior.scaleDown</code> if your workload needs different behavior.</p>
<h2 id="how-the-hpa-distinguishes-zero-from-paused">How the HPA distinguishes zero from paused<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-the-hpa-distinguishes-zero-from-paused" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Scaling from zero creates an ambiguity. A replica count of zero can mean that the HPA
scaled the workload down, or that an operator manually paused it.</p>
<p>The controller resolves this with a <code>ScaledToZero</code> status condition. When the HPA
scales a workload from one or more replicas to zero, it records
<code>ScaledToZero=True</code>. The condition tells later reconciliation loops that the
controller owns the zero state and should continue evaluating object or external
metrics.</p>
<p>After scaling the workload back up, the controller changes the condition to
<code>ScaledToZero=False</code> with the reason <code>NotScaledToZero</code>. A workload at zero without
the <code>ScaledToZero=True</code> condition remains paused.</p>
<p>You can inspect the conditions with:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl describe hpa queue-worker
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>If the adapter cannot return the configured metric, the HPA reports
<code>ScalingActive=False</code> with a reason such as <code>FailedGetExternalMetric</code>. Restore the
metric or manually scale the workload to recover capacity.</p>
<h2 id="before-upgrading-or-rolling-back">Before upgrading or rolling back<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#before-upgrading-or-rolling-back" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In Kubernetes v1.37, the <code>HPAScaleToZero</code> feature gate is enabled by default on both the
<code>kube-apiserver</code> and <code>kube-controller-manager</code>. The API server accepts
<code>minReplicas: 0</code>; the controller manager performs the condition-based scaling.</p>
<p>During a version-skewed control plane upgrade, wait until both components support the
feature and have it enabled before creating HPAs with <code>minReplicas: 0</code>. A controller
manager with the feature disabled treats <code>replicas: 0</code> as a manual pause and may leave
a workload at zero.</p>
<p>Before disabling the feature gate or downgrading to a version without the
condition-based implementation:</p>
<ul>
<li>Change affected HPAs to <code>minReplicas: 1</code> or higher.</li>
<li>Scale any workload currently at zero to at least one replica.</li>
</ul>
<p><code>minReplicas: 0</code> also requires at least one object or external metric. The API server
rejects an HPA that only contains resource metrics such as CPU or memory.</p>
<h2 id="from-alpha-to-beta">From Alpha to Beta<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#from-alpha-to-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The first Alpha implementation shipped in Kubernetes v1.16. Kubernetes v1.36 added
the <code>ScaledToZero</code> condition and the controller behavior needed to distinguish an
automatic scale-down from a manual pause.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 enables the feature by default after adding integration and end-to-end
coverage for scaling down to zero and back up from an external metric. The next step is
to gather operational feedback before considering graduation to GA.</p>
<h2 id="how-can-i-learn-more">How can I learn more?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-can-i-learn-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>Read the documentation for
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/#scaling-to-and-from-zero">scaling to and from zero</a>.</li>
<li>Read
<a href="https://kep.k8s.io/2021">KEP-2021: HPA supports scaling to and from zero pods for object and external metrics</a>.</li>
<li>Learn how to configure the
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter/blob/v0.12.0/docs/externalmetrics.md">Prometheus Adapter for external metrics</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="how-to-get-involved">How to get involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This feature is owned by
<a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/autoscaling/">SIG Autoscaling</a>.
Join <a href="https://slack.k8s.io/">Kubernetes Slack</a> and the
<a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C09R1LV8S"><code>#sig-autoscaling</code> channel</a> to share
feedback from Beta usage.</p>
<h2 id="acknowledgements">Acknowledgements<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#acknowledgements" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Thanks to the SIG Autoscaling contributors who took this feature from the original
v1.16 implementation to the condition-based redesign and Beta graduation. Thanks
also to <a href="https://github.com/gjtempleton">Guy Templeton</a> and
<a href="https://github.com/adrianmoisey">Adrian Moisey</a> for reviewing the KEP, and to the
release, documentation, and production-readiness reviewers who helped prepare it for
Kubernetes v1.37.</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: etcd RangeStream Cuts Memory Use on Large List Reads</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/01/kubernetes-v1-37-etcd-range-stream/</link><pubDate>Tue, 01 Sep 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/09/01/kubernetes-v1-37-etcd-range-stream/</guid><description>
<p>I am excited to announce that etcd RangeStream is graduating to beta in
Kubernetes v1.37. Paired with etcd v3.7, it reduces the memory the API server and
etcd need to read a large collection, and makes peak usage more predictable.</p>
<h2 id="the-cost-of-large-reads">The cost of large reads<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-cost-of-large-reads" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The API server serves most list and watch requests from its in-memory watch cache.
Populating that cache requires reading a resource's full state from etcd, at
startup and on every re-initialization. For a resource with many objects, or large
ones, such as Pods, that read is expensive.</p>
<p>The API server already paginated these reads, asking etcd for a fixed number of
keys at a time rather than the whole collection at once. But a page bounded by key
count has no awareness of object size, so a page of large objects can still be
very large. That makes memory usage hard to predict, and a bad combination of
object size and concurrent reads can be enough to trigger an OOM. etcd's unary
<code>Range</code> assembles each page in full before sending it, and the API server holds it
while decoding, so the same payload sits in memory on both sides at once. Most of
that cost lands on etcd, which is also where streaming helps most.</p>
<h2 id="streaming-reads-with-rangestream">Streaming reads with RangeStream<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#streaming-reads-with-rangestream" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>etcd v3.7 adds a streaming version of that read, the <code>RangeStream</code> RPC. It takes
the same <code>RangeRequest</code> as <code>Range</code> and returns the same result set, but instead of
building the whole response up front, etcd splits it into chunks and streams them.
Chunk size is tuned adaptively to the values being returned, so a collection of
large objects is bounded by bytes rather than by a key count, and memory is freed
as the stream progresses instead of being held until a whole page is assembled.</p>
<p>When the feature is enabled, the API server uses <code>RangeStream</code> wherever it reads a
whole collection out of etcd. This includes watch cache initialization, and the
fallback paths where a list request cannot be served from the cache and reads etcd
directly. In either case the API server decodes each chunk as it arrives and
releases it before pulling the next one, so neither side ever holds the whole
collection.</p>
<h2 id="requirements">Requirements<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#requirements" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>Kubernetes v1.37 or later</li>
<li>etcd v3.7 or later</li>
</ul>
<p>RangeStream is used when the <code>EtcdRangeStream</code> feature gate is enabled on the
kube-apiserver, which is beta and on by default in v1.37, and etcd is v3.7 or
later. The API server resolves etcd's support at startup
and also falls back at runtime if a call returns <code>Unimplemented</code>, so an API server
paired with an older etcd keeps using the paginated <code>Range</code> path on its own. To
turn it off, disable the gate:</p>
<pre tabindex="0"><code>--feature-gates=EtcdRangeStream=false
</code></pre><h2 id="confirming-rangestream-is-in-use">Confirming RangeStream is in use<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#confirming-rangestream-is-in-use" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The API server records streamed reads under their own operation label on its etcd
metrics. A non-zero count here means <code>RangeStream</code> is in use:</p>
<pre tabindex="0"><code>etcd_request_duration_seconds_count{operation=&#34;listStream&#34;}
</code></pre><p>If it stays at zero, the API server is still using the paginated <code>Range</code> path, most
likely because etcd is older than v3.7.</p>
<h2 id="learn-more">Learn more<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#learn-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5966">KEP-5966: etcd RangeStream</a></li>
<li><a href="https://etcd.io/docs/v3.7/learning/api/">RangeStream in the etcd API guide</a></li>
<li><a href="https://etcd.io/blog/2026/announcing-etcd-3.7/">Announcing etcd v3.7</a></li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/master/sig-etcd">SIG etcd</a></li>
</ul>
<p>If you have questions or feedback, join the <code>#sig-etcd</code> channel on
<a href="https://slack.k8s.io/">Kubernetes Slack</a>.</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Storage Version Migration Enabled by Default</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/31/kubernetes-v1-37-storage-version-migration-ga/</link><pubDate>Mon, 31 Aug 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/31/kubernetes-v1-37-storage-version-migration-ga/</guid><description>
<p>I am excited that <em>storage version migration</em> (SVM) has graduated to General Availability (GA) in Kubernetes v1.37!</p>
<p>After a number of releases of work and testing, the built-in StorageVersionMigration API (<code>storagemigration.k8s.io/v1</code>)
and control plane controller are now fully stable and enabled by default across all v1.37 Kubernetes clusters.</p>
<h2 id="the-problem-with-stale-storage-versions">The problem with stale storage versions<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-problem-with-stale-storage-versions" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>In Kubernetes, stored API resources are written using a specific <em>storage version</em> (schema representation). The way Kubernetes interacts with object storage fundamentally requires mutation of a resource in order to ensure that the latest storage version is used for all resources. This creates problems when you want to change the storage version of a resource.</p>
<p>One example of a scenario where you may want to change the storage version of a resource is when you are promoting a CRD to drop an older API version (such as <code>v1alpha1</code>) to a newer version (leaving just <code>v1beta1</code> and <code>v1</code>). It's a problem to drop the older API version whilst there are still resources stored with the old alpha version.</p>
<p>To avoid problems, you designate <code>v1</code> as the new storage version; but, on it's own, that's not enough. While new writes are stored as <code>v1</code>, any existing resource could remain stored as <code>v1alpha1</code> or <code>v1beta1</code> in storage. You cannot safely remove <code>v1alpha1</code> from the CRD's <code>.status.storedVersions</code> or drop serving support until every single resource in storage has been re-written to not be serialized and stored with the alpha version.</p>
<p>Another relevant example is <em>encryption at rest</em> and, related, <em>key rotation</em>.
When you configure encryption at rest or rotate encryption keys, existing resources in storage remain <strong>unencrypted</strong> (or encrypted under old keys) until they are actively
re-written through the Kubernetes API server.</p>
<p>Historically, cluster administrators and CRD authors had to rely on manual
<code>kubectl get</code> / <code>kubectl replace</code> scripts, or to deploy the out-of-tree <code>kube-storage-version-migrator</code> component to force re-writes.
These approaches were often tedious, error-prone, and difficult to monitor.</p>
<h2 id="how-storage-version-migration-works">How storage version migration works<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-storage-version-migration-works" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Initiating a storage version migration is as simple as creating a declarative StorageVersionMigration object.
The built-in StorageVersionMigrator controller in the Kubernetes control plane watches for these objects, and automatically migrates existing resources to the default storage version for that API.</p>
<h3 id="example-custom-resources">Example: Migrating a custom resource API<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#example-custom-resources" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Suppose you have updated a CustomResourceDefinition (<code>crontabs.example.com</code>) to use <code>v1</code> as its storage version.
To migrate all existing stored resources off older versions, create a StorageVersionMigration:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">storagemigration.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">StorageVersionMigration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">crontabs-migration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resource</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">group</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example.com</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resource</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">crontabs</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Apply the manifest using <code>kubectl</code>:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl apply -f crontabs-migration.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="monitoring-and-verifying-migrations">Monitoring and verifying migrations<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#monitoring-and-verifying-migrations" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The StorageVersionMigrator controller updates the <code>status</code> of the StorageVersionMigration object as migration progresses.
You can inspect the migration status using <code>kubectl</code>:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get storageversionmigration.storagemigration.k8s.io/crontabs-migration -o yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>A successful migration will report a <code>Succeeded</code> condition set to True:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">status</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">conditions</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Running</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">status</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;False&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">lastUpdateTime</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;2026-08-02T10:05:00Z&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">reason</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">StorageVersionMigrationInProgress</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Succeeded</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">status</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;True&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">lastUpdateTime</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;2026-08-02T10:05:00Z&#34;</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">reason</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">StorageVersionMigrationSucceeded</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Once the migration has succeeded, you can be confident that all instances of the resource in storage are stored in the current storage version. For
CRDs, the stored version should be updated in the CRD's <code>.status.storedVersions</code> to only contain the preferred version. If the
<code>.status.storedVersions</code> is not updated following a successful migration then that means that the CRD was updated during the migration. In
that case, the migration should be retried in order to safely deprecate an older storage version.</p>
<h2 id="including-migrations-in-your-crd-manifests">Including migrations in your CRD manifests<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#including-migrations-in-your-crd-manifests" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Because StorageVersionMigration is a standard declarative Kubernetes API, CRD authors can bundle or trigger migrations directly
alongside CRD upgrades. For example, you can include the migration in the same manifest as your updated CustomResourceDefinition:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">apiextensions.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">CustomResourceDefinition</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">crontabs.example.com</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">group</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example.com</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="c"># Updated versions list where v1 has storage: true</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">...</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">storagemigration.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">StorageVersionMigration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">crontabs-migration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resource</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">group</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example.com</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">resource</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">crontabs</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="what-s-next">What's next?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>Learn more about the concepts behind <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/storage-version/">Storage Versions</a>.</li>
<li>Read the step-by-step task guide: <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/storage-version-migration/">Migrate Kubernetes Objects Using Storage Version Migration</a>.</li>
</ul>
<p>SIG API Machinery would love to hear your feedback as you adopt built-in Storage Version Migration in your clusters. Reach out to us on the <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/messages/sig-api-machinery">#sig-api-machinery</a> Slack channel or participate in our community discussions!</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Pod Certificates and Cluster Trust Bundles</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/28/kubernetes-v1-37-pod-certificates-and-cluster-trust-bundles/</link><pubDate>Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/28/kubernetes-v1-37-pod-certificates-and-cluster-trust-bundles/</guid><description>
<h2 id="pod-certificate-cluster-trust-bundles-blog-post">Pod Certificate / Cluster Trust Bundles Blog Post<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#pod-certificate-cluster-trust-bundles-blog-post" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Kubernetes brings a wealth of features that make it easy to run your production
workloads securely and reliably. While aspects like scheduling, health checks
and resource limits are probably at the front of your mind, one other important
feature of Kubernetes is production identity — how your workload can
authenticate to other systems in order to do its job.</p>
<p>Up until now, the primary production identity mechanism built into Kubernetes
has been service account JWTs (JSON Web Tokens). These are
cryptographically-signed tokens, issued by the control plane of your cluster,
that let anyone in the world understand who is calling when your workload uses
them.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes 1.37, the foundations of a new built-in production identity
