technology have gone GA. Pod Certificates (and the closely-associated Cluster
Trust Bundles) build X.509 certificate issuance for TLS and mTLS directly into
core Kubernetes.</p>
<p>Why?</p>
<p>Service account JWTs have a lot going for them:</p>
<ul>
<li>They are built directly into Kubelet, and work pretty magically. They are
written to your workload container’s filesystem before your workload starts
up, and automatically kept up to date.</li>
<li>The issuance system follows least-privilege principles; the node restriction
admission plugin ensures that tokens can only be requested by the Kubelet that
is actually currently running your pod.</li>
<li>They can be federated, allowing you to use them to authenticate to other
systems outside of Kubernetes. Service account JWTs underpin the pod-to-cloud
authentication store for all of the largest cloud providers, and have
widespread support across many additional services and software packages. If
it can understand JWTs, you can authenticate to it with a service account
token.</li>
</ul>
<p>However, service account JWTs have one big downside — they are bearer tokens.
With bearer tokens, if you <em>have</em> the token, then you <em>are</em> the identity
asserted by the token. And since you necessarily have to hand copies of the JWT
to all your peers in order to authenticate to them, <em>they</em> can be you, too.</p>
<p>There are partial mitigations for this, and service account tokens make use of
them (time-, object-, and audience-binding), but none are complete defences.</p>
<p>A solution to this problem lies in proof-of-possession credentials, where you
don’t send your <em>entire</em> credential to your peer, but only a proof that you
possess the credential. In practice, these schemes are always built on
asymmetric cryptographic signatures (RSA, ECDSA, and friends).</p>
<p>There are few different standard approaches, such as request signing (AWS SigV4,
JWT DPoP, RFC 9421), but the most widely-deployed and understood solution is
X.509 certificates, as used in TLS. In TLS, your credential is split into two
pieces</p>
<ul>
<li>A private key, which for maximum security should be generated within your
workload (or within a hardware security module), and never leave.</li>
<li>A certificate, which is a description of your identity and public key, signed
by a Certificate Authority.</li>
</ul>
<p>The goal of Pod Certificates is to make using X.509 certificates from your
Kubernetes workload just as easy as using service account JWTs, while
maintaining Kubernetes’ high security bar. I think we’ve hit this target.</p>
<p>As I’ll cover in the architecture and example sections below, there are many
similarities between the design of service account JWT issuance and Pod
Certificates. One significant place they diverge, however, is that Pod
Certificates is a much more flexible mechanism. Kubernetes only offers one
flavor of service account JWTs, with standardized claims.</p>
<p>The X.509 ecosystem is significantly more varied than the JWT ecosystem, and
X.509 certificates used for different purposes contain different extensions and
information. For this reason, Pod Certificates has common machinery built into
Kubelet, but offers a pluggable interface so that many different types of
certificates can be issued within a single cluster, at the same time.</p>
<p>In the fullness of time, I expect Kubernetes to offer at least two built-in
certificate providers:</p>
<ul>
<li>One that issues server TLS certificates for the DNS names used by Kubernetes
services.</li>
<li>One that offers SPIFFE client certificates, filling the same role that service
account JWTs fill today.</li>
</ul>
<p>In the remainder of this article, I’ll take you through the overall architecture
of a Kubernetes workload using Pod Certificates, as well as give you an example
of installing and using a real (toy) Pod Certificates signer controller.</p>
<h2 id="architecture">Architecture<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#architecture" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>When you use Pod Certificates and Cluster Trust Bundles, there are the following
major components:</p>
<ul>
<li>Your application, which requests certificates in its pod spec, and reads the
keys, certificates and trust bundles from the container filesystem to use for
(m)TLS.</li>
<li>Kubelet, which issues PodCertificateRequest objects and reads
ClusterTrustBundle objects on behalf of your workload.</li>
<li>The signer controller, which answers PodCertificateRequests and publishes
ClusterTrustBundles.</li>
</ul>
<figure class="diagram-large ">
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/28/kubernetes-v1-37-pod-certificates-and-cluster-trust-bundles/pod-certificates-architecture.svg"
alt="Block diagram of an application using Pod Certificates"/> <figcaption>
<p>Architecture of an application using Pod Certificates</p>
</figcaption>
</figure>
<p>The best way to get a sense of what these components each do is to follow the
issuance process chronologically:</p>
<ol>
<li>Once your application pod is scheduled to a node, Kubelet identifies all of
the podCertificate and clusterTrustBundle projected volumes sources in its
spec.</li>
<li>For each podCertificate source:
<ol>
<li>Kubelet generates a new private key according to the keyType field.</li>
<li>Kubelet creates a PodCertificateRequest addressed to the signer named in
the source.</li>
<li>The signer controller sees the PodCertificateRequest and decides whether
or not to issue the certificate.</li>
<li>The signer controller issues the certificate by filling out the
status.certificateChain field.</li>
<li>The signer controller also fills out the status.beginRefreshAt field to
instruct Kubelet when it should begin trying to refresh the certificate.<br>
certificate to the container filesystem.</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>For each clusterTrustBundle source:<br>
6) Kubelet retrieves the issued certificate, and writes the private key and
<ol>
<li>Kubelet collects all the ClusterTrustBundles that match the signer name</li>
<li>Kubelet unifies all of the certificates from all matching
ClusterTrustBundles, and (stably) reorders them (to prevent applications
from accidentally depending on a particular ordering).<br>
and label selectors in the source.</li>
<li>Kubelet writes the certificates to the file path named in the source.<br>
and trust anchors from the filesystem.</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Your application pod starts up, and the application reads keys, certificates,</li>
<li>Kubelet periodically updates the files from clusterTrustBundle sources as the
contents of the selected ClusterTrustBundles changes. The application must
pick up the changes using inotify or polling.</li>
<li>As each certificate’s beginRefreshAt time passes, Kubelet repeats the process
in step 2 to refresh the certificates, and write the update private keys and
certificate chains to the filesystem. As in step 5, the application must
pick up changes using inotify or polling.</li>
</ol>
<p>Some key takeaways:</p>
<ul>
<li>Automatic rotation is built in. Applications <em>must</em> properly handle it. Any
signers eventually shipped in core Kubernetes will issue certificates with a
max lifetime of 24 hours. The maximum lifetime allowed for other signers is
91 days.</li>
<li>To make automatic rotation support as simple as possible, Kubelet supports
writing the private key and certificate chain to a single file (a <em>credential
bundle</em>) This allows the application to simply subscribe to inotify events for
(or poll) the single file, read the contents, and use them. Kubelet does
support writing the private key and certificate chain to separate files, but
then the application needs to carefully manage the potential race conditions
of reading the files mid-rotation.</li>
<li>Wherever possible, security checks are built into kube-apiserver, rather than
burdening signer or application developers. As an example, the built-in node
restriction admission plugin enforces node isolation, ensuring that one
compromised node cannot spread access by requesting certificates for pods that
aren’t scheduled to it.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="try-it-out">Try it out<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#try-it-out" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Because the Kubernetes project does not yet ship any Pod Certificate signers in
core, in order to try these features out, you will need to install a third-party
signer into your cluster. To make this easier, I have written
<a href="https://github.com/ahmedtd/tinycert">Tinycert</a>, which you can install into your
cluster (or a Kind cluster).</p>
<p>Tinycert is not a full production solution, but it’s a good starting point for
experimenting with Pod Certificates, as well as a base for creating your own
signers.</p>
<p>Tinycert provides:</p>
<ul>
<li>The
<a href="https://ahmedtd.github.io/tinycert-service">ahmedtd.github.io/tinycert-service</a>
signer, which issues certificates with DNS SANs for all of the Kubernetes
Services your Pod is part of.</li>
<li>The
<a href="https://ahmedtd.github.io/tinycert-spiffe">ahmedtd.github.io/tinycert-spiffe</a>
signer, which issues SPIFFE-compatible certificates that identify the
namespace and service account of your Pod. These can be used as both client
and (with effort) server certificates.</li>
<li>A Go library,
<a href="https://github.com/ahmedtd/tinycert/lib/spiffefsd">github.com/ahmedtd/tinycert/lib/spiffefsd</a>
to help your applications load SPIFFE certificates and trust bundles from a
<a href="https://github.com/spiffe/spiffe/pull/376">SPIFFE Filesystem Delivery (Draft
Standard)</a> folder, as well as
configure the Go TLS library for proper client and server authentication.</li>
<li>An example of a SPIFFE client and server application communicating using
mutual TLS and SPIFFE certificates.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="what-next">What next?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>Take a look at the documentation for <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#pod-certificate-requests">Pod
Certificates</a>
and <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#cluster-trust-bundles">Cluster Trust
Bundles</a>.</li>
<li>Review and offer feedback on the <a href="https://github.com/spiffe/spiffe/pull/376">SPIFFE Filesystem Delivery draft
standard</a>, which aims to make it as
easy as possible to use SPIFFE certificates directly on native Kubernetes.</li>
<li>Participate in Kubernetes SIG Auth to help shape the future of signers that
are built directly in to core Kubernetes.</li>
<li>Try building your own signer based on Tinycert.</li>
</ul>
<p>Happy hacking!</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Metrics API graduates to stable</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/27/kubernetes-v1-37-metrics-api-ga/</link><pubDate>Thu, 27 Aug 2026 10:30:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/27/kubernetes-v1-37-metrics-api-ga/</guid><description>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 promotes the <code>metrics.k8s.io</code> API to stable (<code>v1</code>). This
API provides CPU and memory usage for nodes and Pods, and is the API behind
commands such as <code>kubectl top</code> and resource-metrics-based autoscaling.</p>
<p>For cluster operators and application developers, this graduation means that
the API now has the stability guarantees associated with a Kubernetes stable
API. The <code>v1</code> API has the same resource types and fields as <code>v1beta1</code>; this is
an API-version graduation, not a change to the metrics that are collected or
returned.</p>
<h2 id="a-long-lived-api-reaches-stable">A long-lived API reaches stable<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#a-long-lived-api-reaches-stable" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The resource Metrics API was introduced as alpha in Kubernetes v1.6 and became
beta in v1.8. It has remained unchanged and has been used in production for
years by clients including the HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) and <code>kubectl top</code>.
Kubernetes v1.37 formally graduates that proven API to <code>metrics.k8s.io/v1</code>.</p>
<p>The API exposes two resource types:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>NodeMetrics</code>, for CPU and memory usage for a node.</li>
<li><code>PodMetrics</code>, for CPU and memory usage for a Pod, with a per-container
breakdown in its <code>containers</code> field.</li>
</ul>
<p>The API remains intentionally small. It provides the resource metrics needed
for autoscaling and basic inspection; it is not a replacement for a full
monitoring pipeline or the custom metrics (<code>custom.metrics.k8s.io</code>) API.</p>
<h2 id="changes">What changed with the v1.37 release?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#changes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The <code>v1</code> API surface is identical to <code>v1beta1</code>, except for the API version.
There are no renamed fields, new fields, or changes to the meaning of the
returned CPU and memory values.</p>
<p>For example, a client can retrieve node metrics from the stable endpoint:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1/nodes
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Likewise, it can retrieve metrics for the pods in a namespace:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/default/pods
</span></span></code></pre></div><p><code>kubectl top</code> supports both API versions. It prefers <code>v1</code> when available and
automatically falls back to <code>v1beta1</code> on clusters that do not yet serve <code>v1</code>.
The HPA controller currently supports only <code>v1beta1</code>. Support for
discovery-based selection between <code>v1</code> and <code>v1beta1</code> is planned, but is not
available in Kubernetes v1.37.</p>
<h2 id="what-you-need-to-do">What you need to do<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-you-need-to-do" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>You don't need to enable any feature gate. The Metrics API is served through the
<a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/configure-aggregation-layer/">API aggregation layer</a>,
by an implementation such as <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server">metrics-server</a>.
You can choose any implementation of <code>metrics.k8s.io</code>; for the v1 metrics API to be
available in your cluster, your chosen implementation must serve the <code>v1.metrics.k8s.io</code> API, and you need to <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/configure-aggregation-layer/">register</a> an associated <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/apiregistration/api-service-v1/">APIService</a>.</p>
<p>During the transition, implementations should serve both <code>v1</code> and <code>v1beta1</code>.
Keeping both versions available maintains compatibility with older clients.
The <code>v1beta1</code> API remains available in Kubernetes v1.37.</p>
<p>You can see which versions your cluster serves with:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/ <span class="p">|</span> jq .
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Once your metrics implementation supports <code>v1</code>, you can also check that its
APIService is available:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get apiservice v1.metrics.k8s.io
</span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="learn-more">Learn more<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#learn-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ul>
<li>Read the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/resource-metrics-pipeline/">Resource metrics pipeline</a>
documentation.</li>
<li>Read <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5207/">KEP-5207</a>, the proposal for (graduating) this API.</li>
<li>Learn about the <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/metrics#resource-metrics-api">Metrics API</a>
and its reference implementation, <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server">metrics-server</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="get-involved">Get involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The Metrics API is maintained by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/instrumentation/">SIG Instrumentation</a>.
To ask questions, share feedback, or contribute, join the
<a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/messages/sig-instrumentation">#sig-instrumentation</a>
channel on Kubernetes Slack or attend a SIG Instrumentation meeting.</p></description></item><item><title>Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/</link><pubDate>Wed, 26 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/</guid><description>
<p><strong>Editors:</strong> Arsh Sharma, Christopher Tineo, Kirti Goyal, Sophia Ugochukwu, Swathi Rao, Troy Connor</p>
<p>Similar to previous releases, the release of <a href="https://kubernetes.io/releases/1.37/">Kubernetes v1.37</a> introduces new Stable, Beta, and Alpha features. The consistent delivery of high-quality releases underscores the strength of our development cycle and the vibrant support from our community.</p>
<p>This release consists of 67 enhancements.
Of those enhancements, 16 have graduated to Stable, 23 have graduated to Beta,
27 are entering Alpha, and 1 is a deprecation/removal.</p>
<h2 id="release-theme-and-logo">Release theme and logo<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#release-theme-and-logo" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2>
<figure class="release-logo ">
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/k8s-v1.37.svg"
alt="Kubernetes v1.37 Garhwal release logo: a ringaal-inspired woven frame surrounds snow-capped Himalayan peaks, terraced fields, deodar trees, a winding river, a mountain house marked 1.37, colourful flags, a Himalayan monal, and red buransh flowers with Kubernetes helm symbols at their centres"/>
</figure>
<p>The theme for Kubernetes v1.37 is <strong>Garhwal</strong> (गढ़वाल, pronounced <em>gaṛhvāl</em>), a Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, India. The snow-capped peaks of the Garhwal Himalaya, deodar forests, terraced fields, rivers and streams, and mountain paths shape both the region and the logo. Together, these elements reflect a community in which every layer, route, and contribution is connected.</p>
<p>The logo is imagined as a window into Garhwal's landscape.<sup>1</sup> Inside, terraced fields climb towards the snowy peaks, each level supported by the one below, much as every Kubernetes release depends on work carried forward. A river winds through the valley and gathers mountain streams, reflecting contributions from many SIGs and communities flowing into one project.</p>
<p>The deodar forest represents the wider Kubernetes ecosystem, where distinct projects share common ground and grow side by side. Stonework and woodcraft shape the path and mountain house, placing people at the centre and evoking shared foundations maintained for those who follow. Above the river, colourful flags catch the wind and bring the scene to life.</p>
<p>Encircling the scene is a patterned frame inspired by basketry woven from <em>ringaal</em>, a flexible dwarf Himalayan bamboo. Individual strips gain strength when interlaced, just as code, reviews, tests, documentation, and coordination come together to make a release.</p>
<p>Within the frame, the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_monal">Himalayan monal</a>, Uttarakhand's state bird, lives at high altitudes in the Himalaya. Its iridescent plumage holds many colours at once, much as the Kubernetes community brings many skills and perspectives into one project. Flowers of red <em>buransh</em> (<em>Rhododendron arboreum</em>), Uttarakhand's state tree, carry Kubernetes helms at their centres, linking a familiar bloom of Garhwal with the symbol shared by the community. The house bears १.३७ (1.37 in Devanagari numerals), grounding the release in the landscape.</p>
<p><sub>1. Keep looking through the window (the logo). Watch the river flow and the flags catch the wind. In 37 seconds, the landscape reveals its magic. 😉</sub></p>
<h2 id="spotlight-on-key-updates">Spotlight on key updates<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#spotlight-on-key-updates" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Kubernetes v1.37 is packed with new features and improvements. Here are a few select updates the <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-release/blob/master/releases/release-1.37/release-team.md">Release Team</a> would like to highlight!</p>
<h3 id="stable-resilient-watchcache-initialization">Stable: Resilient watchcache initialization<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#stable-resilient-watchcache-initialization" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 completes the work on <em>resilient watch cache initialization</em>: the
<code>ResilientWatchCacheInitialization</code> feature gate reached Stable back in v1.34, and in v1.37 the remaining
<code>WatchCacheInitializationPostStartHook</code> gate graduates to Stable and is locked on. It has defaulted to
enabled since v1.36, hardening the API server at startup and during
recovery. Watchcache initialization and reinitialization no longer create a traffic spike of requests against <code>etcd</code>, and
requests are handled gracefully instead of piling up while the cache warms.</p>
<p>Instead of allowing expensive list and watch requests to overload <code>etcd</code> or exhaust API Priority and Fairness capacity, <code>kube-apiserver</code> now safely delegates bounded requests and rejects others with HTTP 429 responses. This reduces the risk of control
plane outages in large clusters. Clients (including custom controllers and operators) should be designed to handle HTTP <code>429 Too Many Requests</code> responses gracefully by respecting <code>Retry-After</code> headers and implementing exponential backoff.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4568/">KEP #4568</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/api-machinery/">SIG API Machinery</a>.</p>
<h3 id="beta-horizontalpodautoscaler-scale-to-zero">Beta: HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale to zero<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#beta-horizontalpodautoscaler-scale-to-zero" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In Kubernetes v1.37, HorizontalPodAutoscaler <em>scale to zero</em> support is graduating to Beta. First introduced in
Kubernetes v1.16, it is now <strong>enabled by default</strong>.
For workloads that are using object or external metrics, this feature allows HorizontalPodAutoscalers to scale down to
zero Pods when idle, then restore them when demand returns. Doing that can reduce costs for queue consumers, batch jobs,
and GPU workloads. Setting <code>spec.minReplicas: 0</code> applies this functionality for workloads.</p>
<p>Scaling to zero based on CPU and memory metrics is <strong>not</strong> supported because those metrics depend on active Pods.
Instead, this feature is for situations such as leaving the replica count at zero until there is queued work to process.</p>
<p>While the HorizontalPodAutoscaler is holding a
workload at zero replicas, it records a <code>ScaledToZero</code> condition with <code>True</code> in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's status. The
<code>HorizontalPodAutoscaler</code> controller then uses this condition to distinguish a workload that it scaled to zero (and will
scale back up when the metric returns) from one that was manually deactivated by setting its replica count to 0. Once the
workload is scaled back up, the condition is set to <code>False</code> with the reason <code>NotScaledToZero</code>.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/2021/">KEP #2021</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/autoscaling/">SIG Autoscaling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="beta-manifest-based-admission-control-configuration">Beta: Manifest-based admission control configuration<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#beta-manifest-based-admission-control-configuration" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 graduates <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/manifest-admission-control/">manifest-based admission control</a>
configuration to Beta. Admission webhooks and CEL-based policies can now be loaded from manifest files on disk, via the
<code>staticManifestsDir</code> field in <code>AdmissionConfiguration</code>, instead of living only in the Kubernetes API. Policies loaded this
way are enforced from API server startup, keep working while <code>etcd</code> is unavailable, and can protect the API-based admission
resources themselves from modification.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5793/">KEP #5793</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/api-machinery/">SIG API Machinery</a>.</p>
<h3 id="alpha-pod-level-checkpoint-and-restore">Alpha: Pod-level checkpoint and restore<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#alpha-pod-level-checkpoint-and-restore" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 introduces Alpha support for <strong>Pod-level</strong> checkpoint and restore,
extending the CRI with <code>CheckpointPod</code> and <code>RestorePod</code> RPCs, which allow the kubelet and compatible container runtimes to create a Pod checkpoint and restore a Pod from it.
To use this feature, your container runtime(s) must also implement these new RPCs.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5823/">KEP #5823</a> led by
<a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h2 id="features-graduating-to-stable">Features graduating to Stable<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#features-graduating-to-stable" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This lists all the features that graduated to Stable (also known as <em>General Availability</em>). For a full list of updates
including new features and graduations from Alpha to Beta, see the release notes.</p>
<p>This release includes a total of 16 enhancements promoted to Stable:</p>
<h3 id="kyaml">KYAML<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kyaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><em>KYAML</em> is a safer and less ambiguous subset of YAML designed specifically for Kubernetes, <strong>not a replacement for it</strong>. Every
KYAML file is valid YAML, so KYAML is a valid input for any version of <code>kubectl</code>, and spec files do not need to be written in
KYAML for the input to be parsed. Your existing manifests, tooling, and pipelines don't need to change.
Introduced as an Alpha feature in v1.34 and graduating to Beta in v1.35, KYAML graduates to Stable in v1.37 with conformance
testing complete, and <code>kubectl get -o kyaml</code> is now Stable.</p>
<p>To learn more about KYAML, check out <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/11/how-to-pretty-print-kubernetes-yaml-as-kyaml/">How to Pretty-Print Your Kubernetes YAML as KYAML and Why You'd Want To</a>.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5295/">KEP #5295</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/cli/">SIG CLI</a>.</p>
<h3 id="the-metrics-k8s-io-api">The metrics.k8s.io API<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-metrics-k8s-io-api" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <em>metrics.k8s.io</em> API graduates to Stable in Kubernetes v1.37 after spending nearly nine years in Beta. The API provides a
standard way to retrieve CPU and memory usage for pods and nodes, powering widely used Kubernetes features such as the
HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) and commands like <code>kubectl top</code>.</p>
<p>The graduation follows the Kubernetes project’s goal of avoiding permanent Beta APIs. Now that <code>v1</code> exists, future
Kubernetes releases will move over to it; <code>v1beta1</code> remains usable throughout the transition, in line with the API
deprecation policy, so you can adopt the Stable API without breaking existing workflows.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5207/">KEP #5207</a> led
by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/instrumentation/">SIG Instrumentation</a>.</p>
<h3 id="selinuxmount-and-selinuxchangepolicy"><code>SELinuxMount</code> and <code>SELinuxChangePolicy</code><a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#selinuxmount-and-selinuxchangepolicy" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In Kubernetes v1.37, <code>SELinuxMount</code> and <code>SELinuxChangePolicy</code> flags reach Stable and are enabled by default: this means that
volumes get mounted with <code>-o context=&lt;label&gt;</code> (the MountOption default) instead of being recursively relabeled, but only when
the volume's CSI driver opts in via <code>.spec.seLinuxMount: true</code> for the CSIDriver object.</p>
<p>A mount can only carry one SELinux context, so <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/1710/#story-3-cluster-upgrade">Pods with different SELinux labels sharing a volume on the same node, which
used to coexist under recursive relabeling, can now fail to start</a>.
To retain the old behavior for a workload, it is advised to set the <code>.spec.seLinuxChangePolicy</code> to <code>Recursive</code> on a Pod.</p>
<p>This behavior itself also isn't locked until v1.38, so disabling it cluster-wide remains an option for one more release.</p>
<p>Clusters without SELinux enabled see no effect at all. To learn more, check <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/04/22/breaking-changes-in-selinux-volume-labeling/">SELinux Volume Label Changes goes GA (and likely
implications in v1.37)</a>.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/1710/">KEP #1710</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/storage/">SIG Storage</a>.</p>
<h3 id="dra-features-graduating-to-stable">DRA features graduating to Stable<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-features-graduating-to-stable" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><h4 id="dra-resourceclaim-status-with-possible-standardized-network-interface-data">DRA: ResourceClaim status with possible standardized network interface data<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-resourceclaim-status-with-possible-standardized-network-interface-data" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>The ResourceClaim <code>.status.devices</code> reaches Stable in Kubernetes v1.37, which allows drivers to report device-specific device
status data for each allocated device in a resource claim. This makes it easier to see how a device is configured,
troubleshoot problems, and use the device with other services.</p>
<p>This is particularly useful for network devices; before this field was added, if a Pod requested a network device via DRA,
there was no way for any other component in the system to learn the IP address that was assigned to that network device.
The new status field provides a standardized way for the DRA driver to export that information to components that need it,
making DRA fully usable for attaching secondary network interfaces to Pods.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4817/">KEP #4817</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a> and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/network/">SIG Network</a>.</p>
<h4 id="dra-handle-extended-resource-requests-via-dra-driver">DRA: handle extended resource requests via DRA Driver<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-handle-extended-resource-requests-via-dra-driver" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>DRA Extended Resource support reaches Stable in Kubernetes v1.37. This feature allows DRA drivers to fulfill requests made
through the traditional <em>extended resource</em> mechanism, such as <code>abc.example/gpu: 3</code> in a Pod spec, without requiring a
separate <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/">device plugin</a>.</p>
<p>With this mechanism, an extended resource name can be assigned directly to a DeviceClass. Pods requesting that resource can then have a device allocated through DRA without needing to define a ResourceClaim in the workload.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5004/">KEP #5004</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h4 id="dra-device-taints-and-tolerations">DRA: device taints and tolerations<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-device-taints-and-tolerations" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Support for <em>taints and tolerations</em> for physical devices managed through DRA is now Stable in Kubernetes v1.37. By default, any available device can be considered for scheduling. This enhancement provides greater control over device scheduling by allowing DRA drivers to mark specific devices as tainted, preventing them from being selected for workloads. Alternatively, cluster administrators can create a DeviceTaintRule to taint devices based on specific selection criteria, such as all devices managed by a particular driver.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5055/">KEP #5055</a>
led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h4 id="dra-standard-numanode-device-attribute">DRA: standard numaNode device attribute<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-standard-numanode-device-attribute" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Kubernetes v1.37 defines a new standard <em>NUMA node device attribute</em>. It standardizes
<code>resource.kubernetes.io/numaNode</code> as a shared attribute name for device NUMA node information, allowing devices managed by
different DRA drivers to be compared based on the same NUMA node. This avoids each driver defining its own attribute name and
provides a consistent way to identify NUMA placement across devices. The enhancement lands directly as Stable because it is a
naming and registration KEP with no feature gate or in-tree behavior changes.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6072/">KEP #6072</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h3 id="node-declared-features">Node declared features<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#node-declared-features" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><em>Node declared features</em> graduate to Stable in Kubernetes v1.37, providing a framework to declare the availability of specific, feature-gated Kubernetes features for Nodes.
This would then be used by control plane components (such as the <code>kube-scheduler</code>, admission controllers, or the API server itself) to manage version skew.</p>
<p>The feature introduces a new <code>.status.declaredFeatures</code> field for Nodes, which is used to declare a feature graduating
through the Alpha → Beta → Stable stages. The control plane can use this to adopt
the correct behavior even in a cluster running a mixture of different node versions.</p>
<p>Once features graduate to Stable and the control plane can assume all nodes support them across the supported version skew
window, nodes stop reporting them.</p>
<p>The <code>kubelet</code> determines its declared features when it starts, based only on feature gates and the node’s static
configuration (so any changes require a <code>kubelet</code> restart).</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5328/">KEP #5328</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h3 id="storage-version-migrator">Storage version migrator<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#storage-version-migrator" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 sees the <em>StorageVersionMigration API</em> (<code>storagemigration.k8s.io/v1</code>) graduate to Stable and become enabled by
default. It helps migrate existing resources, both built-in and custom, from an older storage version to the new storage
version after an API upgrade, such as when the preferred storage version changes from <code>v1beta1</code> to <code>v1</code>. It can also be used to rewrite existing
data after a change to encryption at rest, so that stale data is stored using the new encryption settings.</p>
<p>Historically, cluster administrators and CustomResourceDefinition authors had to use manual <code>kubectl get</code> or
<code>kubectl replace</code> scripts, or deploy the out-of-tree <code>kube-storage-version-migrator</code> component to rewrite existing resources. These
approaches were often tedious, error-prone, and difficult to monitor.</p>
<p>To start a storage version migration, users would need to create a declarative StorageVersionMigration object. The built-in
<code>StorageVersionMigrator</code> controller in the Kubernetes control plane watches for these objects and automatically migrates
existing resources to the default storage version for that API. Since StorageVersionMigration is a standard Kubernetes API,
CRD authors can trigger migrations as part of a CRD upgrade instead of managing the migration separately.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4192/">KEP #4192</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/api-machinery/">SIG API Machinery</a>.</p>
<h3 id="pod-certificates-and-clustertrustbundles">Stable: Pod certificates and Cluster Trust Bundles<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#pod-certificates-and-clustertrustbundles" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#pod-certificate-requests">Pod certificates</a> and the closely related <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#cluster-trust-bundles">ClusterTrustBundles</a>
both graduate to Stable in Kubernetes v1.37, providing first-class support for distributing private keys, X.509
certificates, and trust bundles to Pods.</p>
<p>To use this, the developer or administrator chooses a signer name and deploys a <em>signer controller</em> that
watches PodCertificateRequest objects, issues and refreshes certificates for eligible Pods, and maintains the corresponding ClusterTrustBundle objects containing the trust anchors needed to verify those certificates.
A workload then opts into this identity by defining a <code>podCertificate</code> projected volume with the chosen signer name. Workloads can also mount a ClusterTrustBundle projected volume to load the trust anchor information.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of two KEPs - <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4317/">KEP #4317</a> and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3257/">KEP #3257</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/auth/">SIG Auth</a>.</p>
<h2 id="features-graduating-to-beta">Features graduating to Beta<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#features-graduating-to-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="gang-scheduling-support-in-kubernetes">Gang scheduling support in Kubernetes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#gang-scheduling-support-in-kubernetes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>As Kubernetes becomes the de facto standard for managing AI/ML workloads at scale, scheduling workloads such as AI/ML training jobs and HPC simulations becomes more important than ever. However, scheduling becomes challenging because the default Kubernetes scheduler schedules Pods individually, which can result in some Pods being scheduled while others remain pending due to insufficient resources. This partial scheduling can lead to deadlocks and inefficient use of cluster resources.</p>
<p><em>Gang scheduling</em> graduates to Beta in Kubernetes v1.37, improving upon native support for gang scheduling through the Workload API and PodGroup concept.
This feature implements an <em>all-or-nothing</em> scheduling strategy, ensuring that a defined group of Pods is scheduled only when the cluster has sufficient resources to accommodate the entire group. The Beta graduation of this enhancement also introduces workload-aware preemption to avoid premature preemptions that do not help a workload make progress, along with PodGroup queueing to better coordinate competing workloads.</p>
<p>Importantly, it addresses livelock scenarios that can occur when multiple workloads are being scheduled simultaneously by the <code>kube-scheduler</code>, preventing them from repeatedly interfering with one another without making progress.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4671/">KEP #4671</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="native-histogram-support-for-kubernetes-metrics">Native histogram support for Kubernetes metrics<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#native-histogram-support-for-kubernetes-metrics" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes exposes hundreds of histogram metrics in <a href="https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/exposition_formats/">Prometheus format</a> across its control plane components, which are essential to
monitor cluster health and debug performance issues. However, classical Prometheus histograms relied on static, pre-defined
buckets that forced a compromise between data accuracy and memory usage. To mitigate this, Prometheus introduced <em>native
histograms</em> that use dynamic exponential bucket boundaries instead of fixed boundaries, providing significant storage efficiency,
improved query performance, and finer-grained visibility into distributions while maintaining full backward compatibility
with existing monitoring infrastructure.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 graduates native histogram support for Kubernetes metrics to Beta. Building on the Alpha implementation,
which introduced the <code>NativeHistograms</code> feature gate, the Beta phase improves the implementation and rollout experience. When
enabled, Kubernetes components expose histograms in both classic and native formats when the requested scrape protocol supports Native
Histograms, (specifically <code>PrometheusProto</code>), allowing existing dashboards and alerts to continue working while users migrate at
their own pace. The implementation also refactored histograms created in <code>init()</code> functions to use lazy initialization,
ensuring native histogram options are correctly applied after feature gates are parsed. These changes provide a more reliable
implementation while retaining safe rollout and rollback through the feature gate or Prometheus-side configuration for
Prometheus 3.x users.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5808/">KEP #5808</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/instrumentation/">SIG Instrumentation</a>.</p>
<h3 id="was-features-graduating-to-beta">WAS: Features graduating to Beta<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#was-features-graduating-to-beta" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><h4 id="workload-aware-preemption">Workload-aware preemption<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#workload-aware-preemption" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Kubernetes traditionally performs preemption at the Pod level, which can be inefficient for workloads made up of multiple
tightly coupled Pods. In Kubernetes v1.37, workload-aware preemption graduates to Beta, allowing the scheduler to consider a
PodGroup when making preemption decisions. This helps the scheduler consider the workload as a whole when preempting lower
priority workloads, reducing cases where individual Pods are disrupted without providing enough capacity for the workload to
make progress.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5710/">KEP #5710</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h4 id="dra-resourceclaim-support-for-workloads">DRA: ResourceClaim support for workloads<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-resourceclaim-support-for-workloads" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) allows Pods to request specialized resources through ResourceClaims. In Kubernetes v1.37,
DRA ResourceClaims support for workloads graduates to Beta, allowing Workload and PodGroup APIs to associate
ResourceClaims and ResourceClaimTemplates with the groups of Pods. This allows ResourceClaims to be shared across a
workload rather than reserved individually for each Pod, while ResourceClaimTemplates can create claims for PodGroups
automatically.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5729/">KEP #5729</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="cadvisor-less-cri-full-stats">cAdvisor-less, CRI-full container and Pod stats<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#cadvisor-less-cri-full-stats" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>kubelet</code> has historically obtained container and Pod statistics from <code>cAdvisor</code>, while the Container Runtime
Interface (CRI) exposes statistics of its own. Having two sources for the same metrics makes it harder to tell where a
particular value came from.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes v1.37, the cAdvisor-less, CRI-full Container and Pod Stats enhancement graduates to Beta. The enhancement
expands the CRI to provide the container and pod statistics needed by Kubernetes, allowing the <code>kubelet</code> to get these metrics
directly from the container runtime instead of relying on <code>cAdvisor</code> for them.</p>
<p>This moves container and pod metrics toward a single source of truth, while reducing duplicated metric collection and
simplifying how the <code>kubelet</code> gathers and exposes these statistics.</p>
<p>This feature is Beta in v1.37 but <strong>off</strong> by default; enable the <code>PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI</code> feature gate to try it.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/2371/">KEP #2371</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h3 id="support-memory-qos-with-cgroups-v2">Support memory QoS with cgroups v2<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#support-memory-qos-with-cgroups-v2" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes is improving its quality of service mechanisms to cover memory protection and isolation for Kubernetes workloads. For nodes running Linux, the <em>memory
QoS</em> feature uses memory requests and limits to configure cgroup controls that can protect requested memory from reclamation and throttle memory usage before
workloads reach their hard limits. This can help reduce the impact of memory pressure on memory-sensitive workloads and improve node stability.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes v1.37, memory QoS support is graduating to Beta. The feature uses cgroups v2 memory controls such as <code>memory.min</code>,
<code>memory.low</code> and <code>memory.high</code> to provide different levels of memory protection and throttling. For example, memory requests
can be used to protect memory from reclamation, while <code>memory.high</code> can be used to throttle workloads that exceed their
configured threshold.</p>
<p>The <code>MemoryQoS</code> feature gate is enabled by default in v1.37. Cluster operators can control memory protection through the <code>kubelet</code>’s
<code>memoryReservationPolicy</code> setting and configure memory throttling with <code>memoryThrottlingFactor</code>. The defaults are designed to
avoid introducing unexpected memory throttling for existing workloads when upgrading to v1.37, while allowing operators to
opt into the additional memory protection capabilities.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/2570/">KEP #2570</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h3 id="pod-level-resource-managers">Pod-level resource managers<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#pod-level-resource-managers" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In Kubernetes v1.37, <em>Pod-level resource managers</em> graduate to Beta behind the <code>PodLevelResourceManagers</code> feature gate,</p>
<p>which stays <strong>disabled by default</strong>. Enabling it allows the topology, CPU, and memory resource</p>
<p>managers to use the resources defined for an entire Pod when making</p>
<p>allocation and NUMA alignment decisions. This makes it possible to manage a Pod as a single resource unit while still
supporting different resource requirements between the containers within it.</p>
<p>With pod-level resource management, a Pod can reserve a NUMA-aligned pool of CPU and memory based on its overall resource budget. Containers that require dedicated resources can receive exclusive portions of that pool, while other containers, such as sidecars or supporting workloads, can share the remaining resources. This is particularly useful for performance-sensitive workloads such as AI/ML and high-performance computing, where keeping resources close to each other on the same NUMA node can improve performance without requiring every container in the Pod to have dedicated resources.</p>
<p>The feature also supports a container scope, where containers can continue to receive independent NUMA-aligned allocations. This provides more flexibility for workloads that combine a performance-sensitive container with other containers that have different resource requirements.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5526/">KEP #5526</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h3 id="watch-based-route-controller-reconciliation">Watch-based route controller reconciliation<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#watch-based-route-controller-reconciliation" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The route controller in the cloud-controller-manager library previously reconciled routes on a fixed interval, by default every 10 seconds. This could result in unnecessary requests to infrastructure providers, even when nothing had changed and could also delay route updates when a new Node is added.</p>
<p><em>Watch-based route controller reconciliation</em> graduated to beta in Kubernetes v1.37. This release also adds observability for this work: the route controller's Alpha <code>route_sync_total</code> metric gains two labels, <code>trigger</code> (<code>periodic</code> or <code>node_change</code>) and <code>outcome</code> (<code>changed</code>, <code>noop</code>, or <code>error</code>), so operators can see whether periodic reconciliation is actually correcting route drift or just running as a no-op, and can track failed reconciles.</p>
<p>With watch-based route controller reconciliation, the route controller can reconcile routes from watch events instead of waiting for the next fixed interval: a reconciliation can start as soon as relevant Node changes occur, such as a Node being added or removed or when its addresses or assigned Pod CIDRs change. A less frequent periodic reconciliation still runs to catch outdated routes and keep the state consistent. This behavior sits behind the <code>CloudControllerManagerWatchBasedRoutesReconciliation</code> feature gate and is disabled by default, so the transition has not changed default behavior.</p>
<p>This reduces unnecessary requests to infrastructure providers while allowing routes for newly added Nodes to be reconciled sooner. The change does not alter the route reconciliation logic itself; it changes when reconciliation is triggered.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5237/">KEP #5237</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/cloud-provider/">SIG Cloud Provider</a>.</p>
<h3 id="storage-capacity-scoring-of-nodes">Storage capacity scoring of Nodes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#storage-capacity-scoring-of-nodes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>VolumeBinding</code> scheduler plugin has always been able to score nodes for statically bound PVs based on free capacity, but that scoring never extended to dynamic provisioning.</p>
<p>When a CSI driver provisions a new volume on demand, the scheduler had no way to prefer a node with more or less free space.</p>
<p>This was a gap for local storage, as an admin might want pods landing on the node with the most free capacity to leave room for a later volume expansion or on the node with the least (but still sufficient) free capacity to bin-pack workloads and cut down on the number of nodes a cloud cluster needs to run.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 graduates storage capacity scoring for dynamic provisioning to Beta behind the <code>StorageCapacityScoring</code>
feature gate. First introduced in Alpha in v1.33, this feature consolidates (and deprecates) the older
<code>VolumeCapacityPriority</code> gate from <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/1845/">KEP #1845</a>. When enabled, the
VolumeBinding plugin's <code>Score</code> extension point reads <code>CSIStorageCapacity</code> objects published by a driver's external
provisioner sidecar and scores nodes for dynamic provisioning the same way it already does for static bindings. Admins choose
the strategy via the <code>Shape</code> setting in <code>VolumeBindingArgs</code>, defaulting to &quot;prefer the node with the maximum allocatable&quot; so
there is room for expansion later.</p>
<p>The feature depends solely on the <code>StorageCapacityScoring</code> gate: scoring for statically
bound PVs runs as soon as it's enabled, independent of any CSI driver. A driver only needs <code>StorageCapacity: true</code> on its
<code>CSIDriver</code> object so that its dynamically-provisioned volumes also get capacity-aware scoring. The feature is fully
reversible, and disabling the gate stops all VolumeBinding capacity scoring — static and dynamic alike — without affecting
already scheduled pods.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4049/">KEP #4049</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/storage/">SIG Storage</a>.</p>
<h3 id="integrate-csi-volume-attach-limits-with-cluster-autoscaler">Integrate CSI volume attach limits with Cluster Autoscaler<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#integrate-csi-volume-attach-limits-with-cluster-autoscaler" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 improves Cluster Autoscaler's integration with CSI volume attach limits, so that when it creates new
nodes for pending Pods, Cluster Autoscaler can more accurately determine how many new nodes are required to attach all
pending Pods that use CSI volumes. Cluster Autoscaler already had visibility into CSI volume attach limits for existing
nodes, but not for the nodes it was about to create, which means it could undershoot scale-ups and leave volume-backed
Pods pending even after adding capacity. The problem compounds on the scheduling side: the <code>NodeVolumeLimits</code> plugin treats a node with no published CSI driver info as having no limits at all, so a freshly created node that hasn't yet reported its <code>CSINode</code> object can get crowded with more volume-backed pods than it can actually mount, which is a race condition that, until now, cluster admins had no way to close.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 graduates CSI-aware autoscaling to Beta behind the <code>VolumeLimitScaling</code> feature gate, first introduced in Alpha in v1.35. Cluster autoscaler now runs its scale-up simulations against templated <code>CSINode</code> objects, so it correctly accounts for attach limits whether it's scaling an existing node group or scaling one from zero. On the scheduler side, admins can opt in per <code>CSIDriver</code>, via a new <code>PreventPodSchedulingIfMissing</code> field, to block pod placement on nodes that haven't reported their driver yet, with dedicated <code>CSIDriverMissingOnNode</code> and <code>CSINodeMissing</code> errors making those scheduling failures easier to debug. The Beta phase adds e2e coverage for scale-down behavior and CSI opt-in scenarios, and updates the <code>failed_scale_ups_total</code> and <code>scaled_up_nodes_total</code> metrics to include CSI driver information. Both the autoscaler and scheduler changes stay strictly opt-in: disabling the feature gate restores today's default of unlimited pod placement on nodes without <code>CSINode</code> data, so distros and admins running autoscalers that aren't CSI-aware yet (e.g. Karpenter) aren't forced into the new behavior.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5030/">KEP #5030</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/autoscaling/">SIG Autoscaling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="report-last-used-time-on-a-pvc">Report last used time on a PVC<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#report-last-used-time-on-a-pvc" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><code>PersistentVolumeClaims</code> tend to outlive the workloads that created them. When an app gets deleted or migrated, its PVC remains behind, consuming storage and increasing costs.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 graduates PVC &quot;last used&quot; tracking to Beta behind the <code>PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime</code> feature gate, which shipped disabled by default in Alpha (v1.36) and is now enabled by default. The feature adds a new <code>Unused</code> condition to <code>PersistentVolumeClaimStatus</code>, managed by the existing PVC protection controller: <code>Status=True (Reason=NoPodsUsingPVC)</code> once the last non-terminal Pod referencing the PVC goes away, and back to <code>Status=False (Reason=PodUsingPVC)</code> as soon as a Pod starts referencing it again. The condition's <code>lastTransitionTime</code> doubles as an &quot;unused since&quot; timestamp, so admins can query how long a PVC has actually been idle without Kubernetes tracking which Pod used it last or making any deletion decision itself; that's left entirely to the admin. One thing worth noting is that the timestamp reflects when the controller observed no Pods using the PVC, not the exact moment the volume unmounted at the infrastructure level, so the reported idle time may run a little short of the true figure but should never overstate it.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5541/">KEP #5541</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/storage/">SIG Storage</a>.</p>
<h3 id="etcd-rangestream-support">etcd RangeStream support<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#etcd-rangestream-support" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><code>etcd</code>'s unary <code>Range</code> RPC builds an entire response in memory before sending it back, which becomes a problem at scale. On a large list, say kube-apiserver's watch cache warming up on a big cluster, the raw key-value slice, its serialized protobuf form, and the gRPC send buffer all have to coexist in memory at once, and the resulting spikes ripple through kube-apiserver too. Pagination doesn't really fix the underlying cost either because each paginated page still walks the entire B-tree index to recompute the total result count, turning what should be an <code>O(limit)</code> operation into an <code>O(total_keys)</code> one on every single page.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 ships <code>etcd</code> <code>RangeStream</code> support directly at Beta, behind the <code>EtcdRangeStream</code> feature gate (<code>kube-apiserver</code> only, <strong>on</strong> by default).
This release adds a new server-streaming <code>RangeStream</code> RPC that reuses the existing <code>RangeRequest</code> but returns chunks instead of one buffered blob: the server paginates internally with adaptive chunk sizing (each chunk's target size adjusts based on <code>MaxRequestBytes</code> and the value sizes observed so far), pins a single MVCC revision so the merged stream stays snapshot-consistent, and derives the total key count from the running tally it builds while streaming, rather than a separate index walk.
<code>kube-apiserver</code>'s watch cache initialization is the primary consumer, and it now decodes each chunk into synthetic <em>created</em> events inline as they arrive instead of assembling the full list in memory first, with the same treatment applied to direct <code>GetList</code> calls when <code>WatchList</code> is disabled.</p>
<p>The feature requires <code>etcd</code> 3.7+; against older <code>etcd</code>, <code>kube-apiserver</code> detects the Unimplemented response and falls back to unary <code>Range</code> automatically, with zero behavior change. If the pinned revision gets compacted mid-stream, <code>kube-apiserver</code> treats it the same as any other watch cache init failure and retries, which is no worse than the compaction races a paginated List call can already hit today. Beta graduation criteria include a scalability test measuring large-list latency on a 5000-node cluster, and <code>etcdctl get --stream</code> ships alongside it for anyone who wants to poke at the new RPC directly.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5966/">KEP #5966</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/etcd/">SIG etcd</a>.</p>
<h3 id="concurrent-watch-object-decode">Concurrent watch object decode<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#concurrent-watch-object-decode" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><code>kube-apiserver</code> decodes and transforms every watch event from <code>etcd</code> one at a time on a single goroutine, so one slow per-event transform, most notably a CRD conversion webhook call, blocks every event queued behind it. That's mostly a nuisance for built-in resources, but for a CRD whose served version differs from its stored version, converting a cold cache serially can take minutes. If that exceeds <code>etcd</code>'s default 5-minute compaction interval, the revision the cache started reading from gets compacted before initialization finishes, the watch can't resume, and init just restarts and never converges for a large enough resource, with every client trying to list or watch it getting errors in the meantime.</p>
<p>The <code>ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode</code> gate has actually been in Beta, off by default, since v1.31, and Kubernetes v1.37 flips it on by default. Enabling it moves the decode/transform step onto a bounded pool of worker goroutines (10 by default, tuned from a sweep that showed gains flattening out around 8–12) instead of a single one, with a collector reassembling events back into their original order before delivery, so event ordering is preserved exactly. In benchmarks over 150k pods, concurrent decode alone cuts cache initialization about 40%, and about 55% combined with the new <code>EtcdRangeStream</code> feature also landing this release (see KEP 5966). The main tradeoff to watch is conversion webhook load. With the feature on, up to 10 conversions can now run concurrently against a webhook during cache init instead of one at a time. The total call volume is unchanged, only how many run at once, so this mainly matters for webhooks that cap their own concurrency below 10.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6178/">KEP #6178</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/api-machinery/">SIG API Machinery</a>.</p>
<h3 id="stale-controller-mitigation">Stale controller mitigation<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#stale-controller-mitigation" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Every controller in <code>kube-controller-manager</code> works off a local cache built from watching the <code>kube-apiserver</code>, and that watch
stream is only eventually consistent. A change can show up in milliseconds, or it can take seconds or even minutes under
load. Today operators have no visibility into that lag and no way to tell a normal delay from a controller that's fallen
dangerously out of sync, so a controller can keep reconciling against a view of the world that's already stale.</p>
<p>Stale controller mitigation has been Beta since v1.36, enabled by default per controller behind a <code>StaleControllerConsistency&lt;Controller&gt;</code>
feature gate; Kubernetes v1.37 extends it to the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller and adds the circuit-breaking variant and
extra metrics described below. The core mechanism
is a <em>read your writes</em> guarantee: client-go's <code>ResourceEventHandlerFuncs</code> gets a new <code>BookmarkFunc</code> callback so a controller
can reliably track the resource version of objects it cares about, even through edge cases the existing add/update/delete
callbacks miss. A controller records the resource version of its own writes and, on its next reconcile, skips and requeues
until its informer cache has actually caught up to that write. The DaemonSet controller is a good example of this. It tracks
DaemonSet → Pod resource versions so it won't re-reconcile against its own stale pod cache. A second, circuit-breaking
variant targets latency-sensitive controllers like node-lifecycle, which can otherwise read a stale node lease from cache and
wrongly decide it's expired; instead, it does a live GET on the disruptive decision and marks its cache &quot;not ready&quot; until
it's caught up, rather than acting on a stale read. <code>StaleControllerConsistency</code> gates the mitigation itself (scoped
initially to controllers KCM has flagged as high-scale), <code>MonitorInformerStaleness</code> is a separate, observation-only gate that
polls the apiserver directly every 5 seconds purely to surface how far behind an informer's cache actually is, and
<code>AtomicFIFO</code> / <code>UnlockWhileProcessingFIFO</code> are the underlying client-go workqueue plumbing the mitigation depends on. None of
this changes default reconciler behavior; a paused-and-requeued controller can look stuck when it's really just waiting on
its cache, and it rolls back cleanly since nothing it does is irreversible.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5647">KEP #5647</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/api-machinery/">SIG API Machinery</a>.</p>
<h3 id="manifest-based-admission-control-config">Manifest-based admission control config<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#manifest-based-admission-control-config" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In Kubernetes, admission control is responsible for enforcing policies on resources before they are accepted by the API
server. However, admission webhooks and policies configured through the Kubernetes API are dependent on the API server and
etcd during cluster startup and cannot protect the admission configuration resources themselves. This creates a gap during
cluster bootstrap and allows critical admission policies to be modified or removed by users with sufficient privileged access.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes v1.37, <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/manifest-admission-control/">manifest-based admission control</a> configuration graduates to Beta, allowing admission webhooks and CEL-based</p>
<p>policies to be loaded from manifest files on disk and enforced from API server startup. Because the configuration is managed
independently of the Kubernetes API, it can also protect API-based admission resources from modification. Manifest files are
watched for changes and valid updates are reloaded automatically, while invalid updates leave the previously loaded
configuration in place.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5793/">KEP #5793</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/api-machinery/">SIG API Machinery</a></p>
<h3 id="improved-handling-for-undecryptable-resources">Improved handling for undecryptable resources<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#improved-handling-for-undecryptable-resources" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes stores resources in etcd, where encryption at rest can be used to protect sensitive data. However, when encrypted
resources can no longer be decrypted, for example because the encryption key is unavailable, the API server cannot read or
manage those resources normally. This can leave resources in the cluster that cannot be accessed through the Kubernetes API,
requiring administrators to manually modify the underlying etcd data to recover them.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 includes Beta support for cluster administrators to identify and remove resources that cannot be decrypted by the API server.</p>
<p>Previously Alpha, and introduced in Kubernetes v1.32, this support allows problem API resources to be removed via</p>
<p>the Kubernetes API rather than directly manipulating the etcd file. This feature also provides safeguards for administrators
to verify affected resources before deletion.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3926/">KEP #3926</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/auth/">SIG Auth</a>.</p>
<h2 id="new-features-in-alpha">New features in Alpha<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#new-features-in-alpha" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="new-recreate-strategy-for-statefulset-rollouts">New <code>Recreate</code> strategy for StatefulSet rollouts<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#new-recreate-strategy-for-statefulset-rollouts" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 introduces the <code>Recreate</code> strategy for StatefulSet rollouts. The StatefulSet API previously only offered two update
strategies: OnDelete (manual) and RollingUpdate (automatic, default). Similar to Deployments, the <code>Recreate</code> update strategy
deletes all of the StatefulSet's Pods before creating new Pods that reflect modifications made to a StatefulSet's
<code>.spec.template</code>. Using this strategy requires the <code>StatefulSetRecreateStrategy</code> <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/#StatefulSetRecreateStrategy">feature gate</a> to be enabled.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3541/">KEP #3541</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/apps/">SIG Apps</a>.</p>
<h3 id="dra-alpha-features-to-look-out-for">DRA: Alpha features to look out for<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-alpha-features-to-look-out-for" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><h4 id="dra-node-allocatable-resource-request">DRA: Node allocatable resource request<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-node-allocatable-resource-request" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Kubernetes v1.37 improves Alpha support for managing node resources such as CPU, memory, and huge pages through DRA. It
unifies standard and DRA resource accounting, helping prevent the same node capacity from being counted twice.</p>
<p>This update introduces distinct API fields for <code>mapping</code> (for devices directly modeling core resources, like CPU/memory DRA drivers) and <code>overhead</code> (like auxiliary host memory for accelerator devices). The kubelet now enforces these allocations across pod and container cgroups, integrates them with Memory QoS, OOM score calculations, and in-place pod resizing.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5517/">KEP #5517</a>,
led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a> with participation from <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h4 id="dra-derived-attributes">DRA: derived attributes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-derived-attributes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Kubernetes v1.37 introduces Alpha support for <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/resource-management/dynamic-resource-allocation/dra-api/#derived-attributes">derived attributes in DRA</a>. Workloads can use CEL expressions to create virtual
attributes from device information and use them when selecting related devices.</p>
<p>This makes it easier to co-locate devices such as GPUs and network interfaces, even when their drivers use different
attribute names or formats. For example, a workload can derive a shared NUMA identifier and use it to select devices with
matching topology.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6080/">KEP #6080</a>, led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a> with participation from <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/network/">SIG Network</a>.</p>
<h4 id="dra-device-compatibility-groups">DRA: device compatibility groups<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dra-device-compatibility-groups" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>DRA can be used to manage devices that support different partitioning or virtualization schemes. However, some of these
configurations cannot be used together on the same physical device, such as MIG and vGPU on a GPU. Previously, these
incompatibilities could only be detected during device preparation, after the scheduler had already made its decision.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes v1.37, DRA adds device compatibility groups, allowing resource drivers to describe which devices can be
allocated together. The scheduler can use this information when making allocation decisions, preventing incomplete devices
from being assigned together and avoiding Pod startup failures caused by incomplete device configurations.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5963/">KEP #5963</a>, led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="scheduler-preemption-in-place-pod-resize">Scheduler preemption for in-place Pod resize<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#scheduler-preemption-in-place-pod-resize" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 introduces <em>scheduler preemption for in-place pod resize</em>, behind the (opt-in, Alpha) <code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption</code> feature gate. This change addresses an important feature gap that remained after the core <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-resize-inplace">in-place Pod vertical scaling</a> feature graduated to Stable: if a running pod requested additional resources that exceeded the node's available capacity, <code>kubelet</code> marked the
request as <code>Deferred</code>, leaving the pod waiting until sufficient resources became available on the node. With this
enhancement, the Kubernetes control plane can actively free up capacity on a fully-utilized node and preempt lower-priority
workloads, enabling the pending in-place resizes of critical, higher-priority applications to succeed.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5836/">KEP #5836</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="dynamic-resize-of-memory-backed-volumes">Dynamic resize of memory-backed volumes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dynamic-resize-of-memory-backed-volumes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Also building upon in-place Pod vertical scaling, the Alpha <em>in-place scaling for memory backed volumes</em> feature extends the pod</p>
<p><code>/resize</code> subresource, which previously only enabled dynamic CPU and memory adjustments without restarting containers, to
support updating the <code>sizeLimit</code> of memory-backed (medium: Memory) <code>emptyDir</code> volumes on running pods. When a volume's <code>sizeLimit</code>
is explicitly adjusted via the /resize subresource, Kubelet dynamically updates the underlying tmpfs mount without container
disruption while safely preventing out-of-memory errors or false-positive eviction triggers. This is particularly useful for
stateful and memory-intensive workloads that rely on in-memory ephemeral storage, allowing them to dynamically scale storage
limits alongside container memory capacity without incurring Pod restarts or application downtime.</p>
<p>This is an opt-in, off-by-default Alpha feature. To try it out, enable the</p>
<p><code>InPlacePodVerticalScalingMemoryBackedVolumes</code> feature gate.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6030/">KEP #6030</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a> and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/storage/">SIG Storage</a>.</p>
<h3 id="specialized-lifecycle-management-for-nodes">Specialized lifecycle management for Nodes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#specialized-lifecycle-management-for-nodes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Several Kubernetes components need to understand a Node's lifecycle state, and today each one infers it from a different mix
of Node readiness, taints, Pod state, labels, annotations, and provider APIs. This enhancement introduces well-known
lifecycle conditions on Nodes, giving administrators a single Kubernetes-owned place to publish lifecycle state that core
controllers and ecosystem tooling can consume. These new Node Conditions are: <code>DrainInProgress</code>, <code>Drained</code>, <code>MaintenancePlanned</code>, <code>MaintenanceInProgress</code>, and <code>GracefulNodeShutdownInProgress</code></p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5683/">KEP #5683</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/node/">SIG Node</a>.</p>
<h3 id="was-alpha-features-to-look-out-for">WAS: Alpha features to look out for<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#was-alpha-features-to-look-out-for" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><h4 id="compositepodgroup-api">CompositePodGroup API<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#compositepodgroup-api" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>While previous releases introduced support for gang scheduling of workloads with
