a flat structure, modern AI/ML workloads are complex and have more sophisticated
scheduling requirements. In Kubernetes v1.37, the new Alpha <code>CompositePodGroup</code>
API allows Kubernetes to describe complex workloads as a hierarchy of groups
instead of a flat set of Pods. This enables multi-level gang scheduling,
workload-aware preemption and topology-aware scheduling.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6012/">KEP #6012</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a></p>
<h4 id="workload-aware-scheduling-controller-apis">Workload Aware Scheduling Controller APIs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#workload-aware-scheduling-controller-apis" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>As an Alpha feature Kubernetes v1.37 provides a common framework for integrating workload controllers (such as JobSet, TrainJob, LWS, and RayJob, along with core workloads such as <code>Job</code>) with <em>Workload-aware Scheduling</em> (WAS).</p>
<p>The framework provides reusable <code>scheduling.k8s.io</code> API primitives, such as <em>topology constraints</em> and <em>disruption policies</em>,
along with shared libraries that handle the creation of scheduling resources. This allows controllers to expose WAS features
natively within their APIs in a consistent way without implementing the same scheduling logic separately.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6089/">KEP #6089</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h4 id="workload-apis-job-controller">Integrate workload APIs with the Job controller<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#workload-apis-job-controller" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Initially introduced in Kubernetes v1.36 with limited functionality, this feature builds on top of the <a href="#workload-aware-scheduling-controller-apis">Workload Aware Scheduling Controller APIs</a> adding a new user-facing <code>spec.scheduling</code> field to the <code>batch/v1</code> Job in Kubernetes v1.37, allowing users
to explicitly configure scheduling policies, topology constraints, disruption modes, and resource claims. If
<code>spec.scheduling</code> is omitted, the Job defaults to Basic scheduling, preserving existing behavior while still creating a Basic
Workload/PodGroup for workload-aware scheduling, without enforcing a minCount gate. Users can explicitly opt into Gang
scheduling, where <code>minCount</code> defaults to the Job’s parallelism, and the controller uses the shared <code>workloadbuilder</code> library
to translate the scheduling configuration into the corresponding Workload and PodGroup objects instead of implementing custom
translation logic.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5547/">KEP #5547</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/scheduling/">SIG Scheduling</a>.</p>
<h3 id="localhost-nodeport-userspace-proxy-for-nftables">localhost NodePort userspace proxy for <code>nftables</code><a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#localhost-nodeport-userspace-proxy-for-nftables" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Kubernetes v1.37 adds an opt-in userspace proxy to the <code>nftables</code> <code>kube-proxy</code> backend, allowing NodePort services to be accessed
through <code>localhost</code> over IPv4 and IPv6. This closes a gap between the <code>nftables</code> and <code>iptables</code> backends, as <code>nftables</code> could not
previously serve localhost NodePorts.</p>
<p>The proxy is enabled when <code>localhost</code> or a loopback address is included in the <code>kube-proxy</code> <code>--nodeport-addresses</code>
configuration. This can be useful for workloads such as local container registries that rely on <code>localhost:&lt;NodePort&gt;</code>
connections. The existing behavior of the <code>iptables</code> and <code>ipvs</code> backends is unchanged.</p>
<p>This work was done as part of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/6032/">KEP #6032</a> led by <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/network/">SIG Network</a>.</p>
<h2 id="other-notable-changes">Other notable changes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#other-notable-changes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="maxunavailable-for-statefulsets-back-on-by-default"><code>maxUnavailable</code> for StatefulSets back on by default<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#maxunavailable-for-statefulsets-back-on-by-default" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>maxUnavailable</code> field for StatefulSets has been re-enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.37 (after a bug was observed
in v1.36).</p>
<p>The bug occurred where a faulty initial StatefulSet revision created a Pod that never became ready, and with
<code>MaxUnavailableStatefulSet</code> enabled, the StatefulSet controller failed to update that Pod to the newer, corrected
revision. When the bug triggered, the affected Pod could end up stuck in a CrashLoopBackOff state indefinitely (see <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137409">kubernetes#137409</a>).</p>
<h3 id="improved-nftables-performance">Improved <code>nftables</code> performance<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#improved-nftables-performance" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>kube-proxy now uses the kernel’s netlink interface for nftables rule operations, bypassing the <code>nft</code> command-line tool. This makes kube-proxy more efficient when inspecting and managing its nftables rules, improving rule-management performance.</p>
<h3 id="context-handling-and-contextual-logging-in-client-go">Context handling and contextual logging in client-go<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#context-handling-and-contextual-logging-in-client-go" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Support for context propagation and contextual logging in client-go is complete, with the exception of a small number of
authentication plugin log calls that still rely on the global klog logger because the underlying APIs do not support context
passing.</p>
<h2 id="graduations-deprecations-and-removals-in-v1-37">Graduations, deprecations, and removals in v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#graduations-deprecations-and-removals-in-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="graduations-to-stable">Graduations to Stable<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#graduations-to-stable" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>This lists all the features that graduated to Stable (also known as general availability). For a full list of updates
including new features and graduations from Alpha to Beta, see the release notes.</p>
<p>This release includes a total of 16 enhancements promoted to Stable:</p>

<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/1710/">Speed up recursive SELinux label change</a></li>

<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4680/">Add Resource Health Status to the Pod Status for Device Plugin and DRA</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5055/">DRA: device taints and tolerations</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5004/">DRA: Handle extended resource requests via DRA Driver</a></li>

</ul>
<h2 id="deprecations-removals-and-community-updates">Deprecations, removals and community updates<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#deprecations-removals-and-community-updates" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>As Kubernetes develops and matures, features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's
overall health.
See the Kubernetes <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/">deprecation and removal policy</a> for more details on this process.
Many of these deprecations and removals were announced in the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/07/31/kubernetes-v1-37-sneak-peek/">Deprecations and Removals blog</a></p>
<h3 id="deprecation-of-kube-dns">Deprecation of <code>kube-dns</code><a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#deprecation-of-kube-dns" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>CoreDNS has been the default cluster DNS add-on since Kubernetes v1.13, and <code>kube-dns</code> has not kept pace since then; features like EndpointSlices and dual-stack Services aren't available in it.</p>
<p>Kubernetes has already retired the kube-dns subproject and has split node-local-dns out into its own <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/node-local-dns">repository</a>, where it continues to be maintained and works with CoreDNS. It is expected that no new packages will be built for kube-dns after v1.40.</p>
<p>If you still run <code>kube-dns</code>, <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/coredns/">start planning to migrate your clusters to CoreDNS</a>.</p>
<h3 id="deprecating-kube-proxy-s-support-for-ipvs-mode">Deprecating <code>kube-proxy</code>'s support for <code>ipvs</code> mode<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#deprecating-kube-proxy-s-support-for-ipvs-mode" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><code>kube-proxy</code> support for <code>ipvs</code> mode was introduced in v1.8 to resolve <code>iptables</code> performance bottlenecks. However, since the
kernel <code>ipvs</code> API alone cannot fully implement Kubernetes Services, <code>ipvs</code> mode continues to use <code>iptables</code> underneath
(<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/3866-nftables-proxy/README.md#the-ipvs-mode-of-kube-proxy-will-not-save-us">KEP-3866, &quot;The ipvs mode of kube-proxy will not save us&quot;</a>).</p>
<p>Clusters running <code>kube-proxy</code> in <code>ipvs</code> mode (or mode: <code>ipvs</code> in KubeProxyConfiguration) now log a deprecation warning on startup. The deprecation timeline looks like this:</p>
<ul>
<li>By v1.40, <code>ipvs</code> mode for <code>kube-proxy</code> is expected to be disabled by default (still selectable via the feature gate)</li>
<li>By v1.43, support for <code>ipvs</code> mode would be removed entirely <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/5495-deprecate-ipvs-mode-in-kube-proxy/README.md#graduation-criteria">KEP #5495, Graduation Criteria</a>.
To confirm which mode you’re currently running, use:</li>
</ul>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o <span class="nv">jsonpath</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s1">&#39;{.data.config\.conf}&#39;</span> <span class="p">|</span> grep <span class="s1">&#39;mode:&#39;</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>To understand the rationale behind this deprecation, see <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5495/">KEP #5495</a>.</p>
<h3 id="kubectl-kubectl-run-filename-f-to-be-deprecated"><code>kubectl</code>: <code>kubectl run --filename/-f</code> to be deprecated<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kubectl-kubectl-run-filename-f-to-be-deprecated" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>--filename</code> (or <code>-f</code>) flag for <code>kubectl run</code> is being deprecated as the generated pod is always built purely from CLI arguments like <code>NAME</code> and <code>--image</code>.</p>
<p>See <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138671">kubernetes/kubernetes#138671</a> for the original issue and discussion.</p>
<h3 id="kubelet-static-pods-can-no-longer-reference-secrets-or-configmaps"><code>kubelet</code>: static Pods can no longer reference Secrets or ConfigMaps<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kubelet-static-pods-can-no-longer-reference-secrets-or-configmaps" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Static Pods were never meant to read API resources directly, since they aren't created through the API server — but a bug let them reference Secrets or ConfigMaps via fields like <code>configMapRef</code> or <code>secretRef</code>. That bug is now fixed: as of v1.37 these references are strictly prohibited, and the <code>PreventStaticPodAPIReferences</code> feature gate that previously let you opt out of the restriction has been removed.</p>
<p>See <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140226">kubernetes/kubernetes#140226</a> for the original issue and discussion.</p>
<h3 id="ongoing-major-change-future-removal-of-cgroup-v1-support">Ongoing major change: Future removal of cgroup v1 support<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#ongoing-major-change-future-removal-of-cgroup-v1-support" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>As modern Linux distributions and container runtimes use <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/cgroups/">cgroup v2</a> as the default,
support for the legacy cgroup v1 is officially being phased out. Since the v1.35 release, the <code>failCgroupV1</code> setting has
defaulted to true. Consequently, the <code>kubelet</code> will fail to initialize on any nodes that still rely on cgroup v1 unless an
explicit configuration override is applied.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">failCgroupV1</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="c"># temporary override</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Using this override should be considered a short-term fix. Advanced resource management capabilities, such as memory QoS and in-place scaling for memory-backed volumes, work only on cgroups v2. While the override remains available in Kubernetes
v1.37, users are encouraged to migrate to cgroups v2, as support for cgroups v1 is planned to be removed in a future release.</p>
<p>To learn more about this deprecation, refer to <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5573/">KEP #5573</a>.</p>
<h3 id="release-notes">Release notes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#release-notes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Check out the full details of the Kubernetes v1.37 release in our <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.37.md">release notes</a>.</p>
<h3 id="availability">Availability<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#availability" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://kubernetes.io/releases/1.37/">Kubernetes v1.37</a> is available for download from
the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/releases/download/">Kubernetes download page</a> or direct from on <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/releases/tag/v1.37.0">GitHub</a>.</p>
<p>To get started with Kubernetes, check out <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/">these tutorials</a> or run local Kubernetes clusters using <a href="https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/">minikube</a>.
You can also easily install v1.37 using <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/independent/create-cluster-kubeadm/">kubeadm</a>.</p>

Each release team is made up of dedicated community volunteers who work together to build the many pieces that make up the

<p>The Release Team's membership ranges from first-time shadows to returning team leads with experience forged over several

<h3 id="project-velocity">Project velocity<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#project-velocity" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The CNCF K8s <a href="https://k8s.devstats.cncf.io/d/11/companies-contributing-in-repository-groups?orgId=1&var-period=m&var-repogroup_name=All">DevStats</a> project aggregates a number of interesting data points related to the velocity of Kubernetes and various sub-projects.</p>
<p>This includes everything from individual contributions to the number of companies that are contributing and is an

<p>YAML has been the standard way to write Kubernetes manifests for years. Every example, tutorial, and configuration file you come across is written in it. The problem isn't that YAML is a bad format. It's that YAML gives you a lot of choices, and not all of them are equally good for writing Kubernetes manifests. Some features make files harder to read, some are easy to misuse and others can lead to surprising behavior.</p>
<p>The interesting part is that Kubernetes doesn't actually need most of those features. It only relies on a small subset of YAML. This led to a simple question: if Kubernetes only needs a small part of YAML, why not <em>standardize</em> on that part and avoid the rest? Instead of introducing a new configuration language, <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/community/tree/main/sig-cli">SIG CLI</a> introduced <strong>KYAML</strong>, a stricter, more consistent way to write YAML.</p>
<h2 id="what-is-kyaml">What is KYAML?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-is-kyaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><em><strong>KYAML is a strict subset (or &quot;dialect&quot;) of standard YAML, designed to be parseable by the existing ecosystem without any changes, as proposed in <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5295/">KEP 5295</a>.</strong></em> It does not introduce a new format or a new parser. It just narrows the scope of choices you make when writing YAML, so everyone ends up making the same ones.</p>
<p>Think of it less like a new language and more like an agreed-upon style. <em><strong>Everything valid in KYAML is valid YAML.</strong></em></p>
<h2 id="how-kyaml-solves-it">How KYAML solves it<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-kyaml-solves-it" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Standard YAML has a few well-known traps and JSON is not without its own.</p>
<p><strong>Whitespace sensitivity.</strong> Indentation defines structure in YAML, which means a wrongly indented file can remain syntactically valid while representing a different object than intended. This gets especially painful with templating tools like Helm, where you are manipulating indentation from outside the YAML context.</p>
<p><strong>Silent type coercion.</strong> String quoting is optional in YAML, which sounds convenient until it is not. Some values that look like strings get coerced into other types without warning. The classic example is the <a href="https://hitchdev.com/strictyaml/why/implicit-typing-removed/">&quot;Norway Bug&quot;</a>.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">country</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">NO</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>In standard YAML, <code>NO</code> is parsed as a boolean <code>false</code>, not the string <code>&quot;NO&quot;</code> and it has caught more than a few people off guard.</p>
<p><strong>JSON is not the answer either.</strong> It lacks comment support, is strict about trailing commas, and requires every key to be quoted, none of which makes for a good config writing experience.</p>
<p><em><strong>KYAML addresses all of these by making structure and types explicit:</strong></em></p>
<ul>
<li>Does not depend on whitespace for structure</li>
<li>Always quotes value strings so no silent type coercion</li>
<li>Always uses <code>{}</code> for maps and structs</li>
<li>Always uses <code>[]</code> for lists</li>
<li>Allows comments and trailing commas, unlike JSON</li>
<li>Includes a <code>---</code> header to distinguish it from JSON at a glance, since both start with <code>{</code></li>
</ul>
<p>YAML calls this <strong>flow style</strong>, as opposed to the conventional <strong>block style</strong> most people use. KYAML sits halfway between JSON and YAML, more explicit than default YAML, friendlier than JSON.</p>
<p>Here is the same Pod manifest written in both formats for comparison.</p>
<h3 id="standard-yaml">Standard YAML<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#standard-yaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">my-pod</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">labels</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">app</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">demo</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">nginx</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">image</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">nginx:1.20</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="kyaml">KYAML<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kyaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span>{<span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;v1&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;Pod&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span>{<span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;my-pod&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">labels</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span>{<span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">app</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;demo&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>}<span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>}<span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span>{<span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">containers</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span>{<span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;nginx&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">image</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">&#34;nginx:1.20&#34;</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>}<span class="p">],</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>}<span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span>}<span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Notice the double-quoted string values, the braces around every mapping, the brackets around the list and the trailing commas. The additional syntax makes the document structure explicit instead of relying on indentation.</p>
<h2 id="how-to-pretty-print-yaml-as-kyaml">How to pretty print YAML as KYAML<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-pretty-print-yaml-as-kyaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>There are different ways to get KYAML output.</p>
<h3 id="option-1-kubectl-o-kyaml">Option 1: kubectl -o kyaml<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#option-1-kubectl-o-kyaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Since Kubernetes 1.34, <code>kubectl</code> supports KYAML as a native output format.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Kubernetes 1.35+ (beta; feature enabled by default, still requires -o kyaml CLI param)</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get deployment my-app -o kyaml
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Kubernetes 1.34 (alpha, opt-in)</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nb">export</span> <span class="nv">KUBECTL_KYAML</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="nb">true</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get deployment my-app -o kyaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>To save the output to a file:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get deployment my-app -o kyaml &gt; my-app.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>There are currently no plans to make KYAML the default output format. If you prefer using KYAML by default, you can configure your preferred default with <code>kuberc</code>. For more details, see the <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/kuberc/">kuberc documentation</a>.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Kubernetes 1.36+</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl kuberc <span class="nb">set</span> --section defaults --command get --option <span class="nv">output</span><span class="o">=</span>kyaml
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Kubernetes 1.33–1.35 (alpha prefix still required)</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl alpha kuberc <span class="nb">set</span> --section defaults --command get --option <span class="nv">output</span><span class="o">=</span>kyaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="option-2-kubernetes-yamlfmt">Option 2: Kubernetes' yamlfmt<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#option-2-kubernetes-yamlfmt" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/yaml">sigs.k8s.io/yaml</a> ships a <code>yamlfmt</code> tool that can convert files to KYAML.</p>
<p>Install via Go:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">go install sigs.k8s.io/yaml/yamlfmt@latest
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Running it against a file prints the KYAML version to <strong>stdout</strong>. It also accepts a directory, in which case it converts and prints every file in that directory.
<em>So you'll need to redirect the output to a file (or files) if you want the conversion to stick.</em></p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">yamlfmt -o<span class="o">=</span>kyaml my-deployment.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>It can also show you a diff instead of a full conversion:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">yamlfmt -o<span class="o">=</span>kyaml -d my-deployment.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="option-3-google-s-yamlfmt">Option 3: Google's yamlfmt<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#option-3-google-s-yamlfmt" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>For converting existing files, Google's <code>yamlfmt</code> added a dedicated <a href="https://github.com/google/yamlfmt/blob/main/docs/config-file.md#kyaml-formatter"><code>kyaml</code> formatter</a> in v0.21.0.</p>
<p>Install via Go, or grab a binary from the <a href="https://github.com/google/yamlfmt/releases">releases page</a>:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">go install github.com/google/yamlfmt/cmd/yamlfmt@latest
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>It is also available as a <a href="https://github.com/google/yamlfmt/blob/main/docs/pre-commit.md">pre-commit hook</a> and as a <a href="https://github.com/google/yamlfmt#basic-usage">Docker image</a> for CI pipelines.</p>
<p>Add a <code>.yamlfmt</code> config to your project root:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">formatter</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kyaml</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Preview the output without modifying your file:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">yamlfmt -dry my-deployment.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>then apply:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">yamlfmt my-deployment.yaml
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>To convert an entire directory:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">yamlfmt ./k8s/
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>The <code>kyaml</code> formatter takes no additional configuration and does not share options with the default formatter so mixing them will cause an error.</p>
<p>For more on the available modes and flags, check the <a href="https://github.com/google/yamlfmt/blob/main/docs/command-usage.md">command usage docs</a>.</p>
<h2 id="is-kyaml-worth-adopting">Is KYAML worth adopting?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#is-kyaml-worth-adopting" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Every valid KYAML file is a valid YAML file. So whatever you write in KYAML, your existing tools, your <code>kubectl</code>, your CI pipelines, none of them need to change. You can even pass KYAML as input to any version of <code>kubectl</code>, not just 1.34+, because at the end of the day it is just YAML.</p>
<p>KYAML is not strictly necessary. You can keep writing block-style YAML and things will work. But it is a <em>deliberate choice</em> to make your configs less error-prone and more consistent especially across a team or a larger repo.</p>
<p><em>It is less of a migration and more of a better habit.</em></p></description></item><item><title>Gateway API v1.6: TCPRoute and UDPRoute Graduate to Standard</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/03/gateway-api-v1-6-release/</link><pubDate>Mon, 03 Aug 2026 08:00:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/03/gateway-api-v1-6-release/</guid><description>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/03/gateway-api-v1-6-release/gateway-api-logo.svg" alt="Gateway API logo"></p>
<p>The Kubernetes SIG Network community is thrilled to share the release of <strong>Gateway API v1.6.0</strong>, which was released on June 30th of this year!</p>
<p>Gateway API has become the standard for modern, role-oriented,
and expressive service networking in Kubernetes.
In previous releases, Gateway API established a production-grade foundation
for HTTP and TLS layer 7 traffic.
With version 1.6.0, Gateway API takes a major step forward by expanding
standard layer 4 protocol routing and introducing cleaner API boundaries for experimental innovation.</p>
<p>Here is a quick summary of what's new in Gateway API v1.6.0:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>TCPRoute and UDPRoute Graduate to Standard</strong>: Raw L4 TCP and UDP traffic routing reach GA stability in the <code>v1</code> API version.</li>
<li><strong>Experimental API Group Separation</strong>: Experimental resources transition to a distinct API group (<code>gateway.networking.x-k8s.io</code>) with an <code>X</code> prefix to make experimental vs. standard boundaries crystal clear.</li>
</ul>
<p>Let's dive into the details!</p>
<h2 id="tcproute-and-udproute-graduate-to-standard">TCPRoute and UDPRoute graduate to Standard<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#tcproute-and-udproute-graduate-to-standard" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Leads: <a href="https://github.com/youngnick">Nick Young</a>, <a href="https://github.com/rikatz">Ricardo Katz</a> and <a href="https://github.com/zac-nixon">Zac Nixon</a></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/geps/gep-2644/">GEP-2644 - TCPRoute</a></li>
<li><a href="https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/geps/gep-2645/">GEP-2645 - UDPRoute</a></li>
</ul>
<p>Until now, Gateway API only offered a stable routing model for HTTP and TLS traffic.
Workloads that speak a raw protocol over TCP or UDP - databases,
DNS, VoIP, gaming, IoT telemetry - had no portable way to plug
into a Gateway. Users either fell back to a plain Kubernetes Service,
or to an implementation-specific CRD that doesn't travel between Gateway controllers.</p>
<p><a href="https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/guides/user-guides/tcp/">TCPRoute</a> and <a href="https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/guides/user-guides/udp/">UDPRoute</a> close that gap: they route traffic to backends based on protocol and port alone, no L7 awareness required.
With this release, both have graduated from the Experimental channel to Standard, and moved to the <code>v1</code> API version.
The <code>v1alpha2</code> version of each was deprecated as of the v1.6 release, and will be removed in a future release.</p>
<h3 id="how-it-works">How it works<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-it-works" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>A Gateway needs a listener that allows TCPRoute attachment:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gatewayClassName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-gateway-class</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">listeners</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">foo</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">protocol</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">TCP</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">port</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">12345</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">allowedRoutes</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kinds</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">TCPRoute</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>A TCPRoute then attaches to that listener and forwards traffic to a backend:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">TCPRoute</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">tcp-app</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">parentRefs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">sectionName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">foo</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">rules</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">backendRefs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">my-foo-service</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">port</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">6000</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Traffic arriving on the Gateway's port <code>12345</code> is proxied to the endpoints of <code>my-foo-service</code> on port <code>6000</code>. Omitting <code>sectionName</code> and <code>port</code> from <code>parentRefs</code> attaches the route to every TCP listener on the Gateway instead of a single one.</p>
<p>UDPRoute follows the same pattern; swap the listener protocol and the route kind:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">gatewayClassName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-gateway-class</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">listeners</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">foo</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">protocol</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">UDP</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">port</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">12345</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">allowedRoutes</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kinds</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">UDPRoute</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">UDPRoute</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">udp-app</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">parentRefs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">example-gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">sectionName</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">foo</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">rules</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">backendRefs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">my-foo-service</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">port</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="m">6000</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="xbackend-arrives-in-experimental">XBackend arrives in Experimental<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#xbackend-arrives-in-experimental" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Leads: <a href="https://github.com/keithmattix">Keith Mattix II</a></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/issues/4894">GEP-4894 - Backend Resource</a></li>
</ul>
<p>Gateway API v1.6 introduces the new <code>XBackend</code> resource, which is a general-purpose decorator for Service (and other backend types) within Gateway API.</p>
<p>The Service resource is an amazing, stable, and flexible object, but that comes with some costs: The flexibility creates a lot of edge cases that Gateway API needs to handle, and the stability makes it impossible to add new concepts to Service.</p>
<p>The XBackend resource builds on the ideas in the upstream <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/6116"><code>EndpointSelector</code> KEP</a>, to add a Gateway API-native object that still targets the backend app, while allowing the community to extend it to handle use cases that are difficult or dangerous to handle with Service.</p>
<p>The first version of XBackend includes support for ExternalHostname destinations, which are ruled out from Service support in Gateway API because of the possibility of confused deputy attacks.</p>
<p>For XBackend, this support is an Extended/Optional feature, allowing implementations and users to opt in once they understand the security tradeoffs.</p>
<p>This support is very useful for egress use cases (which are most commonly used for cluster-hosted agentic workloads), which the community is also working towards formalizing in GEPs about Gateways for Egress (work in progress, stay tuned!)</p>
<p><strong>The XBackend API is experimental and its behavior can change, do not assume it is ready for production</strong></p>
<p>An example of a Gateway with an ExternalName backend that can be used for egress to a cloud AI API is as follows:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c"># Gateway-level TLS remains authoritative for incoming connections</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">Gateway</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">listeners</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">https</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">protocol</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">HTTPS</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">tls</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">certificateRefs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway-cert</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c"># Backend resource for external destination</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">XBackend</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">metadata</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">ai-provider-api</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">namespace</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">ai-apps</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">type</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">ExternalHostname</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">externalHostname</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">hostname</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">api.ai-provider.com</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="c"># HTTPRoute referencing XBackend</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">HTTPRoute</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">spec</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">rules</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">backendRefs</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span>- <span class="nt">name</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">ai-provider-api</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">XBackend</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">group</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">gateway.networking.x-k8s.io</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>The community is also working on moving Session Persistence config from <code>XBackendTrafficPolicy</code> into <code>XBackend</code>, along with other use cases like retries, TLS origination and similar config that is useful to be able to configure per-application rather than per-Route.</p>
<h2 id="experimental-resources-move-off-the-standard-api-group">Experimental resources move off the standard API group<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#experimental-resources-move-off-the-standard-api-group" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Previously, experimental resources shared the same API group as standard ones - <code>gateway.networking.k8s.io</code> - distinguished only by a <code>v1alpha2</code>-style version. TCPRoute and UDPRoute were the last resources to graduate under that scheme.</p>
<p>Going forward, new experimental resources are defined in a separate group,
<code>gateway.networking.x-k8s.io</code>,
and the names of their API types get an <code>X</code> prefix - for example XBackend and XMesh.
When one of these graduates to Standard, it's renamed into the <code>gateway.networking.k8s.io</code> group
and drops the <code>X</code> prefix, the same way XMesh is expected to become Mesh.</p>
<p>This separation makes the experimental/standard boundary explicit at the API group level, rather than relying on version strings alone.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-next-getting-involved">What's next &amp; getting involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next-getting-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The graduation of TCPRoute and UDPRoute to Standard marks an essential milestone
in making Gateway API a complete, universal ingress and mesh networking API
for Kubernetes workloads across layer 4 and layer 7 protocols.</p>
<h3 id="try-it-out">Try it out<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#try-it-out" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>You can start using Gateway API v1.6.0 today with your favorite Gateway controller implementation:</p>
<ul>
<li>Check out the <a href="https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/">Gateway API Documentation</a> for detailed guides and API references.</li>
<li>View the <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/tag/v1.6.0">v1.6.0 Release Notes</a> for complete details on the CRD installation and changes.</li>
</ul>
<p>Gateway API relies on an extensive conformance test suite to ensure consistent,
portable behavior across all implementations.
Here is a list of the implementations that are conforment with v1.6 on the day we published the article:</p>

<h3 id="get-involved">Get involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Gateway API is an open, community-driven project built under Kubernetes SIG Network. We welcome contributions, feedback, and participation from everyone!</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Join our Slack Channel</strong>: Join <code>#sig-network-gateway-api</code> on the <a href="https://slack.k8s.io/">Kubernetes Slack</a>.</li>

<p>As we get closer to the release date for Kubernetes v1.37, the project develops and matures,
features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's overall
health. This blog outlines some of the planned changes for the Kubernetes v1.37 release that the
release team feels you should be aware of for the continued maintenance of your Kubernetes
environment and keeping up to date with the latest changes. The information below reflects the
current status of the v1.37 release and may change before the actual release date.</p>
<h2 id="deprecations-and-removals-for-kubernetes-v1-37">Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#deprecations-and-removals-for-kubernetes-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="kubectl-kubectl-run-filename-f-to-be-deprecated">Kubectl: <code>kubectl run --filename/-f</code> to be deprecated<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kubectl-kubectl-run-filename-f-to-be-deprecated" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>--filename</code> (or <code>-f</code>) flag for <code>kubectl run</code> is being deprecated as the generated pod is always built purely from CLI arguments like <code>NAME</code> and <code>--image</code>.</p>
<p>See <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138671">kubernetes/kubernetes#138671</a> for the original issue and discussion.</p>
<h3 id="kubelet-static-pods-can-no-longer-reference-secrets-or-configmaps">Kubelet: Static Pods can no longer reference Secrets or ConfigMaps<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kubelet-static-pods-can-no-longer-reference-secrets-or-configmaps" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Static Pods were never meant to read API resources directly, since they aren't created through the API server — but a bug let them reference Secrets or ConfigMaps via fields like <code>configMapRef</code> or <code>secretRef</code>. That bug is now fixed: as of v1.37 these references are strictly prohibited, and the <code>PreventStaticPodAPIReferences</code> feature gate that previously let you opt out of the restriction has been removed.</p>
<p>See <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140226">kubernetes/kubernetes#140226</a> for the original issue and discussion.</p>
<h3 id="deprecating-kube-proxy-s-support-for-ipvs-mode">Deprecating kube-proxy's support for <code>ipvs</code> mode<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#deprecating-kube-proxy-s-support-for-ipvs-mode" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><code>kube-proxy</code> support for <code>ipvs</code> mode was introduced in v1.8 to resolve <code>iptables</code> performance bottlenecks. However, since the kernel <code>ipvs</code> API alone cannot fully implement Kubernetes Services, <code>ipvs</code> mode continues to use <code>iptables</code> underneath (<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/3866-nftables-proxy/README.md#the-ipvs-mode-of-kube-proxy-will-not-save-us">KEP-3866, &quot;The ipvs mode of kube-proxy will not save us&quot;</a>).</p>
<p>Clusters running <code>kube-proxy</code> in ipvs mode (or mode: ipvs in KubeProxyConfiguration) would now be logging a deprecation warning on startup. The deprecation timeline looks like this:</p>
<ul>
<li>By v1.40, <code>ipvs</code> mode for <code>kube-proxy</code> is expected to be disabled by default (still selectable via the feature gate)</li>
<li>By v1.43, support for <code>ipvs</code> mode would be removed entirely <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/5495-deprecate-ipvs-mode-in-kube-proxy/README.md#graduation-criteria">KEP-5495, Graduation Criteria</a>.
To confirm which mode you’re currently running, use:</li>
</ul>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o <span class="nv">jsonpath</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s1">&#39;{.data.config\.conf}&#39;</span> <span class="p">|</span> grep <span class="s1">&#39;mode:&#39;</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>To understand the rationale behind this deprecation, see <a href="https://kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5495">KEP-5495: Deprecate ipvs mode in kube-proxy</a>.</p>
<h2 id="ongoing-major-changes">Ongoing major changes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#ongoing-major-changes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="cgroup-v1-support">Future removal of cgroup v1 support<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#cgroup-v1-support" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>As modern Linux distributions and container runtimes use <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/cgroups/">cgroup v2</a> as the default, support for the legacy cgroup v1 is officially being phased out. Since the v1.35 release, the <code>failCgroupV1</code> setting has defaulted to true. Consequently, the <code>kubelet</code> will fail to initialize on any nodes that still rely on cgroup v1 unless an explicit configuration override is applied.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nt">apiVersion</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">kind</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l">KubeletConfiguration</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="w"></span><span class="nt">failCgroupV1</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="c"># temporary override</span><span class="w">
</span></span></span></code></pre></div><p>Using this override should be considered a short-term fix. Advanced resource management capabilities, such as In-Place Pod Resizing and Tiered Memory Protection, depend entirely on cgroup v2. While the override remains available in Kubernetes v1.37, users are encouraged to migrate to cgroup v2, as support for cgroup v1 is planned to be removed in a future release.</p>
<p>To learn more about this deprecation, refer to <a href="https://kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5573">KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support</a>.</p>
<h2 id="breaking-changes-in-kubernetes-v1-37">Breaking changes in Kubernetes v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#breaking-changes-in-kubernetes-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="SELinuxMount-GA">SELinux volume relabeling (&quot;SELinuxMount&quot;) graduates to GA<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#SELinuxMount-GA" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>SELinuxMount is expected to reach GA and be enabled by default in v1.37. Volumes would then be
mounted with <code>-o context=&lt;label&gt;</code> (the mount option default) instead of being recursively
relabeled, but <strong>only</strong> when the volume's CSI driver opts in via a CSIDriver that sets <code>.spec seLinuxMount: true</code>.</p>
<p>Because a single mount can only hold one SELinux context, pods with different SELinux labels sharing a volume on the same node (which previously coexisted under recursive relabeling) may now fail to start. To retain the previous recursive behavior for a specific workload, set <code>seLinuxChangePolicy: Recursive</code> in the Pod spec.</p>
<p>Clusters without SELinux enabled see no effect at all. To learn more, check <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/04/22/breaking-changes-in-selinux-volume-labeling/">SELinux Volume Label Changes goes GA (and likely implications in v1.37)</a></p>
<h2 id="featured-enhancements-of-kubernetes-v1-37">Featured enhancements of Kubernetes v1.37<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#featured-enhancements-of-kubernetes-v1-37" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="metrics-api-ga">Metrics API goes GA<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#metrics-api-ga" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The <code>metrics.k8s.io</code> API is expected to graduate to Stable (GA) in Kubernetes v1.37 after spending nearly nine years in Beta. The API provides a standard way to retrieve CPU and memory usage for pods and nodes, powering widely used Kubernetes features such as the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and commands like <code>kubectl top</code>.</p>
<p>This graduation recognizes the API's stability and widespread adoption, with no functional changes expected. Both <code>v1</code> and <code>v1beta1</code> will remain usable during the transition, enabling developers to adopt the stable API at their own pace without breaking existing workflows.</p>
<p>To learn more about this enhancement, refer to <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/5207/">KEP-5207: metrics.k8s.io API definition</a>.</p>
<h3 id="kubelet-in-userns-a-k-a-rootless-mode">Kubelet in UserNS a.k.a. Rootless Mode<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kubelet-in-userns-a-k-a-rootless-mode" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Traditionally, Kubernetes node components such as the <code>kubelet</code> run with root privileges on the host. While necessary for many deployments, this also means that a vulnerability in one of these components could potentially have a greater impact on the underlying system.</p>
<p>With Kubernetes v1.37, kubelet in User Namespace (Rootless Mode) is expected to graduate to
Beta. This enhancement allows Kubernetes node components to run inside a Linux user namespace as an unprivileged user on the host while still behaving as root within the namespace. By reducing the need for host-level root privileges, it adds an extra layer of isolation and helps limit the impact of potential vulnerabilities affecting node components.</p>
<p>To learn more about this enhancement, refer to <a href="https://kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/4960">KEP-2033: Kubelet in UserNS(aka Rootless Mode)</a>.</p>
<h3 id="volume-health-monitor">Volume health monitor<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#volume-health-monitor" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Historically, Kubernetes has lacked an API for CSI drivers to report storage failures, which become evident only through
failed mounts or hung I/O. Since remediation controllers had nothing machine-readable to act upon, the only way to figure out the root cause behind this failure was to cross-reference Kubernetes objects alongside external vendor dashboards.</p>
<p>In Kubernetes v1.37, this KEP resets graduation to Alpha after an initial implementation in v1.21 and introduces four new CSI
RPCs. The controller plugin reports the health of storage volumes using <code>ControllerListVolumeHealth</code> (lists unhealthy volumes) and <code>ControllerGetVolumeHealth</code> (checks a specific volume). A controller-side health monitor polls these CSI controllers and stores the results in
<code>PersistentVolumeClaim.status.healthStatus</code>.</p>
<p>On the node side, the kubelet calls <code>NodeGetVolumeHealth</code> to obtain the health of individual volumes on that node and records
it in <code>Pod.status.volumeHealth</code>, while <code>NodeGetStorageHealth</code> reports the health of the drivers registered to a node in
<code>CSINode.status.storageHealth</code>.</p>
<p>The error vocabulary is kept simple, extensible, and machine-parsable (<code>Inaccessible</code>, <code>Degraded</code>, etc.), with further driver-specific elaboration available via <code>reason</code> and <code>message</code>. Finally, the controller-side and node-side reports are kept independent and are hence displayed separately, providing a more holistic view of storage health to consumers.</p>
<p>To learn more about this enhancement, refer to <a href="https://kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/1432">KEP-1432: Volume Health Monitor</a>.</p>
<h2 id="want-to-know-more">Want to know more?<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#want-to-know-more" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>New features and deprecations are also announced in the Kubernetes release notes. We will formally announce what's new in <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.37.md">Kubernetes v1.37</a> as part of the CHANGELOG for that release.</p>
<p>Kubernetes v1.37 release is planned for <strong>Wednesday, August 26th, 2026</strong>. Stay tuned for updates!</p>
<p>You can see the announcements of changes in the release notes for:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.36.md">Kubernetes v1.36</a></p>
</li>

</li>

</li>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.33.md">Kubernetes v1.33</a></p>
</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="get-involved">Get involved<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#get-involved" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The simplest way to get involved with Kubernetes is by joining one of the many <a href="https://kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/">Special Interest Groups</a> (SIGs) that align with your interests.</p>
<p>If you don't know where to start, join our monthly <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/docs/orientation/">New Contributor Orientations</a>
where we teach the community how the project is structured, and we'll guide you on how to make your first contribution to the project.</p>

</ul></description></item><item><title>How the controller-runtime Cache Actually Works, and Why Your Controller Does Not Crash the API Server</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/07/29/controller-runtime-cache-explained/</link><pubDate>Wed, 29 Jul 2026 10:00:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/07/29/controller-runtime-cache-explained/</guid><description>
<div class="pageinfo pageinfo-primary">
<p>This article has been revised since it was first published, to correct several significant technical inaccuracies in the original text.</p>
</div>
<p>Kubernetes has long been the default platform for distributed workloads, and writing your own
controller for it is now a matter of a few hours. The common path — Golang, using <code>kubebuilder</code> on top of
<code>controller-runtime</code> — gives you a project scaffold, types, and a reconciler. For typical
scenarios that is more than enough. But as soon as load grows or the controller starts behaving
in ways you did not expect, a whole class of edge cases shows up. Most of them trace back to
the same root cause: a fuzzy mental model of how <code>controller-runtime</code> works inside. If you
write Kubernetes controllers in Go, this article should help you build a coherent picture and
avoid expensive surprises in production.</p>
<p>This article walks through the internals of <code>controller-runtime</code> and, along the way, shows which
architectural decisions are baked into Kubernetes itself. The starting point is how
controllers actually read objects from the Kubernetes API.</p>
<p>A common misconception goes like this: <code>r.Get()</code> inside <code>Reconcile</code> queries <code>kube-apiserver</code>
directly; <code>r.List()</code> returns a fresh, live view of the world; and after <code>r.Update()</code> you can
re-read the object and immediately see the new state. In practice the model is the opposite:
<code>controller-runtime</code> operates against a local copy of the data populated through <strong>list</strong> + <strong>watch</strong>.
Reads inside a reconciler cost almost nothing and do not load the control plane even at
hundreds of calls per second — but the price of this design is that a controller can quietly
consume gigabytes of memory, perform hidden O(n) scans, and regularly trip over stale reads.</p>
<p>This post is aimed at engineers who already write controllers in Go with <code>controller-runtime</code>
but want to consolidate the pieces into a single mental model rather than carry around a bag
of isolated observations. The focus is the practical impact on production clusters: memory,
network traffic, read consistency, and reconciler behavior.</p>
<h2 id="tl-dr">TL;DR<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#tl-dr" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>If you take only one idea from this article, take this:</p>
<p><code>r.Get()</code> and <code>r.List()</code> inside a reconciler typically do not read from the API server. They
read from a local in-memory cache, which the manager warms up with <strong>list</strong> and then keeps
current through <strong>watch</strong>.</p>
<p>Almost every other property of the system follows from that one fact:</p>
<ul>
<li>Reads are cheap, but not strongly consistent immediately after a write.</li>
<li>Writes go straight to the API server, not through the cache.</li>
<li>The size of the local cache and the set of indexes directly drive memory consumption.</li>
<li>An incorrectly written <code>List()</code> can silently turn into a linear scan over tens of thousands
of objects.</li>
<li><code>APIReader</code> is rarely needed — but in some places you really cannot do without it.</li>
</ul>
<p>The rest of the article unpacks why this is so and how the model is wired underneath.</p>
<h2 id="a-bit-of-context-what-a-reconciliation-loop-is">A bit of context: what a reconciliation loop is<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#a-bit-of-context-what-a-reconciliation-loop-is" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>To avoid arguments about terminology, start with the basic model.</p>
<p>A controller in Kubernetes lives inside a reconciliation loop: it continuously compares the
desired state of an object with the actual state and tries to bring one in line with the
other. The idea is described in the original
<a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/design-proposals-archive/blob/main/architecture/principles.md">architectural notes</a>
on Kubernetes. In practice it looks like this:</p>
<ul>
<li>A user or another controller mutates an object.</li>
<li>An event lands in a queue.</li>
<li><code>Reconcile</code> reads the current state.</li>
<li>The controller decides what to create, update, or delete.</li>
<li>The system produces a new event and the loop repeats.</li>
</ul>
<p>What matters here is not that the controller &quot;does something&quot; — it is <strong>where it learns about
changes from</strong> and <strong>where it reads state from</strong>. That is exactly where the cache comes in.</p>
<p>On a live cluster, the easiest way to see this in action is:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">kubectl get pods --watch
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>In watch mode, <code>kubectl</code> subscribes to the same event stream that controllers consume.
You create or delete a Pod and you see not a single &quot;final&quot; object but a chain of states: the
scheduler assigns a node, the kubelet updates status, other controllers contribute their
changes. Kubernetes controllers do not poll continuously — they consume an event stream and
maintain a local state that is kept current.</p>
<p>For a visual walkthrough, see <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P50otWVh7w4">Reconciliation loop pattern in visual representation</a>,
a talk that shows how the reconciliation loop plays out on a real Pod and the states it
passes through.</p>
<h2 id="why-the-cache-exists-in-controller-runtime-at-all">Why the cache exists in <code>controller-runtime</code> at all<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-the-cache-exists-in-controller-runtime-at-all" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Imagine the simplest possible controller:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-go" data-lang="go"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="kd">func</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">r</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="nx">Reconciler</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="nf">Reconcile</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">ctx</span> <span class="nx">context</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">Context</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">req</span> <span class="nx">ctrl</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">Request</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">ctrl</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">Result</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="kt">error</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"> <span class="kd">var</span> <span class="nx">pod</span> <span class="nx">corev1</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">Pod</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"> <span class="k">if</span> <span class="nx">err</span> <span class="o">:=</span> <span class="nx">r</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">Get</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">ctx</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">req</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">NamespacedName</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="o">&amp;</span><span class="nx">pod</span><span class="p">);</span> <span class="nx">err</span> <span class="o">!=</span> <span class="kc">nil</span> <span class="p">{</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nx">ctrl</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">Result</span><span class="p">{},</span> <span class="nx">err</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"> <span class="p">}</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"> <span class="c1">// ... meaningful logic ...</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="p">}</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Looks straightforward. But what happens when you call <code>r.Get</code>? Does it fire an HTTP request at
the API server? If it did, picture the scene: a dozen controllers, each issuing a <strong>get</strong> and
a <strong>list</strong> per reconcile, with hundreds of reconciles per second. The API server and <code>etcd</code>
