<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/archive/refs/tags/v3.7.0.tar.gz">Source code</a></li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/releases/tag/v3.7.0">Binaries</a></li>
<li><a href="https://gcr.io/etcd-development/etcd">Official container images</a></li>
</ul>
<p>This release also includes new versions of the two core etcd dependencies, <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/bbolt/releases/tag/v1.5.0">bbolt v1.5.0</a> and <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/releases/tag/v3.7.0">raft v3.7.0</a>.</p>
<p>For instructions on installing etcd, see the <a href="https://etcd.io/docs/v3.7/install/">install documentation</a>. For the full list of changes, see the <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/main/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-3.7.md">etcd v3.7 changelog</a>.</p>
<p>A heartfelt thank you to all the contributors who made this release possible!</p>
<h2 id="major-features">Major features<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#major-features" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The most significant changes in v3.7.0 include:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="#rangestream"><strong>RangeStream</strong></a> — stream large result sets in chunks instead of buffering the whole response.</li>
<li><strong>Keys-only range requests, faster and more reliable leases,</strong> and several other <a href="#performance-improvements"><strong>performance improvements</strong></a>.</li>
<li>etcd now <a href="#bootstrap-from-v3store">boots entirely from v3store</a>, eliminating a long-standing dependency on the legacy v2 store</li>
<li>A completed <a href="#protobuf-overhaul"><strong>protobuf overhaul</strong></a>, replacing outdated protobuf libraries with fully supported ones.</li>
<li>etcd v3.7 ships with <a href="#bbolt-v151">bbolt v1.5.1</a> and <a href="#raft-v370">raft v3.7.0</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="features">Features<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#features" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><h3 id="rangestream">RangeStream<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#rangestream" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In etcd v3.6 and earlier, it is challenging to work with requests that return large result sets. The database would buffer the full result set before sending, leading to unpredictable latency and memory usage, both on the server and the client. <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-etcd/5966-etcd-range-stream">The RangeStream RPC</a> lets calling applications accept result sets in chunks, reducing latency and making buffering memory usage more predictable.</p>
<p>Instructions on how to use RangeStream <a href="https://etcd.io/docs/v3.7/learning/api/#rangestream">in gRPC calls</a> and <a href="https://etcd.io/docs/v3.7/dev-guide/interacting_v3/#read-keys">in etcdctl</a> can be found in the etcd documentation. Users should try it out for their own applications.</p>
<p>In coordinated releases, the RangeStream feature will become available to users running the upcoming v1.37 of Kubernetes by enabling the <code>EtcdRangeStream</code> feature gate. This early and planned adoption is possible thanks to the merger of etcd and Kubernetes development in 2023.</p>
<h3 id="performance-improvements">Performance improvements<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#performance-improvements" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>v3.7 delivers multiple specific performance improvements, both for the Kubernetes control plane and for other use cases. Kubernetes users should see a significant decrease in overall CPU usage by the etcd members, compared with v3.6.</p>
<h4 id="keys-only-range-optimization">Keys-only range optimization<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#keys-only-range-optimization" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>etcd v3.7.0 includes a keys-only Range optimization (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21791">#21791: keys-only Range optimization</a>). When processing a keys_only Range request or <code>etcdctl get --keys-only</code>, etcd reads solely from its in-memory index. It returns the matched keys without loading all serialized values from bbolt as it did previously. The only exception where loading from bbolt is still required is when <code>keys_only</code> Range requests must be sorted by value (i.e., when SortTarget is set to VALUE).</p>
<p>This reduces unnecessary backend reads and memory use for workloads that only need key names, making large keys-only range requests more efficient.</p>
<h4 id="faster-more-reliable-etcd-leases">Faster, more reliable etcd leases<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#faster-more-reliable-etcd-leases" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>v3.7 improves lease expiration and renewal:</p>
<ul>
<li>LeaseRevoke requests are now prioritized to ensure timely lease expiration during overload (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20492">#20492: stability enhancement during overload conditions</a>).</li>
<li>The new FastLeaseKeepAlive feature enables faster lease renewal by skipping the wait for the applied index (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20589">#20589: etcdserver: improve linearizable renew lease</a>).</li>
</ul>
<h4 id="faster-find-operations">Faster find() operations<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#faster-find-operations" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>etcd 3.7 improves the performance of concurrent watches on keys by making find() operations faster (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/19768">#19768: adt: split interval tree by right endpoint on matched left endpoints</a>).</p>
<h3 id="other-features">Other features<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#other-features" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><h4 id="protobuf-overhaul">Protobuf overhaul<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#protobuf-overhaul" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>v3.7 migrates and replaces multiple outdated protobuf libraries with fully supported dependencies. This includes replacing <code>github.com/golang/protobuf</code> and <code>github.com/gogo/protobuf</code> with the fully-supported <code>google.golang.org/protobuf</code> (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/14533">#14533: Protobuf: cleanup both golang/protobuf and gogo/protobuf</a>), and migrating grpc-logging to grpc-middleware v2 (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20420">#20420: Migrate grpc-logging to grpc-middleware v2</a>).</p>
<p>As well as improving security and maintainability, this refactor has been shown to reduce CPU usage by etcd components.</p>
<p>While these changes are not expected to directly affect users running etcd via official binaries or container images, they may affect users who depend on etcd Go modules, such as the client SDK or packages under <code>api/</code> or <code>pkg/</code>. These consumers may need to update their code or dependencies due to protobuf and related API changes introduced in this release. More detailed information is available from <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/website/issues/1162">the API change tracking issue</a>.</p>
<h4 id="unix-socket-support">Unix socket support<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#unix-socket-support" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>etcd now supports Unix socket endpoints (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/19760">#19760: Add Support for Unix Socket endpoints</a>), enabling local communication without a TCP port. Since this is restricted to single-member clusters, it is mainly aimed at development, testing, and edge device use-cases.</p>
<h4 id="bootstrap-from-v3store">Bootstrap from v3store<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#bootstrap-from-v3store" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>One of the major changes in etcd v3.7 is that the server now bootstraps entirely from the v3 store (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/20187">#20187 Bootstrap etcdserver from v3store</a>), eliminating its dependency on the legacy v2 store during startup.</p>
<p>This milestone is the result of a long-term effort spanning multiple releases, from v3.4 through v3.7. It resolves a long-standing technical debt, significantly simplifies the bootstrap workflow, and lays the foundation for future improvements to etcd.</p>
<p>To maintain backward compatibility, etcd v3.7 continues to generate v2 snapshots. As a result, the <code>--snapshot-count</code> flag is also retained in v3.7. This is the last remaining dependency on the legacy v2 store, and both the v2 snapshot generation and the <code>--snapshot-count</code> flag will be removed in v3.8.</p>
<h4 id="etcdutl-timeouts">etcdutl timeouts<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#etcdutl-timeouts" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>All etcdutl commands now have a timeout command line argument (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20708">#20708: etcdutl: enable timeout functionality for all commands</a>), so offline utility commands no longer block indefinitely when holding a lock.</p>
<h4 id="setting-the-authentication-token-directly">Setting the authentication token directly<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#setting-the-authentication-token-directly" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Client v3 now allows users to set the JWT directly, offering more flexibility in authentication options (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/16803">#16803: clientv3: allow setting JWT directly</a>, <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20747">#20747: clientv3: disable auth retry when token is set</a>),</p>
<h4 id="retrieve-authstatus-without-authenticating">Retrieve AuthStatus without authenticating<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#retrieve-authstatus-without-authenticating" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>Clients can check their AuthStatus without attempting to authenticate first, eliminating some application overhead (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20802">#20802: etcdserver: remove permission check on AuthStatus api</a>).</p>
<h4 id="new-watch-metrics">New watch metrics<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#new-watch-metrics" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>v3.7 adds optional watch send-loop metrics (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21030">#21030: Instrument watchstream send loop</a>) for better observability of the watch path:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>etcd_debugging_server_watch_send_loop_watch_stream_duration_seconds</code></li>
<li><code>etcd_debugging_server_watch_send_loop_watch_stream_duration_per_event_seconds</code></li>
<li><code>etcd_debugging_server_watch_send_loop_control_stream_duration_seconds</code></li>
<li><code>etcd_debugging_server_watch_send_loop_progress_duration_seconds</code></li>
</ul>
<p>There is also a new <code>etcd_server_request_duration_seconds</code> metric (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21038">#21038: Add metric <code>etcd_server_request_duration_seconds</code></a>).</p>
<h4 id="etcdctl-command-cleanup">etcdctl command cleanup<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#etcdctl-command-cleanup" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h4><p>etcdctl commands were reorganized for clarity (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20162">#20162: etcdctl: organize etcdctl subcommand</a>) and global command line arguments are now hidden to streamline help output (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20493">#20493: etcdctl: hide global flags</a>).</p>
<h2 id="upgrading">Upgrading<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#upgrading" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This release contains breaking changes, particularly around the removal of legacy v2 components. Users should review the <a href="https://etcd.io/docs/v3.7/upgrades/upgrade_3_7/">upgrade guide</a> before upgrading their nodes. As with all minor releases, perform a rolling upgrade one member at a time and confirm cluster health between steps.</p>
<h3 id="experimental-flags-removed">Experimental flags removed<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#experimental-flags-removed" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>All deprecated experimental flags have been removed (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/19959">#19959: Cleanup the deprecated experimental flags</a>). Features in etcd now follow the Kubernetes-style feature-gate lifecycle (Alpha → Beta → GA) introduced in v3.6, rather than the old <code>--experimental</code> prefix. If your configuration still relies on <code>--experimental-*</code> command line arguments, migrate to using the corresponding feature gates or stable command line arguments before you upgrade to etcd 3.7.</p>
<h3 id="legacy-v2-api-packages-and-code-cleanup">Legacy V2 API packages and code cleanup<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#legacy-v2-api-packages-and-code-cleanup" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>To remove the dependencies on v2store, the following components have been removed:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20109">v2 discovery</a> (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20109">#20109: Remove v2discovery</a>) packages removed,</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21263">v2 request</a> support (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21263">#21263: Remove v2 Request and apply_v2.go</a>)</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20117">v2 client</a> support (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20117">#20117: Remove client/internal/v2</a>).</li>
</ul>
<p>These changes may create some breakage for users, particularly those who have not already updated to v3.6.11 or later. Users should report any blockers encountered, or cases that need better upgrade documentation.</p>
<h3 id="non-blocking-client-creation">Non-blocking client creation<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#non-blocking-client-creation" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>etcd no longer honors the deprecated <code>grpc.WithBlock</code> dial option ( <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21942">#21942: Make the etcd client creation non-blocking</a>). To preserve the previous blocking behavior when needed, follow the guidance in grpc-go's <a href="https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/master/Documentation/anti-patterns.md#especially-bad-using-deprecated-dialoptions">anti-patterns documentation</a>.</p>
<h3 id="multiarch-container-images-only">Multiarch container images only<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#multiarch-container-images-only" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>For users relying on the official etcd container images, v3.7 will be distributed <strong>only</strong> as multiarch containers. Architecture-tagged images will not be available, so adjust deployments accordingly.</p>
<h3 id="api-changes">API changes<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#api-changes" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>As with every etcd release, there are a number of API changes. These are designed to be backwards-compatible to the extent possible, but may require adjustment by some users. See our <a href="https://etcd.io/docs/v3.7/learning/api/">API documentation</a> page for full information.</p>
<h2 id="bbolt-v1-5-1">bbolt v1.5.1<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#bbolt-v1-5-1" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>etcd v3.7 depends on, and includes, <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/bbolt/blob/main/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.5.md">v1.5.1</a> of the bbolt storage engine. v1.5 includes several improvements to functionality and performance, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/bbolt/pull/929">Database file size limits</a>: users may set, and bbolt will enforce, file size limits. When a bolt database exceeds these limits it will refuse to accept writes until the database is compacted or the limit is changed.</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/bbolt/pull/977">Disable statistics for performance</a>: users may set <code>NoStatistics</code> to limit overhead from locks taken by the database statistics viewer.</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/bbolt/pull/1179">More efficient hashmap processing</a>: merge spans faster and with less overhead.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="raft-v3-7-0">raft v3.7.0<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#raft-v3-7-0" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>etcd 3.7 depends on, and includes, v3.7.0 of the raft consensus engine. v3.7 includes several improvements, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/pull/370">Update the bootstrap process</a>: v3.7 now allows booting from partly initialized snapshots, supporting etcd's initializing directly from v3store.</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/pull/397">Improve the ReadIndex flow to prevent stale reads</a> by injecting a unique identifier into the heartbeat context for read-only operations.</li>
</ul>
<p>raft v3.7.0 also includes the <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/14533">same protobuf library updates</a> and refactoring as etcd does.</p>
<h2 id="dependency-updates">Dependency updates<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dependency-updates" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Other dependency updates include a bump to <code>golang.org/x/crypto</code> v0.52.0 for CVE resolution (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21903">#21903: [release-3.7] Bump golang.org/x/crypto to v0.52.0</a>), an OpenTelemetry contrib update to v0.61.0 (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20017">#20017: Update otelgrpc to v0.61.0</a>), and compilation with Go 1.26.4 (<a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/21891">#21891: [release-3.7] Update Go to 1.26.4</a>).</p>
<h2 id="contributors">Contributors<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#contributors" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>etcd v3.7.0 is the product of more than a hundred contributors across the community. Thank you to everyone who wrote code, reviewed PRs, filed and triaged issues, and helped test the alpha, beta, and release candidates.</p>
<h3 id="leads">Leads<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#leads" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The SIG etcd leads for the v3.7 release are <a href="https://github.com/ivanvc">ivanvc</a>, <a href="https://github.com/serathius">serathius</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ahrtr">ahrtr</a>, <a href="https://github.com/fuweid">fuweid</a>, <a href="https://github.com/siyuanfoundation">siyuanfoundation</a>, and <a href="https://github.com/jberkus">jberkus</a>. Ivan leads our release team.</p>
<h3 id="other-contributors">Other contributors<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#other-contributors" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p><a href="https://github.com/ah8ad3">ah8ad3</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ajaysundark">ajaysundark</a>, <a href="https://github.com/aladesawe">aladesawe</a>, <a href="https://github.com/amosehiguese">amosehiguese</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ArkaSaha30">ArkaSaha30</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ashikjm">ashikjm</a>, <a href="https://github.com/AwesomePatrol">AwesomePatrol</a>, <a href="https://github.com/dims">dims</a>, <a href="https://github.com/Elbehery">Elbehery</a>, <a href="https://github.com/gangli113">gangli113</a>, <a href="https://github.com/henrybear327">henrybear327</a>, <a href="https://github.com/Jille">Jille</a>, <a href="https://github.com/jmhbnz">jmhbnz</a>, <a href="https://github.com/joshuazh-x">joshuazh-x</a>, <a href="https://github.com/kishen-v">kishen-v</a>, <a href="https://github.com/lavishpal">lavishpal</a>, <a href="https://github.com/liggitt">liggitt</a>, <a href="https://github.com/marcelfranca">marcelfranca</a>, <a href="https://github.com/miancheng7">miancheng7</a>, <a href="https://github.com/mmorel-35">mmorel-35</a>, <a href="https://github.com/MrDXY">MrDXY</a>, <a href="https://github.com/mrueg">mrueg</a>, <a href="https://github.com/purpleidea">purpleidea</a>, <a href="https://github.com/qsyqian">qsyqian</a>, <a href="https://github.com/redwrasse">redwrasse</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ronaldngounou">ronaldngounou</a>, <a href="https://github.com/skitt">skitt</a>, <a href="https://github.com/spzala">spzala</a>, <a href="https://github.com/tcchawla">tcchawla</a>, <a href="https://github.com/tjungblu">tjungblu</a>, <a href="https://github.com/vivekpatani">vivekpatani</a>, <a href="https://github.com/wenjiaswe">wenjiaswe</a></p>
<h3 id="new-contributors">New contributors<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#new-contributors" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>A special welcome to the contributors who made their first etcd contribution in this cycle — including <a href="https://github.com/jefftree">Jeffrey Ying</a>, whose work drove the RangeStream feature. New contributors can have a substantial impact on etcd; if you’d like to get involved, see the <a href="https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md">contributor guide</a>.</p>

href="https://github.com/abdurrehman107">abdurrehman107</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ABin-Huang">ABin-Huang</a>, <a href="https://github.com/adeptvin1">adeptvin1</a>, <a <p>AI has really changed the game around software development.
More people are leveraging AI than ever to contribute patches to projects they use.
To me, this is a good thing as more folks will contribute patches rather than fork or not fix them.
The main problem is that AI has made generating code fast but there has been very little improvement in maintaining code bases.
In this post, we will highlight the ways the Kubernetes community is adapting to the world of AI assisted coding.</p>
<p>The first step of this journey was to develop an AI policy. This seems mundane and bureaucratic but there were many PRs that derailed into discussions around AI usage.
The AI policy helps steer the conversation around the project's stance on AI and provides a clear signal to contributors on how to use these tools responsibly.</p>
<h2 id="kubernetes-ai-policy">Kubernetes AI policy<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kubernetes-ai-policy" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The Kubernetes project has established <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/docs/guide/pull-requests/#ai-guidance">clear guidelines for AI-assisted contributions</a> that balance innovation with accountability.
These policies are designed to maintain code quality and ensure human oversight while acknowledging that AI tools can be valuable aids in the development process.</p>
<h3 id="transparency-first">Transparency first<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#transparency-first" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Contributors must disclose when AI tools have been used to assist with a pull request. A simple statement in the PR description such as &quot;This PR was written in part with the assistance of generative AI&quot; is sufficient. This transparency helps reviewers understand the context and apply appropriate scrutiny.</p>
<h3 id="human-accountability">Human accountability<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#human-accountability" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>While AI tools can assist, the human contributor remains fully responsible for every change. The policy explicitly prohibits:</p>
<ul>
<li>Listing AI as a co-author on commits</li>
<li>Using AI co-signing on commits</li>
<li>Adding trailers like &quot;assisted-by&quot; or &quot;co-developed&quot; that attribute work to AI</li>
</ul>
<p>This isn't about diminishing AI's role as a tool—it's about maintaining clear accountability. If something breaks, there needs to be a human who understands why and can fix it.</p>
<h3 id="cla-enforcement-for-co-authors">CLA enforcement for co-authors<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#cla-enforcement-for-co-authors" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The CNCF provides a <a href="https://github.com/cncf/cla">tool</a> for verifying the contributor license agreements on each pull request.
AI agents are not able to solve these contributor license agreements so one enforcement the project made is to enable the CLA check for co-authors.
This provides a flag to reviewers that the PR is not ready to merge.</p>
<h3 id="human-engagement-required">Human engagement required<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#human-engagement-required" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Perhaps the most critical aspect of the policy: reviewers expect to engage with humans, not with AI.
Contributors cannot rely on AI to respond to review comments.
If you cannot personally explain changes that AI helped generate, your PR will be closed.
This requirement ensures that knowledge transfer happens and that contributors genuinely understand the code they're submitting.</p>
<h3 id="verification-obligations">Verification obligations<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#verification-obligations" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Contributors must verify AI-generated changes through code review, testing, and personal understanding.
It's not enough for the code to work—you need to know why it works and be able to maintain it.</p>
<p>These policies reflect a mature approach to AI: embrace it as a tool, but never let it replace human judgment, understanding, or responsibility.</p>
<h2 id="automated-ai-reviews">Automated AI reviews<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#automated-ai-reviews" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>There exist many tools to aid in reviewing code. AI pull request tools introduce governance challenges so one of the first tasks the community took on was to <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/github-management/ai-code-review-tools.md">document the process</a> for what is needed to bring in new AI tools.
One of the major evaluation criteria for these tools is to find maintainers willing to test drive them in kubernetes-sigs repositories. Kueue, JobSet and Agent-Sandbox have been experimenting with these tools to provide more support for maintainers.</p>
<h3 id="copilot">Copilot<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#copilot" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>One tool that many maintainers started using was GitHub Copilot.
The CNCF provides <a href="https://contribute.cncf.io/blog/2025/12/16/github-copilot-enterprise-for-maintainers/">access for maintainers</a> so this ended up being the first tool many started using.
It provides some good experience on tuning reviews but there were some growing pains with this tool.
The biggest blocker for community adoption is relying on contributors to have a copilot license. Only maintainers were able to request copilot reviews and automated reviews of pull requests was out of reach for the community.
One of the goals of AI review tools is to provide an automated review tool that maintainers don't need to request.
This demonstrated the need for organization control rather than relying on contributors having access.</p>
<h3 id="coderabbit">CodeRabbit<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#coderabbit" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>In mid 2026, the Kubernetes community has rolled out CodeRabbit to a few projects.
As with copilot, some tuning has been required to provide better reviews but the overall feedback has been positive.
There is a lot of configuration available for this tool and one of the most interesting uses of this tool comes from agent-sandbox.</p>
<p>AI pull request tools can be a quality gate. Contributors can at least get a quick spot check review without waiting for a maintainer.
Agent-sandbox has added a label on PRs to reflect that there is still a need to resolve some of the comments from AI tools.</p>
<h2 id="next-steps">Next steps<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#next-steps" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The reality is that leveraging AI in open source projects is an area of active exploration.
The community could use your help in tuning reviews tools, evaluating tools or evaluating emerging technologies in the AI space.</p>
<p>Some areas we are exploring more:</p>
<ul>
<li>The use of AI skills to reduce maintainer burnout.</li>
<li>AI assisted triage of failing tests.</li>
<li>Skills to aid the operational aspects of Kubernetes.</li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Introducing the Cluster API plugin for Headlamp</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/</link><pubDate>Thu, 25 Jun 2026 14:00:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/</guid><description>
<p><a href="https://headlamp.dev/">Headlamp</a> is an open-source, extensible Kubernetes SIG UI
project designed to let you explore, manage, and debug cluster resources directly
from a browser.</p>
<p><a href="https://cluster-api.sigs.k8s.io">Cluster API (CAPI)</a> is a Kubernetes sub-project
that brings declarative, Kubernetes-style APIs to cluster lifecycle management. It
lets platform teams provision, upgrade, and manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes
clusters using standard Kubernetes objects stored and reconciled in a management
cluster.</p>
<p>Managing Cluster API resources has historically required raw <code>kubectl</code> commands and
deep familiarity with ownership hierarchies. The Headlamp Cluster API plugin brings
visual clarity, faster debugging, and simplified operations for platform teams,
directly inside Headlamp.</p>
<h2 id="what-this-plugin-provides">What this plugin provides<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-this-plugin-provides" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The Cluster API plugin adds a dedicated Cluster API section to Headlamp and brings
full visibility into core CAPI resources through consistent list and detail views.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Feature</th>
<th>Description</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Cluster overview</strong></td>
<td>View clusters with live control plane and worker replica status.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Machine visibility</strong></td>
<td>Inspect MachineDeployments, MachineSets, Machines, and MachinePools with status and conditions.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Cluster API dashboard</strong></td>
<td>Get a centralized view of Cluster API resource health, active condition issues, provider information, and remediation guidance.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Control plane monitoring</strong></td>
<td>Track KubeadmControlPlane replicas, versions, and associated Machines.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Scale from the UI</strong></td>
<td>Scale MachineDeployments and MachineSets directly from Headlamp.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Owned resource hierarchy</strong></td>
<td>Trace relationships between clusters, deployments, sets, and machines.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>KubeadmConfig inspection</strong></td>
<td>View bootstrap configs, files, kubelet args, and join/init settings.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Topology awareness</strong></td>
<td>Automatically detect and label ClusterClass-managed resources.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Map view</strong></td>
<td>Visualize Cluster, Control Plane, and Worker relationships.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Dynamic API versioning</strong></td>
<td>Supports both v1beta1 and v1beta2 Cluster API versions.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Prometheus metrics</strong></td>
<td>View live metrics from the <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/tree/main/prometheus">Headlamp Prometheus plugin</a> inline on Cluster API resource detail pages.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h2 id="a-tour-of-the-plugin">A tour of the plugin<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#a-tour-of-the-plugin" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The Headlamp Cluster API plugin brings core Cluster API resources into a consistent,
visual interface inside Headlamp. Here are some of the key views included in the
first release.</p>
<h3 id="cluster-api-dashboard">Cluster API dashboard<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#cluster-api-dashboard" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The dashboard provides a centralized view of Cluster API resources and their
health across a management cluster.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/cluster-api-dashboard.png" alt="Cluster API dashboard showing overall resource health"></p>
<p>The overview summarizes the status of clusters, Machines, MachineDeployments,
MachinePools, MachineSets, and control planes. It also highlights active
condition issues, provider information, and configuration template counts to
help operators quickly identify degraded or unhealthy resources.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/cluster-health-cards.png" alt="Cluster details and remediation guidance"></p>
<p>Selecting a cluster opens a detailed health view showing control plane and
worker status, machine information, infrastructure details, and resource
conditions. When issues are detected, the dashboard provides remediation
guidance and diagnostic commands to assist with troubleshooting.</p>
<h3 id="bring-full-cluster-api-visibility-into-headlamp">Bring full Cluster API visibility into Headlamp<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#bring-full-cluster-api-visibility-into-headlamp" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The cluster list view shows all Cluster resources in the management cluster,
including control plane and worker replica status. This gives you an at-a-glance
understanding of overall cluster health.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/cluster-list-view.png" alt="Cluster list view showing control plane and worker replica status"></p>
<p>The cluster detail view provides resource status, conditions, infrastructure
references, control plane references, and related Machines on a single page.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/cluster-detail-overview.png" alt="Cluster detail view showing resource status and conditions"></p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/cluster-detail-machines.png" alt="Cluster detail view showing related machines"></p>
<h3 id="explore-cluster-api-resources-in-a-visual-interface">Explore Cluster API resources in a visual interface<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#explore-cluster-api-resources-in-a-visual-interface" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Dedicated views are available for MachineDeployments, MachineSets, Machines, and
MachinePools. These pages surface replica counts, ownership relationships, provider
IDs, versions, and conditions to support day-to-day operations and debugging.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/machine-resources-view.png" alt="MachineDeployment list view showing replica counts, ownership, and conditions"></p>
<h3 id="scale-workloads-directly-from-headlamp">Scale workloads directly from Headlamp<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#scale-workloads-directly-from-headlamp" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>MachineDeployments and MachineSets include a built-in Scale action, allowing you to
adjust replica counts directly from Headlamp without using terminal commands.</p>
<p>For topology-managed clusters, the plugin also indicates when scaling should be
performed at the Cluster level.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/scale-machine-deployments.png" alt="Scale dialog for a MachineDeployment"></p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/scale-machine-sets.png" alt="Topology-managed cluster showing scaling guidance at the Cluster level"></p>
<h3 id="inspect-bootstrap-configuration-without-raw-yaml">Inspect bootstrap configuration without raw YAML<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#inspect-bootstrap-configuration-without-raw-yaml" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>Bootstrap configurations can be viewed in a structured format, including inline
files, kubelet arguments, extra volumes, and join or init settings. This removes
the need to inspect raw YAML or secrets manually.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/bootstrap-config-view.png" alt="KubeadmConfig detail view showing bootstrap configuration in structured format"></p>
<h3 id="visualize-cluster-relationships-with-map-view">Visualize cluster relationships with map view<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#visualize-cluster-relationships-with-map-view" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>A visual map view displays the relationships between Cluster, control plane, and
worker resources. It offers a faster way to understand ownership hierarchies and
overall cluster structure.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/topology-map-view.png" alt="Map view showing Cluster, Control Plane, and Worker resource relationships"></p>
<h3 id="prometheus-metrics-integration">Prometheus metrics integration<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#prometheus-metrics-integration" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h3><p>The Cluster API plugin integrates with the
<a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/tree/main/prometheus">Headlamp Prometheus plugin</a>
to surface metrics directly inside Cluster API resource detail pages.</p>
<p>When the Prometheus plugin is installed and configured, metrics are embedded inline
on the detail pages for Clusters, MachineDeployments, MachineSets, and Machines.
You can view resource health and performance data alongside status conditions and
ownership relationships, without switching to a separate dashboard.</p>
<p>This makes it easier to correlate infrastructure state with live metrics during
debugging or day-to-day cluster operations, all from within Headlamp.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-cluster-api-plugin/prometheus-metrics-view.png" alt="Prometheus metrics embedded inline on a Cluster detail page"></p>
<h2 id="how-to-use">How to use<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-use" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>See the
<a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/blob/main/cluster-api/README.md"><code>plugins/cluster-api/README.md</code></a>
for installation and usage instructions.</p>
<h2 id="developed-during-lfx-mentorship">Developed during LFX Mentorship<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#developed-during-lfx-mentorship" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This plugin was developed as part of the CNCF LFX Mentorship program under the
Headlamp project. The mentorship provided an opportunity to work closely with the
Headlamp community while building features to improve the Cluster API management
experience.</p>
<p>The focus was not only on implementing features but also on understanding real-world
usability challenges around Cluster API operations. Discussions with mentors and
community members helped shape the plugin's direction, improve the user experience,
and prioritize features most useful to platform teams.</p>
<p>The mentorship also provided valuable experience contributing to large open-source
projects: collaborating with maintainers, participating in design discussions,
handling release feedback, and iterating on features based on community input.</p>
<p>Work on the plugin is ongoing, with additional improvements and features planned
beyond the initial Alpha release.</p>
<h2 id="feedback-and-questions">Feedback and questions<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#feedback-and-questions" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This is an Alpha release, and community feedback directly shapes what comes next.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Bug reports:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/headlamp/issues">Open an issue</a></li>
<li><strong>Feature requests:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/headlamp/discussions">Start a discussion</a></li>
<li><strong>Contributing:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/headlamp/pulls">PRs are welcome</a></li>
<li><strong>Kubernetes Slack:</strong> <a href="https://slack.k8s.io/">Join the #headlamp channel</a> for questions and discussion</li>
</ul></description></item><item><title>Inspect Volcano workloads faster with Headlamp</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/</link><pubDate>Thu, 25 Jun 2026 12:00:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/</guid><description>
<p><a href="https://volcano.sh/">Volcano</a> is a cloud native batch scheduler for Kubernetes, built for high-performance computing, AI/ML, and other batch workloads.</p>
<p><a href="https://headlamp.dev/">Headlamp</a> is an extensible Kubernetes web UI. With its plugin system, Headlamp can surface APIs and workflows beyond the built-in Kubernetes resources. The Volcano plugin brings core Volcano resources into Headlamp so you can inspect workload state, queue behavior, and gang scheduling details in one place.</p>
<p>Kubernetes was originally designed around long-running services, where applications are expected to start and remain available over time. Batch, AI/ML, and HPC workloads often behave differently: jobs arrive dynamically, compete for limited resources, and may need multiple workers to start together before useful work can begin.</p>
<p>Volcano extends Kubernetes with concepts such as queues, priorities, quotas, and gang scheduling. Instead of treating every Pod independently, Volcano schedules workloads with awareness of the job as a whole and the resources it needs to make progress.</p>
<p>To make these workloads easier to operate and troubleshoot, the Volcano plugin brings that scheduling context directly into Headlamp.</p>
<p>Watch this short walkthrough to see the Volcano plugin in Headlamp:</p>
<div style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;">
<iframe allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen" loading="eager" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Mqm1EyAa7TY?autoplay=0&amp;controls=1&amp;end=0&amp;loop=0&amp;mute=0&amp;start=0" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Volcano plugin for Headlamp walkthrough"></iframe>
</div>
<h2 id="visual-context-helps-teams-understand-volcano-jobs-queues-and-podgroups-faster">Visual context helps teams understand Volcano jobs, queues, and PodGroups faster<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#visual-context-helps-teams-understand-volcano-jobs-queues-and-podgroups-faster" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Working with Volcano often means moving across several related resources while trying to understand a batch workload. You might start with a Job, then look at the related PodGroup, inspect the Pods behind it, check the Queue, and finally return to the Job again. All of that is possible with CLI tools like <code>kubectl</code> and the Volcano CLI, but it can become fragmented very quickly.</p>
<p>The Volcano plugin for Headlamp makes that workflow easier by bringing the key resources together in a single UI. Instead of reconstructing relationships manually, you can move directly between Jobs, Queues, PodGroups, Pods, and events from the same interface.</p>
<p>Volcano introduces its own resources on top of core Kubernetes objects:</p>
<dl>
<dt>Job</dt>
<dd>Describes a batch workload as a set of tasks and the Pods they create.</dd>
<dt>Queue</dt>
<dd>Divides cluster capacity between teams or workloads using quotas and priorities.</dd>
<dt>PodGroup</dt>
<dd>Ties a group of Pods together so the scheduler can treat them as a single unit for gang scheduling.</dd>
</dl>
<p>The plugin surfaces all three resource types directly in Headlamp, providing dedicated list and detail views for each of them under a Volcano section in the sidebar.</p>
<h2 id="jobs-workload-status-actions-and-logs">Jobs: workload status, actions, and logs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#jobs-workload-status-actions-and-logs" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The Job view is the center of the plugin experience. In the list view, you can quickly understand the basics of a workload, including its status, queue, running versus minimum-available values, task count, and age.</p>
<figure>
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/volcano-jobs-list.png"
alt="Volcano Jobs list in Headlamp"/>
</figure>
<p>The detail view goes further by surfacing the information you usually need while debugging a Job: task details, Pod status, related Queue and PodGroup links, conditions, events, and more. Instead of forcing you to jump between several CLI commands, the plugin keeps that context together in a single page.</p>
<p>The Job page also adds supported lifecycle actions for appropriate states, including <strong>Suspend</strong> and <strong>Resume</strong>, so you can act on a Job directly from the UI.</p>
<p>Another useful addition is direct <strong>Job logs</strong> access. You can open logs for Pods created by a Volcano Job without leaving the Job detail page. The logs viewer supports both single-Pod and all-Pods views, along with container selection and common log controls such as line count, previous logs, timestamps, and follow.</p>
<figure>
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/volcano-job-logs.png"
alt="Volcano Job logs in Headlamp"/>
</figure>
<h2 id="queues-scheduling-capacity-and-resource-context">Queues: scheduling capacity and resource context<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#queues-scheduling-capacity-and-resource-context" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The Queue view provides much more than a small set of top-level fields. It helps you understand how resources are being allocated and constrained by surfacing capacity, allocated resources, deserved and guaranteed resources, reservation details, child queues, and more.</p>
<p>This makes the Queue page much more useful when trying to understand how resources are being shared and limited across queues.</p>
<figure>
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/volcano-queue-detail.png"
alt="Volcano Queue details in Headlamp"/>
</figure>
<h2 id="podgroups-gang-scheduling-state-and-blockers">PodGroups: gang scheduling state and blockers<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#podgroups-gang-scheduling-state-and-blockers" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>PodGroups are central to understanding gang scheduling in Volcano, and the plugin makes that state easier to inspect. The PodGroup view highlights progress, conditions, minimum resource requirements, and more.</p>
<p>This also gives you a clearer picture of whether a workload is blocked because it has not yet met the scheduling conditions required to run as a group.</p>
<figure>
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/volcano-podgroup-detail.png"
alt="Volcano PodGroup details in Headlamp"/>
</figure>
<h2 id="map-view-jobs-queues-podgroups-and-pods-in-one-place">Map view: jobs, queues, PodGroups, and pods in one place<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#map-view-jobs-queues-podgroups-and-pods-in-one-place" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The map view shows how Volcano resources are connected. Instead of inspecting each resource separately, you can see how Jobs, PodGroups, Queues, and Pods relate to one another.</p>
<p>This is especially useful when a workload is pending or not progressing as expected. The map can show the Job, its related PodGroup, the Pods created for the workload, and the Queue context around it. Warning and error states also make it easier to spot resources that need attention.</p>
<figure>
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/volcano-map-view.png"
alt="Volcano resources in the Headlamp map view"/>
</figure>
<h2 id="why-use-this-alongside-cli-tools">Why use this alongside CLI tools<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#why-use-this-alongside-cli-tools" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The plugin is not trying to replace <code>kubectl</code> or the Volcano CLI. Those remain important for automation, scripting, and raw object inspection. What the plugin improves is the interactive troubleshooting experience: discovering related resources more quickly, understanding structured detail pages, and moving from scheduling state to runtime output without switching tools constantly.</p>
<h2 id="what-s-next">What’s next<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#what-s-next" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>This work brings the main Volcano workflow into Headlamp, including Jobs, Queues, PodGroups, and the map view. Possible future work includes Prometheus integration, richer scheduling insights, and more workflow-oriented visibility across Volcano workloads.</p>
<h2 id="try-it-and-share-feedback">Try it and share feedback<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#try-it-and-share-feedback" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>To try the plugin:</p>
<ol>
<li>Install Headlamp.</li>
<li>Open the Plugin Catalog from the Headlamp UI.</li>
<li>Search for Volcano.</li>
<li>Install the Volcano plugin.</li>
<li>Connect Headlamp to a Kubernetes cluster where Volcano is already installed.</li>
</ol>
<figure>
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/visual-context-volcano-headlamp-plugin/volcano-plugin-catalog.png"
alt="Volcano plugin in the Headlamp Plugin Catalog"/>
</figure>
<p>If you have ideas, feature requests, or bug reports, open an issue in the <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins">Headlamp plugins repository</a>. Feedback from real Volcano users will help shape what comes next.</p></description></item><item><title>See your serverless: introducing the Headlamp plugin for Knative</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/</link><pubDate>Thu, 25 Jun 2026 10:00:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/</guid><description>
<p><a href="https://headlamp.dev/">Headlamp</a> is an open-source, extensible Kubernetes SIG UI project designed to let you explore, manage, and debug cluster resources.</p>
<p><a href="https://knative.dev/">Knative</a> brings serverless workloads to Kubernetes, handling traffic routing, autoscaling, and revision management so teams can deploy and iterate without fighting infrastructure. But operating Knative workloads day-to-day can be difficult, there's still a lot of jumping between the <code>kn</code> CLI, <code>kubectl</code>, and the Kubernetes UI to get a full picture of what's running.</p>
<p>We built the <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/tree/main/knative">Headlamp Knative plugin</a> to bridge that very gap, allowing operators to inspect, understand and act on their workloads all from a single place. This plugin was built as part of the LFX mentorship. Here's a tour of what we shipped.</p>
<p>Here is a short walkthrough of the Knative plugin for Headlamp:</p>
<div style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;">
<iframe allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen" loading="eager" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9HAcUsopSYE?autoplay=0&amp;controls=1&amp;end=0&amp;loop=0&amp;mute=0&amp;start=0" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Headlamp Knative plugin walkthrough"></iframe>
</div>
<h2 id="integrating-knative-resources-with-headlamp-s-map-view">Integrating Knative resources with Headlamp's map view<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#integrating-knative-resources-with-headlamp-s-map-view" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Headlamp's resource mapping works for Knative CRDs too. You can see how KServices, Revisions, and DomainMappings relate to each other in a single graph view.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-map-view.png" alt="Knative resources in Headlamp Map View"></p>
<h2 id="kservice-management-edit-traffic-splits-restart-pods-and-view-logs">KService management: edit traffic splits, restart pods, and view logs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#kservice-management-edit-traffic-splits-restart-pods-and-view-logs" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>A KService is the top-level resource in Knative: it manages the lifecycle of Routes, Configurations, Revisions, and everything needed to run and expose your application.</p>
<p>The plugin gives KServices a full detail view with an <strong>Edit Mode</strong> toggle for making live changes to traffic splits, autoscaling annotations, and more. Common actions like viewing the YAML, opening logs, triggering a redeploy, or restarting backing pods are surfaced in the header, gated by your current RBAC permissions.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-kservice-view.png" alt="Knative Service Detail View"></p>
<h2 id="traffic-splitting-route-across-revisions-for-gradual-rollouts-and-testing">Traffic splitting: route across revisions for gradual rollouts and testing<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#traffic-splitting-route-across-revisions-for-gradual-rollouts-and-testing" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Knative makes it possible to route traffic across multiple Revisions of the same service. This is useful for canary releases, gradual rollouts, tagged preview URLs, and A/B testing.</p>
<p>The plugin shows the traffic assigned to each Revision, the latest ready Revision, readiness status, age, and configured tags. In edit mode, you can adjust percentages and tags inline. The plugin validates that traffic sums to 100% and that tags are unique before saving. Tagged routes with a reported URL render as clickable links.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-traffic-view.png" alt="Traffic Splitting between Revisions"></p>
<h2 id="autoscaling-configuration-view-effective-settings-and-cluster-defaults">Autoscaling configuration: view effective settings and cluster defaults<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#autoscaling-configuration-view-effective-settings-and-cluster-defaults" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Knative's autoscaler supports a range of settings: concurrency targets, target utilization, RPS targets, min/max scale, initial scale, stable window, scale-down delay, and more. The effective value for any workload is a combination of KService-level annotations and cluster-wide ConfigMaps.</p>
<p>The plugin reads <code>config-autoscaler</code> and <code>config-defaults</code> and shows the effective configuration per KService in context, so you can see at a glance whether a setting is explicitly configured or falling back to the cluster default.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-autoscaling-view.png" alt="Autoscaling and Concurrency View"></p>
<h2 id="prometheus-metrics-monitor-request-rates-latency-and-resource-utilization">Prometheus metrics: monitor request rates, latency, and resource utilization<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#prometheus-metrics-monitor-request-rates-latency-and-resource-utilization" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>When paired with the <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/tree/main/plugins/prometheus">Prometheus plugin for Headlamp</a>, the plugin renders request rate, latency, and resource utilization graphs on KService and Revision detail pages. The per-revision request rate breakdown is particularly useful when validating a traffic split in progress.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-revision-metrics-graph.png" alt="Knative metrics filtered by revision"></p>
<h2 id="dashboard-for-other-crds">Dashboard for other CRDs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#dashboard-for-other-crds" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The plugin also includes list and detail views for Revisions, DomainMappings, ClusterDomainClaims, and a cluster-level Networking overview (reading <code>config-network</code> and <code>config-gateway</code> to surface the effective ingress class, gateway settings, and backing services). These give operators a complete picture of Knative's state without leaving Headlamp.</p>
<p><img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-revisions-view.png" alt="Knative Revision List View">
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-domain-mapping-view.png" alt="Knative Domain Mapping List View">
<img src="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/25/headlamp-knative-plugin/knative-cluster-domain-claim-view.png" alt="Knative Cluster Domain Claim List View"></p>
<h2 id="how-to-install-the-knative-plugin-in-headlamp">How to install the Knative plugin in Headlamp<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#how-to-install-the-knative-plugin-in-headlamp" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><ol>
<li>Make sure <a href="https://knative.dev/docs/install/">Knative is installed</a> in your cluster.</li>
<li>In Headlamp Desktop, open the <strong>Plugin Catalog</strong>, search for Knative, and click Install.</li>
<li>Reload Headlamp, a new Knative entry will appear in the sidebar.</li>
</ol>
<p>For development or source-level setup, see the <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/tree/main/plugins/knative">Knative plugin README</a>. The current release is <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/releases/tag/knative-0.3.0-beta"><strong>0.3.0-beta</strong></a>.</p>
<h2 id="share-your-feedback">Share your feedback<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#share-your-feedback" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>We'd love feedback from Knative operators and users. If you hit a bug or want support for a workflow we haven't covered, <a href="https://github.com/headlamp-k8s/plugins/issues">please open an issue</a>. You can also find us in the <a href="https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/headlamp">Kubernetes Slack #headlamp channel</a>.</p></description></item><item><title>Spotlight on WG Device Management</title><link>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/24/wg-device-management-spotlight-2026/</link><pubDate>Wed, 24 Jun 2026 10:00:00 -0800</pubDate><guid>https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/24/wg-device-management-spotlight-2026/</guid><description>
<p>The rising popularity of AI, Edge, and Telecommunications workloads on Kubernetes has led to new requirements for hardware management. We now need hardware specification beyond CPU time and memory allocations. This includes allocating GPUs, TPUs, network interfaces, and other hardware, sometimes after pod start and occasionally through time-sharing.</p>
<p>Efficiently managing this specialized hardware is the mission of the <strong><a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/wg/device-management/">Device Management Working Group</a></strong>. Their cornerstone project, <strong><a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/resource-management/dynamic-resource-allocation/">Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)</a></strong>, recently graduated to GA, marking a fundamental shift in how the project handles hardware-intensive workloads at scale.</p>
<p>In this spotlight, we sit down with working group chairs <strong><a href="https://github.com/klueska">Kevin Klues</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://github.com/pohly">Patrick Ohly</a></strong>, and
<strong><a href="https://github.com/johnbelamaric">John Belamaric</a></strong> to discuss the limitations of the legacy device model,
the <em>NP-hard</em> challenges of scheduling, and how they’re building a more programmable, hardware-aware future for Kubernetes.</p>
<h2 id="introducing-device-management">Introducing Device Management<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#introducing-device-management" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p><strong>Natalie Fisher: Can you introduce yourself, your role, and how you got involved in the Device Management Working Group?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Kevin Klues:</strong> My name is Kevin Klues. I am a Distinguished Engineer at NVIDIA. I have been a co-chair of the device management working group since its inception at Kubecon EU 2024. I have also been involved with DRA (the working group's primary deliverable) since its inception in 2019 / 2020.
I have also been a kubelet maintainer since 2019, with a focus on its device manager, CPU manager, and topology manager subcomponents. The challenges we saw with using these components for workloads that relied on external accelerators (e.g., GPUs) are what triggered us to start working on DRA in the first place.</p>
<p><strong>Patrick Ohly:</strong> I am a Principal Engineer at Intel. In Kubernetes, I am a Tech Lead for <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/testing/">SIG Testing</a> and <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/instrumentation/">SIG Instrumentation</a> and co-chair of the Device Management WG. I was co-chair of the WG Structured Logging and a member of the Steering Committee. Some of my early contributions to Kubernetes include <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/ephemeral-volumes/">ephemeral CSI volumes</a> and storage capacity tracking, so I had some experience with API design, implementation, and scheduling. We knew that introducing a major new API for accelerators would be hard. Somewhat foolishly, I accepted that challenge in 2020, wrote the initial DRA KEP (now known as “classic DRA”) and implemented most of it, then started over with a second KEP for today’s &quot;structured parameters DRA&quot;. Initially, it was an uphill battle to convince maintainers that this work was necessary. It was only around 2023 that interest in DRA picked up, leading to the formation of the working group.</p>
<p><strong>John Belamaric:</strong> I am a Senior Staff SWE at Google, and the third co-chair of WG Device Management, also since its inception. I am also a co-chair of <a href="https://www.kubernetes.dev/community/community-groups/sigs/architecture/">SIG Architecture</a> since 2019. As Patrick mentioned, in late 2023, interest in DRA really picked up. The initial implementation, made autoscaling very challenging, and so there was some concern in the community about advancing it to beta. I got involved to try to help address some of those concerns, and the three of us, along with Tim Hockin, worked hard over the next few months to build a consensus around a new design. To facilitate this collaboration, we formed the working group after discussion at KubeCon in Paris in 2024.</p>
<h2 id="the-problem-and-the-solution">The problem and the solution<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#the-problem-and-the-solution" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>The working group emerged from a fundamental rethink of how Kubernetes interacts with specialized hardware. At the heart of this evolution is <strong>Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)</strong>. Rather than treating devices as simple integers, DRA provides a structured framework that breaks device management into four distinct stages:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Modeling:</strong> Vendors use the <strong>ResourceSlice API</strong> to advertise the granular capabilities and capacity of their hardware.</li>
<li><strong>Requesting:</strong> Users define their specific hardware needs—such as GPU memory or interconnect requirements—through the <strong><code>ResourceClaim</code> API</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Scheduling:</strong> The Kubernetes scheduler uses these APIs to match workload requirements against available hardware intelligently.</li>
<li><strong>Actuation:</strong> Once a match is made, the system handles the &quot;handshake&quot; that prepares and secures the device for the Pod's use.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>NF: For readers who may not be familiar, what is the Device Management Working Group, and what problems is it trying to solve?</strong></p>
<p><strong>KK:</strong> The Device Management Working Group was chartered to enable simple and efficient configuration, sharing, and allocation of accelerators and other specialized hardware across Kubernetes workloads. Think GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs, and similar devices that don't fit neatly into Kubernetes' traditional resource model.</p>
<p>The problem we set out to solve is that the legacy Device Plugin API (which has been the primary mechanism for exposing hardware accelerators in Kubernetes) is fundamentally limited. It treats devices as opaque integers: you can request &quot;2 GPUs,&quot; but you can't say anything meaningful about which GPUs you need, how they should be connected to each other, whether they can be shared, or how they should be partitioned. That was fine for simple cases, but modern AI/ML workloads are anything but simple. They span multiple nodes, require specific interconnect topologies, and increasingly need to share or partition hardware dynamically.</p>
<p>The working group's primary deliverable is Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), a new framework that replaces the rigid device plugin model with a flexible, declarative API.
With DRA, workloads can describe their hardware requirements (e.g., GPU type, memory capacity, interconnect topology, desired partitioning) and drivers can publish fine-grained device attributes that the scheduler can act on.
DRA <a href="https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/01/kubernetes-v1-34-dra-updates/">graduated</a> to GA in Kubernetes 1.34, and the ecosystem around it (e.g., drivers, tooling, and new API extensions) is growing rapidly.</p>
<p><strong>PO:</strong> As Kevin said, the working group was formed around the existing effort to develop DRA. The initial work was done with only a handful of people actively involved, and perhaps also could only be done successfully in such a setup. But because it touches on so many different areas of Kubernetes, we also needed a place to discuss that and get the broader community of Kubernetes maintainers, device vendors, and, to a lesser extent, also end-users involved. The working group provides that place, with regular meetings online (one slot for Americas/EMEA, one for EMEA/Asia) and at KubeCon.</p>
<p><strong>JB:</strong> DRA is the first problem the WG has addressed. It is focused on selection, allocation, and configuration of the devices. We broke the problem down into four parts: how does the vendor model the device and advertise capacity, how does the user request it, how do we schedule that request on top of the advertised capacity, and how do we actuate that result (that is, how do we make the device ready and available to the Pod).</p>
<p>One thing that is fundamental to the approach we took is an awareness of the incredible diversity of hardware and the rapid rate of change in the hardware industry. We knew that we couldn’t keep up with the change if the Kubernetes APIs had to change for every type of hardware. Instead, we created a general approach where we address the hardware aspects that are important to Kubernetes. What we have done so far is focus on the scheduling and configuration aspects of devices. We build a device modeling API (the ResourceSlice API) that vendors use to model the scheduling characteristics of their devices, and allow users to pass through arbitrary configurations to those devices. By doing this, Kubernetes can be “programmed” to understand these aspects of the devices, without needing to be modified.</p>
<p>But DRA, as it stands right now, is very focused on scheduling. There are other aspects of Device Management that are in scope for the WG. In particular, we are looking into device failure detection and mitigation, and whether there is some better support we can build into Kubernetes to help.</p>
<p>Also, as Kevin alluded to, devices are often allocated and used in groups, rather than individually. Choosing the right devices to work together in a group depends on how they are interconnected; for example, NVIDIA GPUs may be in an any-to-any fabric arrangement in an NVLINK domain, whereas TPUs may have a 3D torus interconnect. This affects the “selection, allocation and configuration” of devices, and we have a lot more work to do to address these use cases.</p>
<h2 id="a-cross-sig-effort">A cross-SIG effort<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#a-cross-sig-effort" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Because device management touches scheduling, node operations, autoscaling, networking, and API design, the work naturally spans multiple SIGs across the Kubernetes project.</p>
<p><strong>NF: How does collaboration across these SIGs work in practice, and why is it necessary?</strong></p>
<p><strong>KK:</strong> Device management touches nearly every layer of the Kubernetes stack, which is why the working group was chartered as a cross-SIG effort from the start. We have five stakeholder SIGs: sig-node, sig-scheduling, sig-autoscaling, sig-network, and sig-architecture.</p>
<p>In practice, the working group serves as a coordination layer. We don't own code directly; instead, our deliverables take the form of KEPs and implementations that live in the respective SIGs. What we provide is a unified forum where the people building the scheduler, the kubelet, the autoscaler, and the network plane can design together rather than in isolation.</p>
<p>Why is this necessary? Consider a simple example: a user requests a set of GPUs that need to communicate via NVLink. That requirement involves the scheduler (place the pods on the right nodes), the kubelet (configure the devices and expose them to the container), and potentially autoscaling (provision the right node type if none exists).</p>
<p>If those three groups design independently, you end up with inconsistent abstractions, duplicated logic, and integration bugs that only surface in production. The working group ensures that a single coherent API and data model flows through all of these components.</p>
<p>The cross-SIG model also means that design decisions are reviewed from multiple angles. Someone from sig-scheduling will catch scheduler complexity that a sig-node contributor might overlook, and vice versa. It slows down individual decisions slightly, but produces much more robust outcomes.</p>
<h2 id="current-focus-areas">Current focus areas<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#current-focus-areas" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>With DRA now generally available, the working group’s focus has expanded to enable more advanced scheduling models, shared semantics, operational visibility, and support for increasingly complex hardware topologies.</p>
<p><strong>NF: What are some of the key initiatives or deliverables the working group is currently focused on?</strong></p>
<p><strong>KK:</strong> We maintain a project board at <a href="https://github.com/orgs/kubernetes/projects/95">Kubernetes Project Board</a> with real-time tracking of our initiatives and their progress.</p>
<p><strong>PO:</strong> The scope and feature set of core DRA were intentionally limited to enable graduation to GA within a reasonable time. Additional KEPs add more features, on their own schedule. Those fall roughly into three categories:</p>
<ol>
<li>Extend the expressiveness of DRA to support more complex devices and scheduling scenarios.</li>
<li>Support <em>day two</em> operations like health monitoring.</li>
<li>Improve multi-node support, primarily by integrating with workload-aware scheduling.</li>
</ol>

<p><strong>NF: One of the core challenges is efficient device utilization and sharing. What progress is being made in this area?</strong></p>
<p><strong>JB:</strong> Good question. One way to think about it is what we are doing in the two primary APIs: ResourceClaim and ResourceSlice.</p>
<p>The ResourceClaim API is how the user asks for devices. We have built some features that allow the user to be more flexible in their requests. For example, instead of asking for a specific model of GPU, they can ask for a GPU with at least a certain amount of memory. Or they can ask for a list of alternatives: &quot;I’d like one A100 (80GB) GPU, but if you don’t have it, I’ll take 2 A100 (40 GB) GPUs.&quot; This gives the scheduler some options to satisfy the request, which can lead to better obtainability and utilization of hardware that otherwise would not be selected.</p>
<p>The ResourceClaim API allows users to explicitly share devices. You can point multiple containers (in the same or different Pods) at a ResourceClaim; this allows the devices allocated by that claim to be used in all of those containers, <em>if the device supports it</em>.</p>
<p>The ResourceSlice API is how vendors model and advertise their devices. This is where we implement support for other sharing models. For example, we have a way to represent &quot;overlapping partitions&quot;, enabling the scheduler to dynamically select a MIG partition, and make any overlapping MIG partitions unavailable automatically. This works well in combination with a request like “give me any GPU with 20GB or more of memory” - the scheduler can satisfy that with a MIG or a real GPU.</p>
<p>Some features require changes in both. We have another sharing method we call “consumable capacity”. In the explicit sharing case described above, a user needs to point containers at the same ResourceClaim; there is one ResourceClaim shared amongst several containers and Pods. With consumable capacity, the device sharing works more like how Pods share a Node. The user creates a ResourceClaim that asks for a certain amount of resources, for example, “I need a NIC with 2Gbps of bandwidth”. The scheduler knows that there is a NIC with 40Gbps of bandwidth available, and so it allocates 2Gbps out of that 40Gbps and gives it to that ResourceClaim. In this case, each Pod has its own ResourceClaim, but the underlying device is shared between those claims. It’s up to the on-node DRA driver to properly set up the device for this sort of sharing (in the NIC case, likely by creating a subinterface). We call this “platform-mediated sharing” to differentiate it from the explicit &quot;user-mediated sharing&quot;.</p>
<h2 id="real-world-impact">Real-world impact<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#real-world-impact" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>While much of the work is deeply technical, the underlying goal is practical: enabling Kubernetes to better support real-world AI/ML and hardware-intensive workloads at scale.</p>
<p><strong>NF: What are the biggest challenges users face today when running hardware-intensive workloads (like AI/ML) on Kubernetes?</strong></p>
<p><strong>PO:</strong> Such workloads depart from traditional container workloads in several ways: they may consist of multiple communicating pods which all need to run at the same time (“gang scheduling”). They are often long-running and expensive to initialize, and their performance is sensitive to where they run (topology within a node and interconnects between nodes for multiple pods). The Kubernetes scheduler traditionally has not supported either of this well because it schedules one pod at a time and is unaware of the topology within a node. Several external schedulers try to fill this gap, which often isn’t ideal, in particular when the Kubernetes scheduler schedules other pods to the same cluster.</p>
<p><strong>NF: How should platform engineers think about device management when designing their Kubernetes platforms?</strong></p>
<p><strong>JB:</strong> We’re still learning here, but one idea of DRA is to enable a shift to more &quot;requirements driven&quot; specifications. This can allow less coupling between end users that write the workload specification and the cluster administrators that set up the clusters. Instead of agreeing on labeling conventions and requiring users to understand the cluster topology, the users can specify what their workload needs, and the scheduler can figure out how to satisfy it. If we can make this work, it can make even complex workloads more portable across clusters.</p>
<h2 id="challenges-and-trade-offs">Challenges and trade-offs<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#challenges-and-trade-offs" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>As with many areas of Kubernetes, increasing flexibility and expressiveness also introduces new layers of complexity, particularly around scheduling and optimization.</p>
<p><strong>NF: What are some of the hardest technical challenges the working group is tackling today?</strong></p>
<p><strong>PO:</strong> There’s an inherent conflict between flexibility and scheduling complexity. The current implementation is focused on finding some solution that satisfies the requested resources, but it’s not necessarily the best one, whatever “best” means, which is also not always clear. The other big challenge is exposing node-allocatable resources (RAM, CPU) as devices with additional metadata; this is necessary to fine-tune scheduling of workloads which need perfect alignment on a node for optimal performance.</p>
<p><strong>JB:</strong> Patrick’s list is good. Complex device modeling is hard, and making sure that we build the right semantics such that they apply to lots of different hardware is always tricky.</p>
<p>On top of that, scheduling in general is very complex and is an NP-hard problem. All the metadata and flexibility DRA adds gives the scheduler more options, which has pros and cons. More options are helpful if you are constrained in your choices, as it means you can schedule something that you otherwise could not. But it also means it is even harder to find an optimal solution when there are many possibilities in a given cluster. DRA works well in our common use cases so far, but we have a lot of work to do to improve the optimality of the chosen scheduling solution and ensure the performance of making that choice.</p>
<h2 id="looking-ahead">Looking ahead<a class="td-heading-self-link" href="#looking-ahead" aria-label="Heading self-link"></a></h2><p>Despite the challenges, contributors across the working group remain excited about the pace of innovation and the growing community forming around device management in Kubernetes.</p>
<p><strong>NF: Looking ahead, what are you most excited about in the future of device management in Kubernetes?</strong></p>
<p><strong>KK:</strong> NVIDIA recently donated its DRA driver for GPUs to the Kubernetes project. I’m personally excited for more community members to start contributing to the project and defining its future direction.</p>
<p><strong>PO:</strong> For me, it’s primarily the number of new contributors and people stepping up to help out. This poses new challenges around reviewing proposals and helping developers get those implemented and merged. It’s nice and rewarding to see others succeed, and it bodes well for the future because more people are familiar with the topic.</p>
<p><strong>JB:</strong> I am excited about a lot of things. The community really has grown and has so many interesting features in the works to enable modeling of more complex devices, and to better model multi-node devices.</p>
<p>I am really excited to see the creative ways people will use these APIs. They were primarily designed to address &quot;devices&quot;, but just like how &quot;everything is a file&quot; in Unix/Linux, the APIs themselves are quite flexible as to what they model. They really build out a more programmable scheduler, which can have interesting applications. For example, I recently prototyped using DRA to schedule pods to nodes where a large AI model is already locally cached.
